2027-04-04.title: Second Sunday of Easter (Sunday of Divine Mercy)
readings: The whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul
Give thanks to the Lord for he is good, his love is everlasting (or: Alleluia)
Whatever is born of God conquers the world
Christians, to the Paschal Victim offer your thankful praises
A week later Jesus came and stood among them
2027-04-04.alt: Second Sunday of Easter, the Octave Day of Easter, which St John Paul II named for the whole Church the Sunday of Divine Mercy (2000). Gloria and Creed. The Easter Sequence may be sung. The double Alleluia is added to the dismissal today for the last time until Pentecost. A plenary indulgence is granted on this day, under the usual conditions (sacramental confession, Holy Communion, prayer for the intentions of the Holy Father), with a spirit detached from all sin, to those who take part in prayers and devotions in honour of Divine Mercy in any church or chapel, or who pray the Our Father and the Creed before the Blessed Sacrament, adding a devout prayer to the merciful Lord Jesus such as “Merciful Jesus, I trust in you” (Apostolic Penitentiary, 2002). St Isidore (4 April) is not observed this year. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-04.verse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
theo: Eight days ago the Church sang, “This is the day that the LORD has made.” Today, on the eighth day, the Octave Day of Easter, she sings the same psalm again, and the refrain falls like a drumbeat of mercy: “Let Israel say, ‘His steadfast love endures forever.’ Let the house of Aaron say, ‘His steadfast love endures forever.’ Let those who fear the LORD say, ‘His steadfast love endures forever.’” The first reading shows what that mercy does when it takes hold of a community. “Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common.” Luke places at the centre of this picture the preaching of the Resurrection: “With great power the apostles gave their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.” And the fruit is very concrete: “There was not a needy person among them.” Easter faith is not only a conviction in the mind; it opens hands and purses. Mercy received becomes mercy shared.

St John's First Letter tells us where this new life comes from. “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the parent loves the child.” To love God is to love his children, and to keep his commandments, which “are not burdensome.” John then gives one of the great Easter sentences of the New Testament: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.” Not our cleverness, not our strength, but faith in the Son of God. Finally John speaks of Jesus as “the one who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ, not with the water only but with the water and the blood.” He is thinking of the Jordan, where Jesus was baptized, and of Calvary, where his side was pierced and “at once blood and water came out” (John 19:34). The Fathers saw in that water and blood the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist, flowing from the Heart of Christ to give birth to the Church. On this Sunday the newly baptized of Easter night come to the end of their first week in Christ, washed in that water and fed with that Blood.

The Gospel is read on this Sunday every year. It is the evening of Easter Day. The disciples are behind locked doors, “for fear of the Jews,” as John puts it; the disciples were Jews themselves, and John means the Temple authorities who had handed Jesus over, not the Jewish people as such. Into that locked room of fear the Risen Lord comes: “Peace be with you.” He shows them his hands and his side, so that they may know the one who stands before them is the one who was crucified. “Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.” And at once he sends them: “As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” He breathes on them, as God breathed the breath of life into Adam at the creation, and says: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.” On the very first Easter night the Risen Lord gives his Church the power to forgive sins in his name. The Council of Trent taught that in these words Christ instituted the sacrament of Penance. Every confessional is a little upper room where the wounded hands of Christ are raised in absolution and the same words are heard: peace be with you.

Thomas was not there. When the others say, “We have seen the Lord,” he answers with hard words: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands, and put my finger in the mark of the nails and my hand in his side, I will not believe.” A week later, on the next first day of the week, the disciples are together again and Thomas is with them. Jesus comes, says “Peace be with you,” and turns to Thomas with his own words: “Put your finger here and see my hands. Reach out your hand and put it in my side. Do not doubt but believe.” The Gospel never says that Thomas touched him. It says only that he cried out the greatest confession of faith in all the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” The doubter becomes the one who names Jesus God. Then the Lord speaks to us, who were not there: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.” In Kerala this Sunday is widely called Puthu Njayar, New Sunday, and many pilgrims climb the hill of Malayattoor, where tradition says St Thomas prayed. And this is why the Church calls it the Sunday of Divine Mercy. The wounds that Thomas was invited to touch are not closed; they have become the open door of mercy. St Faustina saw the Lord with two rays streaming from his Heart, pale and red, the water and the blood, and beneath him the prayer every sinner may make: Jesus, I trust in you. John tells us why he wrote: “so that you may come to believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that through believing you may have life in his name.”
conn: The Octave Day.
Easter is so great that the Church celebrates it as one day for eight days. Today the Octave ends and the fifty days of the Easter season continue until Pentecost (16 May 2027).
Divine Mercy Sunday.

At the canonization of St Faustina Kowalska on 30 April 2000, St John Paul II declared that the Second Sunday of Easter would be called Divine Mercy Sunday throughout the Church. The readings and prayers of the day remain those of the Second Sunday of Easter.
Of one heart and soul.
Acts gives three such summaries of the life of the first community (2:42–47; 4:32–35; 5:12–16). Sharing was voluntary and generous, not imposed: Acts 5:4 shows that property remained one's own.
Water and blood.

1 John 5:6 recalls Jesus' baptism in the Jordan and his death on the cross, when blood and water flowed from his side (John 19:34). The Fathers saw there the birth of the Church from the side of the new Adam, and the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist.
“For fear of the Jews.”

In John's Gospel “the Jews” often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus. Jesus, Mary, the Apostles and the first believers were all Jews; the phrase must never be read as blame on the Jewish people (CCC 597).
He breathed on them.
The same verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) and for the breath that raises the dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9). Easter evening is a new creation.
The power to forgive sins.
The Council of Trent (Session 14, canon 3) taught that by John 20:22–23 Christ instituted the sacrament of Penance, giving the Apostles and their successors the power to forgive and retain sins.
Thomas the Twin.

Didymus means “twin.” Earlier Thomas had said, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” (John 11:16), and asked, “Lord, we do not know where you are going” (John 14:5). The tradition of the St Thomas Christians holds that he preached the Gospel in India, arriving at Kodungallur and dying a martyr near Mylapore.
“A week later.”
Literally “after eight days.” From the beginning the disciples gathered on the first day of the week, and the Risen Lord met them there. Sunday is the weekly Easter.
altar: The hands and side that Thomas was invited to touch are present on our altar. In the Eucharist we receive the risen, glorified body of the Lord, still marked with the wounds of love. With Thomas we may say in silence at the elevation: My Lord and my God!

The Lord's first word on Easter evening was “Peace be with you,” and his first gift was the forgiveness of sins. Divine Mercy Sunday invites us to come to the altar through the confessional, washed in the mercy that flows from his side.
outline: Opening
Ask: what locked room are you sitting in today, and what are you afraid of?
Point 1 · Peace and the wounds
He shows them his hands and side.
Point 2 · Receive the Holy Spirit
The gift of forgiveness on Easter night.
Point 3 · My Lord and my God
Thomas, the doubter who confessed.
Point 4 · Of one heart and soul
Mercy received becomes mercy shared.
Closing image
An open door in a locked room, and two rays of light, pale and red.
Take-home line
“Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
live: Receive the mercy
If you have not yet made your Easter confession, go this week; if you have, pray for someone who has stayed away for many years.
Pray “Jesus, I trust in you”
Say this prayer at three o'clock each afternoon this week, the hour of mercy, or pray the Divine Mercy Chaplet with your family.
Say Thomas's prayer at Mass
At the elevation of the Host and the chalice, say silently: “My Lord and my God.”
Make sure no one is needy
Like the first Christians, share with one family in your parish or neighbourhood that is in real need this month.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (Homily 26 on the Gospels, in substance)

It was not by chance that Thomas was absent. The unbelief of Thomas has done more for our faith than the faith of the disciples who believed; for when he is brought back to faith by touching, our minds are freed from doubt and made firm.
St Augustine (Tractates on John 121, in substance)
He saw and touched the man, and he confessed the God whom he could neither see nor touch. What he saw and touched led him to believe what he could not see.
St John Chrysostom (On the Priesthood 3, in substance)

Priests have received a power that God has given neither to angels nor to archangels. Christ said: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven. What priests do here below, God confirms above; the Master ratifies the sentence of his servants.
St Cyril of Alexandria (On John, in substance)
As in the beginning man was formed from the earth and received the breath of life, so now Christ, renewing our nature, breathes the Holy Spirit upon his disciples. We are created anew.
magis: Catechism 644
Even when faced with the reality of the risen Jesus the disciples still doubted; Thomas was brought to faith by the Lord himself.
Catechism 976–983 and 1441–1442
Only God forgives sins; Christ gave this power to his Apostles and their successors, so that the Church is the place of reconciliation.
Catechism 1485–1486
On Easter evening the Lord gave the Apostles the Holy Spirit and the power to forgive sins; the sacrament of Penance.
Catechism 1471
An indulgence is a remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins whose guilt has already been forgiven.
Dives in Misericordia (St John Paul II, 1980)
The Church lives an authentic life when she professes and proclaims mercy and brings people close to the sources of the Saviour's mercy.
Misericordiae Vultus 1 (Pope Francis, 2015)
Jesus Christ is the face of the Father's mercy.
saints: St Faustina Kowalska

Polish religious of the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy (1905–1938). In her Diary she records the Lord's request for an image with the words “Jesus, I trust in you” and for a Feast of Mercy on the Sunday after Easter. Canonized on 30 April 2000; her memorial is on 5 October.
St Thomas the Apostle
The Twin, whose doubt became the confession “My Lord and my God.” Tradition holds that he brought the Gospel to India. His feast is on 3 July.
This week

5 Apr: the Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March): Gloria and Creed, with a genuflection at “and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate.” 7 Apr: St John Baptist de la Salle. 11 Apr: Third Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-04.prayer: God of everlasting mercy, who in the very recurrence of the paschal feast kindle the faith of the people you have made your own, increase, we pray, the grace you have bestowed, that all may grasp and rightly understand in what font they have been washed, by whose Spirit they have been reborn, by whose Blood they have been redeemed. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Merciful Jesus, you came through the locked doors of our fear and showed us your wounds. Breathe your Spirit upon us, forgive our sins, heal our doubts, and make us one heart and one soul in your Church. With Thomas we confess you: my Lord and my God. Jesus, I trust in you. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-11.title: Third Sunday of Easter
readings: You killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead
Lord, let your face shine on us (or: Alleluia)
He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world
Thus it is written, that the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day
2027-04-11.alt: Year B. Third Sunday of Easter. Gloria and Creed; in Eastertide the Rite for the Blessing and Sprinkling of Water may replace the Penitential Act. The Regina Caeli is prayed at noon. St Stanislaus, bishop and martyr (11 Apr), is not celebrated this year because the Sunday prevails. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-11.verse: Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.
theo: On the Third Sunday of Easter the Church sits us down in Jerusalem on the evening of the first Easter day. The two disciples have just run back from Emmaus and are telling “how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.” Before St Luke shows us the risen Lord again, the first reading lets us hear what the apostles did with that experience. In Solomon's Portico, after the healing of the lame man, Peter speaks to the crowd: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our ancestors has glorified his servant Jesus.” He names the tragedy plainly: “you rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked to have a murderer given to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses.” Then his tone changes completely: “And now, friends, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.” These are not words of condemnation but of a brother; they echo Jesus' own prayer from the cross, “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.” Peter, who denied the Lord three times, is in no position to accuse anyone. The Church has always taught that the sins of all of us brought Christ to the cross and that the Jewish people may not be held collectively responsible for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597–598). Peter's purpose is the same as ours today: “Repent therefore, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out.” The Psalm is the prayer of one who has turned back: “Let the light of your face shine on us, O LORD!”

The second reading, from the First Letter of St John, is tender and strong. “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.” The Easter life is a life without sin, and John does not lower the standard. But he knows his children: “But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.” The Greek word for advocate is parakletos, the same word Jesus uses for the Holy Spirit. Jesus is our first advocate, standing before the Father with the wounds of his love; and the word for atoning sacrifice, hilasmos, recalls the mercy seat of the Ark, where the blood of atonement was sprinkled. He is not only the lawyer who pleads for us; he is himself the offering that reconciles. Then John gives a simple test for a living faith: “Now by this we may be sure that we know him, if we obey his commandments.” Knowing Christ is not a feeling but a life: “whoever obeys his word, truly in this person the love of God has reached perfection.”

Then the Gospel. “While they were talking about this, Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, ‘Peace be with you.’” They are “startled and terrified,” thinking they see a ghost. Jesus' answer is one of the most important texts in the Bible for our faith in the bodily Resurrection: “Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” He shows them his wounds. And while “in their joy they were disbelieving and still wondering,” he asks a homely question: “Have you anything here to eat?” They give him a piece of broiled fish, “and he took it and ate in their presence.” The risen Christ is not a memory, not an idea, not a spirit only: he is the same Jesus, body and soul, now glorified, never to die again. Then he opens their minds to understand the Scriptures: “everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled.” The whole Old Testament, all three parts, points to him. And he gives them their mission: “repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.” This Sunday has the same shape as every Mass: the Lord stands among us and says Peace; he opens the Scriptures; he gives himself as food; and he sends us out as witnesses.
conn: “The Author of life.”
Greek archegos, the pioneer or founder who leads the way (Acts 3:15; Hebrews 12:2). The irony is deliberate: men put to death the very source of life, and God raised him.
“You acted in ignorance.”

Peter's words echo Jesus' prayer on the cross (Luke 23:34). The Church teaches that responsibility for the Passion may not be laid on all Jews then or now, and that all sinners are its authors (Catechism 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4).
“Advocate.”
Greek parakletos, one called to stand beside another, especially in court. In 1 John 2:1 it is Jesus; in John 14:16 Jesus promises “another Advocate,” the Holy Spirit (Catechism 692).
“Atoning sacrifice.”
Greek hilasmos, linked with the mercy seat (hilasterion) over the Ark, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Christ is both priest and victim.
“Flesh and bones.”
The risen Jesus is not a ghost. His body is real, can be touched and can eat, yet is glorified, no longer bound by space and time (Catechism 645).
The piece of broiled fish.
He eats not because he needs food but to show that he is truly alive and the same Jesus they knew. The fish (Greek ichthys) later became an early Christian symbol of Christ.
The law, the prophets and the psalms.
The three parts of the Jewish Scriptures (Torah, Prophets, Writings, of which the Psalms are the best known). Jesus says that all of it speaks of him (Luke 24:44).
“Beginning from Jerusalem.”
The programme of the Acts of the Apostles: from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The word witnesses, martyres, would come to mean those who gave their blood.
altar: The Lord who said “Touch me and see” and ate the broiled fish gives us at this altar not a symbol but his own risen Body and Blood. We do not see his hands and feet, but we receive him truly, really and substantially present.
Jesus is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and the Mass makes that one sacrifice present. Here our Advocate pleads for us, and from here we are sent as witnesses of repentance and forgiveness.
outline: Opening
Ask: if the risen Jesus stood in your house tonight, what would you want to touch, and what would you want to ask him?
Point 1 · The Author of life
Peter's preaching: tragedy named, mercy offered.
Point 2 · Repent and turn
Ignorance forgiven, sins wiped out.
Point 3 · An advocate with the Father
Jesus our defender and our sacrifice.
Point 4 · Flesh and bones
The risen body, the opened Scriptures, the mission.
Closing image
A table at night, a plate with a piece of fish, and a pair of wounded hands.
Take-home line
“You are witnesses of these things.”
live: Go to confession
John says: if anyone does sin, we have an advocate. Make a good confession this Easter season and receive the peace of the risen Lord.
Read the Scriptures with him
Each day this week read one Old Testament passage that points to Christ (for example Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Psalm 16) and ask him to open your mind.
Eat with someone
The risen Lord ate with his friends. Invite to your table this week someone who usually eats alone.
Speak of what you have seen
Tell one person this week, simply, how you have met the risen Lord in your life.
fathers: St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)

I know and believe that he was in the flesh even after the resurrection. When he came to Peter and those with him, he said to them: take hold of me, handle me, and see that I am not a bodiless spirit. And at once they touched him and believed.
St Augustine (in substance)

John did not say, you have an advocate, but we have an advocate. He placed himself among the sinners, so that he might have Christ as his advocate. Let no one say: Peter is my advocate, or Paul; we have one Advocate, Christ.
St Augustine (in substance)

The Lord ate after his resurrection not out of need but out of power. The earth absorbs water in one way, and the burning sun in another: the one from thirst, the other by its strength. So his risen body took food without any need.
magis: Catechism 643–645
The appearances of the risen Christ; his real body, which can be touched and shares their meal, yet glorified.
Catechism 999
“It is I myself”: Christ rose with his own body, and so shall we.
Catechism 597–598
Responsibility for the death of Jesus is not to be laid on the Jews as a people; all sinners are its authors.
Catechism 692
Jesus, the first Advocate, and the Holy Spirit, “another Advocate.”
Catechism 1427–1429
Conversion and repentance, to which the risen Lord calls every Christian.
saints: St Stanislaus (11 Apr, not celebrated this year)
Bishop of Kraków, killed in 1079, according to tradition while celebrating Mass, after he had rebuked King Bolesław II. Patron of Poland; his memorial gives way to the Sunday this year.
This week

12–17 Apr: Easter weekdays of the Third Week, with the Bread of Life chapter of John. 13 Apr: St Martin I, pope and martyr (optional). 18 Apr: Fourth Sunday of Easter, Good Shepherd Sunday, World Day of Prayer for Vocations.
2027-04-11.prayer: May your people exult for ever, O God, in renewed youthfulness of spirit, so that, rejoicing now in the restored glory of our adoption, we may look forward in confident hope to the rejoicing of the day of resurrection. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Risen Lord Jesus, you stood among your frightened disciples and said, Peace be with you. Show us your hands and your feet; open our minds to understand the Scriptures; feed us with your Body; and make us witnesses of repentance and forgiveness to all nations, beginning from our own homes. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-18.title: Fourth Sunday of Easter (Good Shepherd Sunday)
readings: There is salvation in no one else; there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved
The stone rejected by the builders has become the cornerstone (or: Alleluia)
See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God; we will see him as he is
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep
2027-04-18.alt: Year B. Good Shepherd Sunday: every year the Gospel of the Fourth Sunday of Easter is taken from John 10 (Year A 10:1–10; Year B 10:11–18; Year C 10:27–30). The Church keeps the World Day of Prayer for Vocations, first kept in 1964 at the wish of St Paul VI; the Holy Father usually publishes a message for the day. The Gloria and the Creed are said; the Regina Caeli is prayed in place of the Angelus. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-18.verse: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
theo: Every year, halfway between Easter and Pentecost, the Church sets before us the face of the risen Christ as the Good Shepherd. The first reading shows us one of his under-shepherds at work. Peter and John have been arrested for healing a man lame from birth at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple and for preaching the resurrection. The next morning they stand before the rulers, the elders and the scribes, the high priestly family among them. And Peter, “filled with the Holy Spirit,” speaks. Only a few weeks earlier, in the courtyard of the high priest, this same man had been frightened by a servant girl into denying that he knew Jesus. Now he says to the most powerful men in Jerusalem: if you are asking how this man was healed, “let it be known to all of you… that this man is standing before you in good health by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead.” Then he quotes the psalm we sing today: “This Jesus is ‘the stone that was rejected by you, the builders; it has become the cornerstone.’” And he ends with one of the boldest sentences in the New Testament: “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved.” The Church has never softened this. Jesus Christ is the one Saviour of all (Catechism 432; 846). At the same time she teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know him, but seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will, can be saved by his grace, which reaches them in ways known to God (Catechism 847; Lumen Gentium 16). Peter's words are spoken to the particular leaders before him at that moment, not to the Jewish people as a whole (Catechism 597); he himself is a son of Israel announcing Israel's Messiah.

The Gospel is the heart of the day. “I am the good shepherd.” The Greek word for “good” here, kalos, also means noble and beautiful: Jesus is the true shepherd, the shepherd as a shepherd should be. Israel knew the image well. God was the shepherd of his people (Psalm 23; Psalm 80:1), and through Ezekiel he had condemned the shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock and promised: “I myself will search for my sheep, and will seek them out” (Ezekiel 34:11). When Jesus says “I am the good shepherd,” he claims to be that promised shepherd, God himself come to seek his sheep. He sets himself against the hired hand, who works for wages, “sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and runs away.” The difference is not skill but love: the hired hand “does not care for the sheep.” The Good Shepherd knows his own, and they know him, “just as the Father knows me and I know the Father.” This is not a list of names on a register; it is the intimacy of the Trinity offered to each of us. Five times in these few verses Jesus speaks of laying down his life. He does it freely: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again.” In the Easter season we hear both halves of that sentence: the Cross and the Resurrection are one act of the Shepherd's love (Catechism 609). And his love is wider than any fold: “I have other sheep that do not belong to this fold. I must bring them also… So there will be one flock, one shepherd.” Today we pray for all who do not yet know him, and for the unity of all Christians in his one flock.

The second reading tells us what the Shepherd's sacrifice has made of us: “See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God; and that is what we are.” Not only called, but made so, in Baptism. And there is more to come: “what we will be has not yet been revealed. What we do know is this: when he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him as he is.” That vision of God face to face is the goal of every Christian life (Catechism 1023). This is why the Church prays today for vocations. The Good Shepherd continues to lead his flock through shepherds he calls: priests who stand in his person at the altar and in the confessional, deacons, men and women in consecrated life, missionaries, and also fathers and mothers who are the first shepherds of the domestic church. God promised through Jeremiah: “I will give you shepherds after my own heart” (Jeremiah 3:15). Kerala has received this gift abundantly, and many of her sons and daughters serve the Church across India and the world. Today let each family ask whether God may be calling one of its own, and let each of us pray for our priests by name. May the Mother of the Good Shepherd, the Blessed Virgin Mary, who gave her whole life to God's call, intercede for all who are called.
conn: Good Shepherd Sunday.

On the Fourth Sunday of Easter the Gospel is always from John 10: in Year A the sheepfold and the gate (10:1–10), in Year B the shepherd who lays down his life (10:11–18), in Year C “my sheep hear my voice” (10:27–30).
World Day of Prayer for Vocations.
First kept in 1964 at the wish of St Paul VI; it is kept on this Sunday. The Holy Father usually writes a message for it each year.
“Good” (kalos).
The Greek word means good, noble and beautiful. Jesus is the model shepherd, the shepherd as God intended.
The hired hand.
A worker paid by the day, with no stake in the flock. Ezekiel 34 and Zechariah 11:17 condemn shepherds who abandon or exploit the sheep.
The cornerstone.
Psalm 118:22, the great Easter psalm. Jesus applies it to himself (Mark 12:10–11), and so do Peter here and in 1 Peter 2:7.
The council.
The Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest; Acts 4:6 names Annas, Caiaphas, John and Alexander.
Other sheep.
The Gentiles who would be brought into the one flock. John 11:52 says Jesus would die “to gather into one the dispersed children of God.”
The Good Shepherd in early art.
A young shepherd carrying a lamb on his shoulders is one of the earliest images of Christ, painted in the Roman catacombs in the third century.
altar: The Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. At every Mass that one sacrifice of the Cross is made present, and the risen Shepherd feeds his flock with his own Body and Blood.
The priest at the altar acts in the person of Christ the Head and Shepherd. Pray for him today, and for all whom God is calling to stand there after him.
outline: Opening
Ask: who has been a good shepherd in my life?
Point 1 · No other name
Peter's courage before the council.
Point 2 · The stone rejected
The Cross and the Resurrection.
Point 3 · The good shepherd
Not a hired hand: one who knows and lays down his life.
Point 4 · Children of God now
We will see him as he is.
Point 5 · Shepherds after his own heart
Pray for vocations.
Take-home line
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
live: Pray for vocations (Matthew 9:38)
As a family, pray each evening this week for one more priest or sister from your parish, and for the seminarians of your diocese by name.
Thank your shepherd
Write a short note, send a message or simply say thank you to your parish priest today.
Listen for his voice (John 10:16)
Give ten silent minutes this week to ask the Good Shepherd: what is my vocation, and how can I live it better?
Be a shepherd at home
Parents: lay down a little of your life this week for your children: one evening without the phone, given entirely to them.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (in substance)

The Lord laid down his life for his sheep and turned his body and blood into our sacrament, so that he might feed with his flesh the sheep he had redeemed. Those of us who are shepherds must at least give our goods to the sheep; if we will not give our possessions, how shall we ever give our lives?
St Augustine (in substance)

All good shepherds are in the one Shepherd; they are his members. Peter is a shepherd, Paul is a shepherd, but in them it is Christ who feeds the flock, for the voice of the Shepherd is heard in all of them.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Nothing so marks the shepherd as care for the flock. The one who loves Christ will feed his sheep, and the proof of love is the willingness to suffer for them.
magis: Catechism 754
The Church is a sheepfold whose one and necessary gate is Christ, and a flock of which God himself foretold that he would be the shepherd.
Catechism 609
Jesus freely lays down his life: “No one takes it from me” (John 10:18).
Catechism 432; 846–847
There is no other name by which we must be saved; and how God's grace may reach those who without fault do not know Christ.
Catechism 1023
Those who die in God's grace will see him “as he is” (1 John 3:2), face to face.
Pastores Dabo Vobis 1 (St John Paul II, 1992)
“I will give you shepherds after my own heart” (Jeremiah 3:15): the promise God keeps in every age through the gift of priests.
saints: St Martin I (13 Apr)
Pope from 649 to 655. He condemned the error that Christ has only one will, was arrested by order of the emperor, exiled to the Crimea and died there of hardship; venerated as a martyr.
St Anselm (21 Apr)
Monk, abbot of Bec in Normandy and Archbishop of Canterbury (1033–1109), Doctor of the Church, who described theology as “faith seeking understanding.”
St George (23 Apr)
Martyr of the early fourth century whose tomb tradition places at Lydda, the town where Peter healed Aeneas (Acts 9:32–35). Much loved in Kerala, where many churches bear his name.
2027-04-18.prayer: Almighty ever-living God, lead us to a share in the joys of heaven, so that the humble flock may reach where the brave Shepherd has gone before. Who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, you laid down your life for us and took it up again. Call many of our young people to follow you as priests and consecrated persons, keep our pastors faithful and joyful, and gather all your sheep into one flock under you, the one Shepherd. Amen. Alleluia.

2027-04-25.title: Fifth Sunday of Easter
readings: Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles
I will praise you, Lord, in the assembly of your people (or: Alleluia)
Let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action
I am the vine, you are the branches
2027-04-25.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. The feast of St Mark the Evangelist (25 April) is not celebrated this year, because a Sunday of Easter takes precedence over a feast; it is not transferred. Regina Caeli at noon until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-25.verse: I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
theo: The first reading shows us Saul of Tarsus after his conversion, trying to join the disciples in Jerusalem. It does not go well. “They were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple.” And who could blame them? Only a short time before he had been dragging Christians to prison. Saul has met the risen Lord, but the Church does not yet trust him. Then one man changes everything: “Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and described for them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.” Barnabas, the “son of encouragement,” takes a risk on a man everyone else feared. Without Barnabas, perhaps there would have been no St Paul as we know him. Soon Saul is preaching boldly in Jerusalem, his life is threatened again, and the believers send him off to Tarsus to keep him safe. Luke ends with a beautiful summary: “the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and was built up. Living in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.”

The Psalm is the second half of Psalm 22, the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” On Palm Sunday of the Passion we sang from its first half, the cry of anguish. In the Easter season the Church sings its second half, the song of thanksgiving of one who has been rescued: “From you comes my praise in the great congregation.” “The poor shall eat and be satisfied.” “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.” The one who was forsaken now praises God in the assembly, and his deliverance will be told “to a people yet unborn.” That is the Resurrection, and that is the Church, the great congregation where the risen Christ praises the Father with us.

The second reading, from the First Letter of John, is short and very practical: “Little children, let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action.” Christian love is not a feeling or a speech; it is shown in deeds. Then John speaks tenderly to troubled consciences: “whenever our hearts condemn us; for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.” When we feel unworthy, our feelings do not have the last word; God does. And he sums up the whole of Christian life in one commandment with two parts: “that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another.” Faith and love are not two separate things; they are one life. “All who obey his commandments abide in him, and he abides in them. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit that he has given us.”

The Gospel gives us one of the richest images of the whole Bible. At the Last Supper Jesus says: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinegrower.” In the Old Testament Israel was God's vine, planted with love and tended with care (Isaiah 5; Psalm 80). Now Jesus says that he himself is the true vine, and we are the branches. The life of the branch is the life of the vine; cut off, it withers. “Abide in me as I abide in you.” The word “abide” appears again and again: to stay, to remain, to make one's home. And the Father prunes: “Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.” Pruning hurts, but it is not punishment; it is the vinegrower's care, so that the branch may bear more. “Apart from me you can do nothing.” We cannot love as 1 John asks by our own effort; we can only love if the life of Christ flows in us. The Barnabas of the first reading is such a branch: his encouragement of Paul was the fruit of Christ's own life in him. Today would ordinarily be the feast of St Mark the Evangelist, the same John Mark who was Barnabas's cousin. This year the Sunday takes its place, but we may thank God for him, who wrote the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, so that it could bear fruit in every age.
conn: Paul in Jerusalem.

Paul himself says he went up to Jerusalem three years after his conversion to visit Cephas, and stayed with him fifteen days (Galatians 1:18). Luke tells the story more briefly and from the Church's side.
Barnabas.
A Levite from Cyprus, the “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36). His trust in Paul is the first of many times he stands up for someone others have rejected (see Acts 15:37–39, with John Mark).
The Hellenists.
Here Greek-speaking Jews in Jerusalem, perhaps the same synagogue circles that had argued with Stephen (Acts 6:9). Paul now stands where Stephen stood.
Tarsus.
Paul's home city in Cilicia, in south-eastern Asia Minor, a centre of learning. He will remain there until Barnabas comes to fetch him for Antioch (Acts 11:25).
Psalm 22.

The psalm whose first verse Jesus cried out on the cross (Mark 15:34). Its second half moves from lament to praise and to a vision of all nations worshipping God. The early Church saw in it the whole paschal mystery.
“Abide.”
The Greek menein appears seven times in John 15:4–7. It means to stay, to remain, to dwell. The same word is used when the first disciples “remained” with Jesus (John 1:39).
The vine.
Israel is God's vine in Isaiah 5:1–7, Jeremiah 2:21, Psalm 80:8–16 and Hosea 10:1. A great golden vine decorated the entrance to the Temple sanctuary in Jesus' day.
Pruning.
In Greek the word for “prunes” (kathairei) is close to the word for “cleansed” (katharoi) in verse 3. The word of Jesus is the knife that cleanses and prunes.
St Mark not kept.
In the Table of Liturgical Days the Sundays of Easter rank above feasts of the Lord's apostles and evangelists. A feast impeded by a Sunday is simply omitted that year.
altar: “I am the vine, you are the branches.” At the Last Supper, where Jesus spoke these words, he took the cup of “the fruit of the vine” and made it his Blood. In Holy Communion the life of the Vine flows into the branches.

The Second Vatican Council calls the Eucharist the source and summit of the Christian life. To abide in Christ is, above all, to abide in his Eucharist: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them” (John 6:56).
outline: Opening
Show a cut branch from a garden: green today, dry in three days. Ask: what keeps me green?
Point 1 · Barnabas took him
Trusting someone others fear.
Point 2 · Not in word, but in truth and action
Love that is shown, and the God who is greater than our hearts.
Point 3 · Abide in me
The vine and the branches.
Point 4 · Pruned to bear more fruit
Suffering in the hands of the vinegrower.
Closing image
A vineyard in harvest, the branches bent low with grapes, and the vinegrower smiling among them.
Take-home line
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
live: Be a Barnabas
Find one person in your parish or family who is distrusted or left out. Speak up for them, introduce them, or simply sit with them.
Love in action
Choose one act of love this week that costs you something: visit, phone, help, pay a bill, forgive. Do it without announcing it.
Stay connected
Make one daily habit of abiding: a short visit to the Blessed Sacrament, the Rosary, or ten minutes with the Gospel. A branch needs the vine every day, not only on Sundays.
Accept the pruning
Bring to the Father one painful loss or limitation in your life, and pray: Prune me, Lord, so that I may bear more fruit.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The branches are in the vine in such a way that they give nothing to the vine but receive their life from it. One of two things belongs to the branch: either the vine or the fire. If it is not in the vine, it will be in the fire; let it be in the vine, that it may not be in the fire.
St Augustine (in substance)

Love, and do what you will. If you keep silence, keep silence out of love; if you cry out, cry out out of love; if you correct, correct out of love; if you spare, spare out of love. Let the root of love be within, for from that root nothing but good can grow.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

Barnabas was a true son of encouragement: he did not let the past of Paul stand between Paul and the Church, but took him by the hand and led him to the apostles. So should we do for those who have turned to God.
St Cyril of Alexandria (in substance)
Christ is the vine; we are joined to him by the Holy Spirit and nourished by his flesh, so that his very life becomes ours.
magis: Catechism 755
The Church is a cultivated field, the vineyard of God; Christ is the true vine who gives life and fruitfulness to the branches.
Catechism 787–789
The Church is communion with Jesus: “Abide in me, and I in you.” The Church is the Body of Christ.
Catechism 2074
“Apart from me you can do nothing”: the fruit of the Christian life comes from union with Christ.
Catechism 1108
The Holy Spirit unites the Church to the life and mission of Christ; the fruit of the Spirit in the liturgy is communion.
Sacrosanctum Concilium 10 / Lumen Gentium 11
The liturgy, and above all the Eucharist, is the source and summit of the Church's life.
Deus Caritas Est 18 (Benedict XVI, 2005)
Love of God and love of neighbour are inseparable: love grows through love, in action.
saints: St Mark the Evangelist (not kept this year)

John Mark, cousin of Barnabas, companion of Paul and of Peter, whom tradition names as the author of the Gospel according to Mark and the founder of the Church of Alexandria. His symbol is the lion. His feast is omitted in 2027 because 25 April is the Fifth Sunday of Easter.
This week

26–30 Apr: Fifth Week of Easter. 28 Apr: St Peter Chanel; St Louis Grignion de Montfort (optional). 29 Apr: St Catherine of Siena (memorial). 30 Apr: St Pius V (optional). 1 May: St Joseph the Worker (optional); May, the month of the Blessed Virgin Mary, begins.
2027-04-25.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, true vine, your Father is the vinegrower and we are the branches. Keep us abiding in you, for apart from you we can do nothing. Nourish us with your word and with your Body and Blood, so that your life may flow in us and bear fruit that lasts. When the Father prunes us, give us trust in his loving hands. Make us like Barnabas, quick to welcome and to encourage; teach us to love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action; and when our hearts condemn us, remind us that God is greater than our hearts. With St Mark, who wrote your Gospel, and with the Blessed Virgin Mary, the fruitful branch who bore you, we praise you in the assembly of your people, now and for ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-01.title: Thursday within the Octave of Easter
readings: You killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses
O Lord, our God, how wonderful your name in all the earth! (or: Alleluia)
Thus it is written, that the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day
2027-04-01.alt: Day within the Octave of Easter, kept with the rank of a solemnity. The Gloria is sung; the Easter Sequence may be sung before the Gospel acclamation; the dismissal has the double Alleluia. Liturgical colour: white. Today is also the first Thursday of the month, kept in many parishes with prayer for priests and for vocations. Seventh day of the Divine Mercy Novena.
2027-04-01.verse: Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.
theo: The lame man who was healed at the Beautiful Gate will not let go of Peter and John. He clings to them, and the whole crowd comes running to Solomon's Portico, “utterly astonished.” Peter sees the faces turned towards him and refuses the glory at once: “why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk?” The power is not theirs. “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our ancestors has glorified his servant Jesus.” Then Peter tells the story of Good Friday in a few sharp words: the Holy and Righteous One was rejected, a murderer was preferred, “and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses.” What a title for the crucified Lord: the Author of life, the one from whom all life begins, put to death, and death could not hold him.

Peter does not speak as an accuser who wants to crush his hearers. He is himself a man who denied the Lord three times only a few weeks before. So his next words are full of tenderness: “And now, friends, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.” They echo the prayer of Jesus on the cross: Father, forgive them. The Church has always refused to lay the death of Christ on the Jewish people as a whole; the Second Vatican Council taught this plainly (Nostra Aetate 4), and the Catechism adds that all sinners were the authors of his Passion, we Christians most of all (CCC 597–598). Peter's call is to everyone, then and now: “Repent therefore, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out, so that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord.” He reminds them that they are heirs of the promise made to Abraham: “in your descendants all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” The Risen One was sent “first to you, to bless you.” The Psalm marvels at the dignity God gives to frail human beings: “what are human beings that you are mindful of them, mortals that you care for them?” The Letter to the Hebrews reads this psalm of Jesus, crowned with glory after the suffering of death.

In the Gospel the two disciples from Emmaus are still telling their story when Jesus himself stands among them and says, “Peace be with you.” Instead of joy there is terror: “They were startled and terrified, and thought that they were seeing a ghost.” The Lord answers their fear with his body: “Why are you frightened, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” Luke adds one of the most human lines in the Gospels: “in their joy they were disbelieving and still wondering.” The news is too good to believe. So Jesus asks, “Have you anything here to eat?” They give him a piece of broiled fish, and he eats it in their presence. The Risen Lord is not a memory, not a vision, not a spirit floating above the earth. He is the same Jesus, with the same body that was nailed to the cross, now raised to a glory that will never die.

Then he does what he did on the road to Emmaus: “he opened their minds to understand the scriptures.” Everything written about him “in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms” had to be fulfilled: the Messiah was to suffer and to rise on the third day, “and that repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.” Notice how today's two readings answer each other. In the Gospel Jesus says, “You are witnesses”; in Acts Peter stands in the Temple and says, “To this we are witnesses.” The Church is born as a community of witnesses to a real, bodily Resurrection. The Collect of the day prays for the newly baptized, that the many nations united in confessing his name may be one in faith and in deeds. That is the Easter mission: to carry repentance and forgiveness to every nation, beginning from our own Jerusalem, our home and our parish.
conn: Solomon's Portico.
A covered colonnade on the east side of the Temple courts. Jesus walked there at the feast of Dedication (John 10:23), and the first Christians often gathered there (Acts 5:12).
“The Author of life.”

The Greek word archēgos means leader, founder, pioneer: the one who goes first and opens the way. Hebrews 2:10 calls Jesus the “pioneer of their salvation.” The one who gives life could not be held by death.
“You acted in ignorance.”

Peter echoes Luke 23:34, “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.” The Catechism quotes this verse (CCC 597) in teaching that the Jews are not collectively responsible for the death of Jesus.
“Times of refreshing” and “universal restoration.”
Peter looks forward to the return of Christ in glory, when God will make all things new (Acts 3:20–21; Revelation 21:5).
“A prophet like me.”
Moses' promise in Deuteronomy 18:15–19. The early Church saw Jesus as the new Moses, the prophet to whom all must listen.
The broiled fish.

The Risen Lord eats not because he needs food but to show that he is truly alive in his body. Peter will later preach that the witnesses “ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41).
The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms.
The three parts of the Hebrew Scriptures as they were known in Jesus' day; the Psalms head the third part, the Writings. Jesus says all of them speak of him.
Psalm 8 and Jesus.
Hebrews 2:6–9 reads this psalm of Christ: made for a little while lower than the angels, “now crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death.”
altar: The Lord who ate the broiled fish before his disciples now gives himself to us as food. The Body we receive at Mass is not a symbol of a departed teacher but the living, risen body of Christ, glorious and real, which once bore the nails.

Before Communion the priest says, “The peace of the Lord be with you always.” It is the Easter greeting of the Risen One standing among his frightened friends. Receive it as he gave it: as peace that drives out fear.
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever received news so good you could not believe it?
Point 1 · Not by our own power
The healed man and Peter's humility.
Point 2 · Touch me and see
The real, bodily Resurrection.
Point 3 · You are witnesses
Repentance and forgiveness to all nations.
Closing image
A piece of broiled fish on a table, and wounded hands taking it.
Take-home line
“Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself.”
live: Give God the glory
When someone praises you today for a good deed, quietly turn it to God, as Peter did: it was not by my own power.
Read with an open mind
Ask the Risen Lord tonight to open your mind to the Scriptures, and read Luke 24:36–48 slowly.
Be a witness at home
Tell one person in your family how the Lord has helped you this Lent or this Easter.
Pray for priests
On this first Thursday, pray for the priest who baptized you and for the priests of your parish.
fathers: St Ignatius of Antioch (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 3, in substance)

I know and believe that he was in the flesh even after the resurrection. When he came to Peter and those with him, he said: take hold of me, handle me and see that I am not a bodiless ghost. And they touched him and believed. After his resurrection he ate and drank with them as one who was in the flesh.
St Augustine (in substance)

The Lord ate after his resurrection not because he was hungry but because he was able. The earth soaks up water in one way; the sun draws it up in another. He took food by power, not by need, so that his disciples might be sure his body was real.
St Leo the Great (Sermon on the Ascension, in substance)

Those days between the Resurrection and the Ascension were not spent idly. In them the Lord let himself be touched, ate with his disciples and opened the Scriptures, so that every doubt might be healed and our faith built on firm ground.
magis: Catechism 645
The risen Jesus invites his disciples to touch him and shares their meal; his body is real, yet now possesses new properties of a glorious body.
Catechism 597–598
The Jews are not collectively responsible for Jesus' death; all sinners were the authors of his Passion.
Nostra Aetate 4 (Second Vatican Council, 1965)
What happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today.
Catechism 999
How do the dead rise? Christ is raised with his own body; we too shall rise with our own bodies.
Dei Verbum 16
The New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made manifest in the New.
saints: St Hugh of Grenoble

Bishop of Grenoble (died 1132), commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 1 April. He welcomed St Bruno and his six companions and gave them the wild valley of the Chartreuse, where the Carthusian Order began in 1084. His day is not kept this year because of the Octave.
This week

2 Apr: Friday within the Octave (no abstinence). 3 Apr: Saturday within the Octave. 4 Apr: Second Sunday of Easter, Sunday of Divine Mercy. 5 Apr: the Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March).
2027-04-01.prayer: O God, who have united the many nations in confessing your name, grant that those reborn in the font of Baptism may be one in the faith of their hearts and the homage of their deeds. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Risen Lord Jesus, you stood among your frightened disciples and said, Peace be with you. Show us your hands and your feet when we doubt, open our minds to understand the Scriptures, and send us out as witnesses of repentance and forgiveness, beginning in our own homes. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-02.title: Friday within the Octave of Easter
readings: There is salvation in no one else: there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved
The stone rejected by the builders has become the cornerstone (or: Alleluia)
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and did the same with the fish
2027-04-02.alt: Day within the Octave of Easter, kept with the rank of a solemnity. The Gloria is sung; the Easter Sequence may be sung before the Gospel acclamation; the dismissal has the double Alleluia. Liturgical colour: white. Although it is a Friday, there is no abstinence today: every day of the Easter Octave has the rank of a solemnity (Code of Canon Law 1251). First Friday of the month. St Francis of Paola (2 April) is not observed this year. Eighth day of the Divine Mercy Novena.
2027-04-02.verse: That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!”
theo: Peter and John are still speaking to the people in the Temple when the priests, the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees arrive, “much annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming that in Jesus there is the resurrection of the dead.” The Sadducees did not believe in any resurrection at all, and here were two Galileans announcing that it had already begun in Jesus. The Apostles spend the night in custody. Yet Luke slips in a quiet line of victory: “many of those who heard the word believed; and they numbered about five thousand.” The word of God is not locked up with its preachers. The next morning the Temple leaders gather, Annas and Caiaphas among them, the same men before whom Jesus stood a few weeks earlier. Their question is the right one, though they ask it in the wrong spirit: “By what power or by what name did you do this?”

Then Peter, “filled with the Holy Spirit,” answers. This is the man who, on the night of the Passion, could not admit to a servant girl that he knew Jesus. Now he stands before the high priest and says: “this man is standing before you in good health by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead. This Jesus is ‘the stone that was rejected by you, the builders; it has become the cornerstone.’ There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved.” The Psalm of the day sings the same verse that Peter quotes: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvelous in our eyes.” The Church has always held this truth firmly: Jesus Christ is the one Saviour of the whole world. The Second Vatican Council adds that God's grace, which always comes through Christ, can reach in ways known to God those who through no fault of their own do not yet know him (Lumen Gentium 16). That is not a reason to be silent; it is a reason to speak his name with love, as Peter did.

The Gospel takes us back to Galilee, to the Sea of Tiberias. Seven disciples are together, and Simon Peter says simply, “I am going fishing.” They go with him, “but that night they caught nothing.” A long, empty night of work: many fishermen, many parents, many young people looking for a job know that night. “Just after daybreak, Jesus stood on the beach; but the disciples did not know that it was Jesus.” He calls to them as a father calls his children: “Children, you have no fish, have you?” They answer, “No.” He tells them to cast the net to the right side of the boat, and now they cannot haul it in for the number of fish. The beloved disciple sees with the eyes of love before anyone else: “It is the Lord!” Peter, impulsive as ever, puts on his clothes and jumps into the sea to reach him first.

On the shore a charcoal fire is already burning, with fish on it, and bread. The only other charcoal fire in John's Gospel is the one in the high priest's courtyard where Peter warmed himself and denied his Master (John 18:18). Now the Lord lights a new fire, of welcome. He asks for some of the fish they have caught, and Peter hauls the net ashore, “full of large fish, a hundred fifty-three of them; and though there were so many, the net was not torn.” Then come the gentlest words: “Come and have breakfast.” None of them dares ask, “Who are you?” They know. “Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and did the same with the fish.” The Fathers saw here a picture of the Church: the boat of Peter, the net that gathers every kind of people and does not tear, and the Lord who feeds his tired disciples with bread from his own hands. Without him the night is empty; with him the net is full, and breakfast is ready on the shore.
conn: The Sadducees.

A priestly party linked with the leading Temple families. They denied the resurrection of the dead (Luke 20:27; Acts 23:8); ancient writers say they held only the five books of Moses as binding. The Pharisees, by contrast, believed in the resurrection.
Annas and Caiaphas.

Annas had been high priest (AD 6–15) and remained powerful; Caiaphas, his son-in-law, was high priest from about AD 18 to 36 (John 18:13). These were particular leaders of the Temple; the five thousand who believed were also Jews.
“By what name?”
In the Bible the name stands for the person and his authority. The whole of Acts 3–4 turns on “the name” of Jesus, mentioned again and again.
The cornerstone.
Psalm 118:22, quoted by Jesus himself (Mark 12:10) and by Peter again in 1 Peter 2:7. The stone thrown away by the builders becomes the stone that holds the whole building together.
The Sea of Tiberias.
Another name for the Sea of Galilee, from the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore in honour of the emperor Tiberius (John 6:1).
“Children.”
Jesus uses the tender word paidia, little ones, as a father speaks to his family.
The charcoal fire.
The Greek word anthrakia appears only twice in the New Testament: at Peter's denial (John 18:18) and here (John 21:9). The scene prepares the threefold “Do you love me?” that follows (John 21:15–17).
153 fish.

Many explanations have been offered. St Jerome mentions a belief of his time that there were 153 kinds of fish, so the catch would stand for every nation; St Augustine saw in it the number of all who are saved. What is certain is John's point: a great catch, and a net that does not tear.
altar: On the shore the Risen Lord “took the bread and gave it to them.” At every Mass he does the same: he prepares the table, he is the host, and he himself is the food, truly present in the Bread of Life.

“Come and have breakfast.” After a night of empty nets, the Lord's first word is an invitation to eat with him. Come to Communion today not as one who has earned it, but as a tired child whom the Father calls to the fire.
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever worked all night and caught nothing?
Point 1 · By what name?
Peter before the council.
Point 2 · It is the Lord!
Love recognizes him first.
Point 3 · Come and have breakfast
The new charcoal fire and the bread from his hands.
Closing image
A full net on the sand that does not tear.
Take-home line
“There is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved.”
live: Say the Name
Pray the name of Jesus slowly ten times today, in the bus, at work or in the kitchen, as an act of faith.
Cast the net again
Take up again, with prayer, one task in which you have failed, and do it as the Lord asks.
First Friday
Visit the Blessed Sacrament today and entrust your family to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.
Feed someone
Like the Lord on the shore, prepare a meal or a cup of tea for someone who is tired.
fathers: St Augustine (Tractates on John 123, in substance)

The roasted fish is Christ who suffered. He is also the bread that came down from heaven. To this meal he invited the seven disciples, and in them all of us, so that we too may share in so great a sacrament and in so great a blessedness.
St Gregory the Great (Homily 24 on the Gospels, in substance)

Peter returned to fishing after the Resurrection, but Matthew did not return to collecting taxes. Work that can be done without sin may be taken up again after conversion; business that cannot be done without sin may not.
St Jerome (Commentary on Ezekiel 47, in substance)

Those who write about the nature of animals say that there are a hundred and fifty-three kinds of fish. All of them were caught by the Apostles, a sign that from every nation, noble and lowly, rich and poor, people are drawn up into the net of the Church.
magis: Catechism 432
The name of Jesus is the divine name that alone brings salvation: “there is no other name under heaven” (Acts 4:12).
Catechism 846–848

Outside the Church no salvation, rightly understood: all salvation comes from Christ through the Church; those who without fault do not know Christ can be saved; the Church still has the duty to evangelize.
Dominus Iesus 13–14 (Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, 2000)
Jesus Christ is the unique and universal Saviour; the Church must hold this firmly as a truth of faith.
Lumen Gentium 6
Images of the Church: the sheepfold, the field, and the building whose cornerstone is Christ.
Lumen Gentium 16
Those who seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try to do his will may attain salvation.
saints: St Francis of Paola

Hermit and founder of the Order of Minims (1416–1507). His motto was Caritas, charity. He died at Tours, in France, on Good Friday, 2 April 1507. His optional memorial is not observed this year because of the Octave.
St John Paul II

Died on 2 April 2005, the eve of Divine Mercy Sunday, the feast he had established for the whole Church in 2000. He was beatified and later canonized on Divine Mercy Sunday. His memorial is on 22 October.
2027-04-02.prayer: Almighty ever-living God, who gave us the Paschal Mystery in the covenant you established for reconciling the human race, so dispose our minds, we pray, that what we celebrate by professing the faith we may express in deeds. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you stood on the shore at daybreak while your friends toiled in vain. Call to us in our empty nights, teach us to cast our nets at your word, and feed us at your fire with the bread of your own hands, so that with the beloved disciple we may say: It is the Lord! Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-03.title: Saturday within the Octave of Easter
readings: We cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard
I praise you, Lord, for you have answered me (or: Alleluia)
Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation
2027-04-03.alt: Day within the Octave of Easter, kept with the rank of a solemnity. The Gloria is sung; the Easter Sequence may be sung before the Gospel acclamation; the dismissal has the double Alleluia. Liturgical colour: white. First Saturday of the month. Ninth and last day of the Divine Mercy Novena. Those who wish to gain the plenary indulgence of Divine Mercy Sunday may go to confession today (sacramental confession within about twenty days before or after is sufficient).
2027-04-03.verse: And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.”
theo: The council looks at Peter and John and is puzzled. These are not scholars trained in the law; they are “uneducated and ordinary men,” fishermen from Galilee. Yet they speak with a boldness that cannot be explained by learning. Then the leaders understand where it comes from: they “recognized them as companions of Jesus.” Time spent with Jesus had left its mark. And there is something they cannot argue against: “When they saw the man who had been cured standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.” A man who had never walked now stands in the middle of the court. So they send the Apostles out and talk among themselves: “What will we do with them? For it is obvious to all who live in Jerusalem that a notable sign has been done through them; we cannot deny it.” Their only plan is to stop the news from spreading: “let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.”

Peter and John give an answer that has inspired Christians in every age of persecution: “Whether it is right in God's sight to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge; for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.” They are respectful; they do not insult the council or stir up the crowd. But they will not be silent about the truth. They have seen the Risen Lord; they have heard his voice; to keep quiet would be to deny what is real. The leaders threaten them again and let them go, because “all of them praised God for what had happened.” The Psalm gives the Apostles' song of victory: “The LORD is my strength and my might; he has become my salvation.” And, from the lips of the risen Christ himself: “I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD.” The Church is bound to obey lawful authority in all that is just; but when any power commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, the Christian must answer as Peter did.

The Gospel is taken from the ending of St Mark, a short summary of the Easter appearances. Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, “from whom he had cast out seven demons.” She goes and tells the disciples, who are “mourning and weeping,” but “they would not believe it.” He appears “in another form” to two of them walking into the country, the Emmaus disciples, and again “they did not believe them.” At last he appears to the Eleven at table, “and he upbraided them for their lack of faith and stubbornness, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.” It is a surprisingly honest page. The first witnesses of the Resurrection were not credulous people looking for a miracle; they were slow, sad and hard to convince. That is why their faith, once it came, is so trustworthy.

And then, to these very men who had doubted, Jesus entrusts the whole world: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” He does not wait for perfect disciples. He sends the forgiven, the slow of heart, the ones who were rebuked a moment earlier. The two readings meet here: the Apostles who once would not believe are now the ones who “cannot keep from speaking.” The Octave of Easter ends tomorrow, but its message is just beginning. The Collect prays that God, who gives increase to the peoples who believe, may clothe the newly baptized with blessed immortality. In ancient Rome the neophytes wore their white baptismal garments all through this week and laid them aside at the end of it; the white garments were put away, but the life of Christ they signified was meant to be carried into every street and home.
conn: “Uneducated and ordinary men.”
The Greek agrammatoi and idiōtai mean men without formal rabbinic training and private persons without office, not that they could not read. The council was surprised that such men spoke so well.
“Companions of Jesus.”
Literally, “they had been with Jesus.” Mark 3:14 says Jesus chose the Twelve first “to be with him,” and then to be sent out to proclaim.
Boldness.
The word parrēsia, freedom and courage of speech, runs all through Acts (4:13, 29, 31; 28:31). It is a gift of the Holy Spirit.
Obeying God rather than human beings.

Peter repeats this principle in Acts 5:29. The Catechism teaches that citizens are obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the moral order or the Gospel (CCC 2242).
The ending of Mark.

Mark 16:9–20 is missing from some of the oldest Greek manuscripts and differs in style from the rest of the Gospel. It was known in the second century and is part of the canonical Scriptures received by the Church as inspired (Council of Trent, 1546).
Mary Magdalene.
All four Gospels place her at the empty tomb; Mark and John say the Risen Lord appeared to her first. The Church calls her “apostle of the apostles,” and since 2016 her day (22 July) is a feast.
“In another form.”
Mark's brief allusion to the Emmaus story (Luke 24:13–35), when the two disciples did not at first recognize the Lord.
In albis.

In the early Church the newly baptized wore white garments throughout Easter week and laid them aside at the end of the Octave; hence the old Latin names of this Saturday and of tomorrow's Sunday, “in albis.”
altar: The Apostles spoke so boldly because they had been with Jesus. Every Mass is time spent with him: the same Lord who sat at table with the Eleven sits at table with us and gives himself to us in the Eucharist.

At the end of Mass we hear “Go forth,” with the double Alleluia. It is a small echo of the Lord's command: go into all the world. We do not leave the altar to go home only; we leave it to take the good news with us.
outline: Opening
Ask: has anyone ever asked you to keep quiet about something you knew was true?
Point 1 · They had been with Jesus
The boldness of ordinary men.
Point 2 · We cannot keep from speaking
Obeying God rather than human beings.
Point 3 · Slow to believe, sent to all
The Eleven rebuked and sent.
Closing image
A white baptismal garment folded away, and a pair of sandals at the door.
Take-home line
“We cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
live: Spend time with Jesus
Give fifteen minutes today to silent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament or with the Gospel.
Prepare for Divine Mercy Sunday
Go to confession today if you can, and finish the Divine Mercy Novena tonight.
Speak gently but clearly
If you are asked to keep silent about what is true and right, at work or among friends, answer respectfully but do not deny the truth.
Honour Our Lady
On this First Saturday, pray the Regina Caeli and a decade of the Rosary in reparation and thanksgiving.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (Homily 29 on the Gospels, in substance)

The disciples were slow to believe the Resurrection, and this was not so much their weakness as our future strength. By their doubts, healed by so many proofs, our faith is made firm. And when the Lord says “to the whole creation,” he means the human being, who shares being with the stones, life with the plants, feeling with the animals and understanding with the angels.
St John Chrysostom (Homilies on Acts 10, in substance)

See how the uneducated put the learned to silence. The rulers came with their power and their threats; the fishermen had only the truth and the name of Jesus, and it was the rulers who were at a loss.
St Bede the Venerable (On Mark, in substance)
The Lord rebuked the hardness of his disciples at table so that, once corrected, they might preach with greater confidence to others what they themselves had come to believe through so many signs.
magis: Catechism 643–644
The disciples' doubts show that the Resurrection was not the product of their faith or credulity; their faith was born of the encounter with the Risen One.
Catechism 849–851
The missionary mandate: the Church is sent by Christ to proclaim the Gospel to every creature.
Catechism 2242
Citizens must not follow directives of civil authority that are contrary to the moral order: we must obey God rather than men.
Evangelii Gaudium 120 (Pope Francis, 2013)
Every baptized person is a missionary disciple; we do not need long training to tell others of the love of God we have met.
Dei Verbum 11
The books of Scripture, with all their parts, are inspired by the Holy Spirit and have God as their author.
saints: St Richard of Chichester

Bishop of Chichester in England (1197–1253), commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 3 April. A humble and generous pastor, remembered for the prayer: may I know you more clearly, love you more dearly, and follow you more nearly, day by day.
This week

4 Apr: Second Sunday of Easter, Sunday of Divine Mercy, Octave Day of Easter. 5 Apr: the Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March), with Gloria and Creed. 7 Apr: St John Baptist de la Salle.
2027-04-03.prayer: O God, who by the abundance of your grace give increase to the peoples who believe in you, look with favour on those you have chosen and clothe with blessed immortality those reborn through the Sacrament of Baptism. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you were patient with disciples who were slow to believe, and you sent them into all the world. Keep us close to you, so that people may see that we have been with you; give us the courage of Peter and John, and let us never keep silent about what we have seen and heard. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-05.title: The Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March)
readings: Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall name him Emmanuel, for God is with us
Here I am, Lord; I come to do your will
See, I have come to do your will, O God
You will conceive in your womb and bear a son
2027-04-05.alt: Solemnity of the Lord, transferred. The Annunciation is normally kept on 25 March, nine months before Christmas. In 2027 that day was Holy Thursday, and no solemnity may be celebrated in Holy Week or in the Octave of Easter; when this happens the Annunciation is moved to the Monday after the Second Sunday of Easter. The readings and Mass of the solemnity replace those of Monday of the Second Week of Easter (Acts 4:23–31; John 3:1–8), and St Vincent Ferrer is not commemorated this year. The Gloria and the Creed are said; at the words of the Creed “and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man” all genuflect (kneel). Because it falls in Eastertide, the Alleluia is added to the antiphons and the Gospel acclamation. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-05.verse: Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
theo: On the day after the Octave of Easter the Church goes back, as it were, nine months before Christmas, to the little house in Nazareth. This year the feast has waited for us. The Annunciation fell on Holy Thursday, and the Church does not let the joy of the Incarnation compete with the Supper, the Cross and the empty tomb; so she keeps it now, in the white light of Easter. The move is not an accident of the calendar but a lesson. The child announced by Gabriel is the same Lord who died and rose. The flesh he received from the Virgin Mary is the flesh that hung on the cross and walked out of the tomb on the third day. In the first reading King Ahaz, frightened by two enemy kings, refuses the sign that God offers him; it sounds pious, “I will not put the LORD to the test,” but it is really fear dressed up as piety. Isaiah answers: “the Lord himself will give you a sign. Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall name him Immanuel.” The Hebrew word, almah, means a young woman of marriageable age; the ancient Greek translation made by Jewish scholars rendered it parthenos, a virgin, and this is the text St Matthew quotes. The Church, with the whole tradition, reads the promise as fulfilled to the letter in the Virgin of Nazareth, and so the Lectionary proclaims it today: “the virgin shall conceive.” The reading ends with the name itself: “God is with us.”
