The Letter to the Hebrews lets us hear what the Son said as he entered the world. It quotes our psalm: “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body you have prepared for me… See, God, I have come to do your will.” The Annunciation has two yeses. Before Mary says “Here am I,” the eternal Son has said “See, I have come.” The Father prepares a body for him in the womb of the Virgin, and that body will be offered once for all on the cross: “it is by God's will that we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” The Incarnation is already turned toward the Passover. That is why this feast sits so naturally in the Easter season: the Son took our flesh in order to offer it, and he offered it in order to raise it up. And every time we kneel at Mass and the priest says “This is my Body,” we are before the same body that began to exist in Mary's womb on this day.

Then the Gospel, which Christians have prayed in the Angelus three times a day for centuries. The angel Gabriel is sent “to a town in Galilee called Nazareth,” a village nobody had heard of, “to a virgin engaged to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David.” He greets her: “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.” The Greek word, kecharitomene, means one who has been and remains filled with grace; the Church sees here the grace that preserved Mary from all stain of sin from her conception. Mary is troubled and ponders; she does not doubt, she asks: “How can this be, since I am a virgin?” The answer reveals the whole Trinity: the Most High is the Father, the Son of the Most High is the child, and “the Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” That word overshadow is the word used for the cloud of God's glory that covered the tent of meeting. Mary becomes the new Ark, the place where God dwells. Gabriel adds a sign, her old relative Elizabeth expecting a child, “for nothing will be impossible with God.” And then the yes on which our salvation hung: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.” In that moment, says the Creed, he “was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man.” That is why we kneel today when we say those words. The Easter Church kneels before the beginning of everything she celebrates.
conn: Why 5 April?

The Universal Norms on the Liturgical Year (no. 60) do not allow a solemnity to be celebrated in Holy Week or the Octave of Easter. When 25 March falls in either, the Annunciation is transferred to the Monday after the Second Sunday of Easter, as in 2027 (25 March was Holy Thursday).
A feast of the Lord.

Since the reform of 1969 the Roman calendar names the day “the Annunciation of the Lord.” It celebrates the Incarnation of the Son, and at the same time Mary's willing consent; St Paul VI called it a joint feast of Christ and of the Virgin (Marialis Cultus 6).
Nine months.
25 March stands nine months before 25 December. Some early Christian writers also linked 25 March with the day of the Lord's death, so that conception and Passover belong together.
Almah and parthenos.

Isaiah 7:14 has the Hebrew almah, a young woman; the Greek Septuagint, made by Jewish translators before Christ, has parthenos, virgin. Matthew 1:23 quotes the Greek, and the Church confesses that the sign is fulfilled in the virginal conception of Jesus.
“Favored one.”

Greek kecharitomene, a perfect participle: one who has been graced and remains so. It is the angel's name for Mary, and a scriptural root of the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception (Catechism 490–491).
“Overshadow.”
The same verb as the cloud that rested on the tent of meeting when the glory of the Lord filled it (Exodus 40:35, Greek text). Mary is the new dwelling place of God.
The genuflection at the Creed.
Only on the Annunciation and on Christmas does the Missal direct all to genuflect at the words “and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man.” On other days we bow.
Angelus and Regina Caeli.

The Angelus prays the Annunciation every morning, noon and evening. In Eastertide it gives way to the Regina Caeli, which asks the Queen of Heaven to rejoice because the Son she bore has risen. Today the two prayers meet.
altar: The body prepared for the Son in Mary's womb is the body offered on the cross and given to us at this altar. The Church prays: “This is my Body,” and the Word made flesh is truly, really and substantially present, as truly as he was present in Nazareth.
Mary welcomed the Word first in faith and then in her womb. Before Communion we too can say her words: let it be with me according to your word.
outline: Opening
Ask: what has God asked of you lately, and what did you answer?
Point 1 · God is with us
Ahaz refuses a sign; God gives one anyway.
Point 2 · A body you have prepared
The Son's yes before Mary's yes.
Point 3 · Here am I, the servant
Mary's faith, willing and whole.
Point 4 · And became man
Why we kneel at the Creed, and why in Easter.
Closing image
A young woman alone in a small house, an angel, and the silence before the yes.
Take-home line
“Let it be with me according to your word.”
live: Pray the Regina Caeli today
At noon, pray the Regina Caeli slowly; then read Luke 1:26–38 and remember that the risen Lord was once a child in Mary's womb.
Kneel with meaning
At Mass today kneel at “and became man” with your whole heart; at home, teach the children why.
Say your own “Here am I”
Name one thing God is asking of you that you have postponed, and say yes to it today.
Honour unborn life
The Word was a hidden child for nine months. Pray today for mothers expecting a child, and help one in a practical way.
fathers: St Irenaeus (in substance)
The knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary; what the virgin Eve bound by unbelief, the Virgin Mary untied by faith.
St Augustine (in substance)
Mary conceived Christ first in her heart by faith before she conceived him in her body. Her motherhood would have profited her nothing had she not first carried him blessedly in her mind.
St Bernard of Clairvaux (in substance)

The angel waits for your answer, O Virgin, and the whole world waits with him, kneeling at your feet: Adam and all his children in exile. Speak the word, receive the Word; say yes, and open the door to the Creator.
magis: Catechism 484–486
The Annunciation: the fullness of time, the Holy Spirit and the conception of the Son.
Catechism 490–494
Mary full of grace; her “Fiat” as the obedience of faith.
Catechism 496–498
The virginal conception of Jesus, a work of God beyond human understanding.
Lumen Gentium 56
Mary, consenting to the divine Word, became the Mother of Jesus and devoted herself wholly to the person and work of her Son.
Redemptoris Mater 13 (St John Paul II, 1987)
At the Annunciation Mary entrusted herself to God completely with the obedience of faith.
saints: The Blessed Virgin Mary
Daughter of Israel, of Nazareth in Galilee, engaged to Joseph of the house of David, chosen to be the Mother of God. Her yes at the Annunciation opened the way for the Incarnation of the Son.
This week
6–10 Apr: Easter weekdays of the Second Week. 7 Apr: St John Baptist de la Salle, memorial. 11 Apr: Third Sunday of Easter. St Vincent Ferrer (5 Apr) is not commemorated this year.
2027-04-05.prayer: O God, who willed that your Word should take on the reality of human flesh in the womb of the Virgin Mary, grant, we pray, that we, who confess our Redeemer to be God and man, may merit to become partakers even in his divine nature. Who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, Word made flesh, you entered our world through the yes of your Mother and rose from the dead in the same flesh you took from her. Give us her faith, that we may hear your word and keep it, and her courage, that we may say each day: let it be with me according to your word. Holy Mary, Mother of God, rejoice, for your Son has risen. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-06.title: Tuesday of the Second Week of Easter
readings: The community of believers was of one heart and soul
The Lord is king; he is robed in majesty (or: Alleluia)
No one has gone up to heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man
2027-04-06.alt: Easter weekday of the Second Week of Easter. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-06.verse: And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.
theo: St Luke paints a second portrait of the first community in Jerusalem: “the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common.” This is not a political programme; it is what the Resurrection does to people. In the middle of the passage Luke places its source: “With great power the apostles gave their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.” Because Christ is risen, nobody needs to cling to land or money as if this life were everything. The result echoes the promise of Deuteronomy, “there will be no one in need among you”: “There was not a needy person among them.” Luke then introduces a man we will meet again and again, a Levite from Cyprus called Joseph, whom the apostles nicknamed Barnabas, “son of encouragement.” He sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet. Before Barnabas ever preaches a sermon, he gives. The Psalm crowns the risen Christ as king: “The LORD is king, he is robed in majesty.”

The Gospel continues the night conversation with Nicodemus, a teacher of Israel who came to Jesus in the dark. Jesus has told him that he must be born from above, of water and the Spirit, and Nicodemus cannot grasp it: “How can these things be?” Jesus answers with an image from the wind, which in Greek is the same word as Spirit: “The wind blows where it chooses, and you hear the sound of it, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” The newly baptized of Easter are exactly this: people born again, whose new life comes from a source the world cannot see. Then Jesus points to the cross. In the desert, when serpents were biting the people, Moses lifted a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived. “So must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.” In John's Gospel “lifted up” means both the cross and the glory: the Son is raised on the wood and raised to the Father. Nicodemus does not understand tonight; but at the end of the Gospel he will come back in daylight, carrying a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes, to bury the One who was lifted up. The Spirit had been blowing in him all along.
outline: Opening
Ask: what would change in our parish if we really believed Christ is risen?
Point 1 · One heart and soul
The Resurrection makes a family that shares.
Point 2 · Born of the Spirit
The wind we cannot see but can hear.
Point 3 · Lifted up
Look at the cross and live; Nicodemus comes back.
Take-home line
“Whoever believes in him may have eternal life.”
live: Be a Barnabas today (Acts 4:36)
Encourage one person by name today: a text, a visit, a word of thanks that lifts them up.
Look at the Crucified (John 3:14)
Spend three minutes before a crucifix and tell the Lord what is biting you; ask to be healed.
2027-04-06.prayer: Lord God, King robed in majesty, you raised your Son and lifted him up to your right hand. Pour out on us the Spirit who blows where he wills, and make us one heart and one soul, generous with what we have, encouraging to one another, and steady in our witness to the Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The Son lifted up on the cross is made present on the altar, and at the elevation we look up at him as Israel looked at the serpent, and live. From the one Bread comes one heart and one soul.

2027-04-07.title: St John Baptist de la Salle, priest (memorial)
readings: The men you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people
The Lord hears the cry of the poor (or: Alleluia)
God sent his Son that the world might be saved through him
2027-04-07.alt: Memorial of St John Baptist de la Salle, priest, founder of the Brothers of the Christian Schools and patron of teachers. The readings are those of Wednesday of the Second Week of Easter; the collect is proper to the saint. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-07.verse: Indeed, God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.
theo: The apostles have been healing and teaching in Solomon's Portico, and the crowds are growing. The high priest and the Sadducees, “filled with jealousy,” arrest them and lock them in the public prison. But at night “an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out, and said, ‘Go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life.’” The angel does not send them to safety; he sends them straight back to the place where they were arrested. At daybreak they are teaching again. Luke tells the rest almost with a smile: the council meets, the guards are sent, and they report a prison “securely locked” with the guards at the doors and nobody inside. The authorities are perplexed; the captain fetches the apostles “without violence,” afraid of the people. The same Lord who left the tomb sealed and empty opens the prison of his witnesses. Luke is describing a struggle with particular leaders of the Temple in that hour, not with the Jewish people, who in this very scene hold the apostles in honour. The Psalm sings what the apostles had just lived: “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.”

The Gospel gives us perhaps the best known verse of the Bible: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” And the next verse tells us what kind of love it is: “God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.” Judgment is not God's wish; it is what happens when people prefer darkness to light, “because their deeds were evil.” Today the Church remembers a man who spent his life bringing light to children who lived in darkness: St John Baptist de la Salle (1651–1719). Born into a wealthy family in Reims, a canon of the cathedral at sixteen and a priest at twenty-seven, he was drawn almost against his will into helping a few poor schoolmasters. Step by step he took them into his own house, gave away his fortune to the hungry in the famine of 1684, resigned his canonry and founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools, lay religious devoted entirely to teaching the poor without fees. He taught in French instead of Latin, grouped pupils in classes, opened schools for working youths on Sundays and trained teachers in what were among the first teacher-training colleges. He met lawsuits, slander and opposition even from churchmen, and he died on Good Friday, 7 April 1719. He was canonized in 1900, and in 1950 Pius XII named him patron of all teachers. He used to tell his Brothers, in substance, that they could work miracles by touching the hearts of the children entrusted to them: that is John 3:17 in a classroom.
outline: Opening
Ask: who was the teacher who opened a door for you?
Point 1 · Doors opened by night
The prison cannot hold the witnesses.
Point 2 · Not to condemn but to save
God's love and our choice of light.
Point 3 · Touching hearts
St John Baptist de la Salle, patron of teachers.
Take-home line
“God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world.”
live: Thank a teacher (Acts 5:20)
Call or write to a teacher who shaped your life, and pray for him or her today; if you teach, offer your work to God for each pupil by name.
Come to the light (John 3:21)
Bring one hidden thing into the light this week, in confession or in an honest conversation.
saints: St John Baptist de la Salle (1651–1719)

Priest of Reims, founder of the Brothers of the Christian Schools (De La Salle Brothers), pioneer of schools for the poor without fees, of teaching in the mother tongue and of teacher training. Canonized 1900; patron of teachers (1950).
2027-04-07.prayer: O God, who chose Saint John Baptist de la Salle to educate young people in the Christian life, raise up teachers in your Church ready to devote themselves with all zeal to the human and Christian formation of the young. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Lord, you so loved the world that you gave your only Son: open the prisons of fear in us, and send us back to tell the whole message of this life. Amen.
altar: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, and the Son gives himself again in the Eucharist. He comes not to condemn but to save; we approach the altar to come into the light.

2027-04-08.title: Thursday of the Second Week of Easter
readings: We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit
The Lord hears the cry of the poor (or: Alleluia)
The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands
2027-04-08.alt: Easter weekday of the Second Week of Easter. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-08.verse: He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.
theo: The apostles, brought back from the Temple, stand before the council. The high priest reminds them: “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name.” He will not even say the name of Jesus. Peter and the apostles answer with a sentence that has given courage to believers in every century: “We must obey God rather than any human authority.” This is not a contempt for authority, which the apostles will later teach Christians to respect; it is the freedom of conscience before God when a human command forbids what God commands. Then Peter proclaims the Easter message once more: “The God of our ancestors raised up Jesus… God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior that he might give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins.” Notice the purpose of his preaching: not accusation but forgiveness, offered first to Israel, the people of the promise. The Church teaches that the responsibility for the Passion cannot be laid on the Jews of that time as a whole, still less on the Jews of today, and that all of us sinners share in it (Catechism 597–598). And Peter adds a second witness beside the apostles: “And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit whom God has given to those who obey him.” The Spirit does not replace our witness; he speaks with it.

The Gospel closes the third chapter of St John with a meditation on the one who comes from above. John the Baptist has just said that he must decrease; now the evangelist explains why. “The one who comes from above is above all.” He does not speak second-hand; “he testifies to what he has seen and heard.” Whoever accepts his testimony “has certified this, that God is true,” like a man who puts his seal on a document. Then a phrase of great richness: “He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.” The prophets received the Spirit by measure, for a time and a task; the Son receives and gives him without limit. “The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands.” Everything the Father has is in the hands that were pierced and are now risen. The chapter ends with a choice: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.” The apostles in the council are living that choice. They have believed, they have received the Spirit, and so, before a powerful court, they can speak the words of God.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last have to choose between pleasing people and pleasing God?
Point 1 · Obey God rather than men
Conscience and courage before the council.
Point 2 · Witnesses with the Spirit
Forgiveness offered, not blame.
Point 3 · The Spirit without measure
All things in the Son's hands.
Take-home line
“We must obey God rather than any human authority.”
live: Speak when it matters (Acts 5:29)
Where you are tempted today to stay silent about what is right, say one clear and gentle word of truth.
Pray for the Spirit (John 3:34)
Pray the Come, Holy Spirit each morning between now and Pentecost.
2027-04-08.prayer: God of our ancestors, you raised up Jesus and exalted him at your right hand as Leader and Saviour. Give us the courage of the apostles to obey you rather than any human voice that would silence your truth, and pour out on us without measure the Spirit of your Son, that we may be faithful witnesses of his Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The Father has placed all things in the Son's hands, and in the Eucharist those risen hands give us his very self. The Spirit called down on the gifts makes them his Body and Blood, and makes us his witnesses.

2027-04-09.title: Friday of the Second Week of Easter
readings: They rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name
One thing I seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord (or: Alleluia)
He distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted
2027-04-09.alt: Easter weekday of the Second Week of Easter. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. Friday: keep the Friday penance as your bishops' conference directs.
2027-04-09.verse: Then Jesus took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated; so also the fish, as much as they wanted.
theo: The council is enraged and wants to put the apostles to death. Then one man stands up: Gamaliel, “a Pharisee in the council… a teacher of the law, respected by all the people.” He is the teacher at whose feet Saul of Tarsus was trained, and later Jewish tradition honours him as one of the great masters of the Law. He has the apostles sent out and gives the council a lesson in patience drawn from recent history: Theudas and Judas the Galilean both gathered followers and both came to nothing. “So in the present case, I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone; because if this plan or this undertaking is of human origin, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them.” Gamaliel is not a Christian, but he is a just man who fears God, and his counsel saves the apostles' lives. The Church has been grateful to him ever since; a later Christian legend even counted him among the friends of the first disciples. The apostles are flogged and released, and Luke records the astonishing reaction: “they rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name. And every day in the temple and at home they did not cease to teach and proclaim Jesus as the Messiah.” The Psalm is their song: “The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

From today until the end of the Third Week of Easter the weekday Gospels walk through the sixth chapter of St John, the great chapter of the Bread of Life. It begins with a sign. “The Passover, the festival of the Jews, was near,” John notes, and a large crowd follows Jesus up the mountain by the Sea of Galilee. Jesus tests Philip: “Where are we to buy bread for these people to eat?” Philip calculates: six months' wages would not be enough. Andrew finds “a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what are they among so many people?” Barley loaves were the bread of the poor, and they recall the prophet Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves. Jesus has the people sit on the green grass; then he “took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them.” The Greek word for giving thanks is eucharistein. The evangelist wants us to see the Eucharist in this meal, celebrated near the Passover. After all have eaten “as much as they wanted,” Jesus says: “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost,” and twelve baskets are filled. The Church still treats every fragment of the consecrated Host with that same care. When the crowd tries to seize him and make him king, Jesus withdraws alone to the mountain. He will not be a king who only hands out bread; he will be the King who gives his own flesh as bread.
outline: Opening
Ask: what small thing do you have that Jesus could multiply?
Point 1 · If it is of God
Gamaliel's wise counsel.
Point 2 · Worthy to suffer for the name
Joy under the lash.
Point 3 · Five loaves and twelve baskets
The sign of the Bread, near Passover.
Take-home line
“Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
live: Offer your five loaves (John 6:9)
Give Jesus one small gift today, an hour, a talent, a sum of money, and let him use it for others.
Waste nothing (John 6:12)
Do not waste food today; share leftovers with someone who needs them, or give the price of one meal to the poor.
2027-04-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you fed the multitude with five barley loaves and gave thanks to the Father for the bread. Give us the wisdom of Gamaliel to recognize the work of God, the joy of the apostles in suffering for your name, and the generosity of the boy who gave you all he had. Feed us with the Bread of Life, and let nothing of your gifts be lost. Who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks and distributed them. At every Mass he does the same, and the bread he gives is no longer bread but his Body. Like the disciples gathering the fragments, the Church reverences every particle of the consecrated Host.

2027-04-10.title: Saturday of the Second Week of Easter
readings: They chose seven men full of the Holy Spirit
Lord, let your mercy be on us, as we place our trust in you (or: Alleluia)
They saw Jesus walking on the sea
2027-04-10.alt: Easter weekday of the Second Week of Easter. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel; the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-10.verse: But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”
theo: The young Church has its first internal crisis, and it is about food and fairness. The disciples are increasing in number, and “the Hellenists complained against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution of food.” The Hellenists were Jewish believers who spoke Greek and had come from the lands of the dispersion; the Hebrews spoke Aramaic and belonged to the land. Two cultures in one community, and the poorest, the widows, were falling between them. The apostles do not ignore the complaint or blame anyone. They call the whole community together and propose a solution: “select from among yourselves seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom,” to serve the tables, “while we, for our part, will devote ourselves to prayer and to serving the word.” All seven chosen have Greek names: the community entrusts the care of the neglected to people from the neglected group. The apostles pray and lay their hands on them. The Church has long seen in this scene the beginnings of the diaconate, a ministry of service ordained by the laying on of hands (Catechism 1569–1571). And the result: “The word of God continued to spread… and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.” A problem honestly faced became a moment of growth.

In the Gospel, after the feeding of the five thousand, the disciples go down to the sea in the evening and set out by boat for Capernaum. John adds a quiet, heavy sentence: “It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.” The sea becomes rough with a strong wind. They have rowed three or four miles when they see Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, “and they were terrified.” Then he speaks: “It is I; do not be afraid.” In Greek it is simply ego eimi, I AM, the name God revealed to Moses at the burning bush. The One who multiplied the loaves is the Lord of creation who walks on the chaos of the waters, as the Psalms say only God can do. When they want to take him into the boat, “immediately the boat reached the land toward which they were going.” The Church has often been pictured as a boat on a dark sea. Today's two readings belong together: in the first, the boat of the Church meets a storm from within, quarrels and neglect; in the second, a storm from outside. In both, the risen Lord comes across the water and says the same words: It is I; do not be afraid.
outline: Opening
Ask: what storm is your family or your parish rowing through right now?
Point 1 · The widows who were forgotten
A complaint heard and a problem solved.
Point 2 · Prayer, the word, and service
The seven and the apostles.
Point 3 · It is I; do not be afraid
The Lord walks on the dark sea.
Take-home line
“It is I; do not be afraid.”
live: Notice who is forgotten (Acts 6:1)
Visit or phone an elderly widow or widower in your parish today, or ask how the parish can help them.
Say his name in the storm (John 6:20)
When fear rises today, stop and pray: Jesus, it is you; I will not be afraid.
2027-04-10.prayer: Lord Jesus, you walked on the stormy sea and said to your frightened disciples: It is I; do not be afraid. Come to us in every storm, from within and from without. Give your Church ministers full of the Spirit and of wisdom, who will care for the forgotten, and keep our pastors faithful to prayer and the service of the word. Let your mercy be on us, as we place our trust in you. Who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: The Lord who walks on the waters comes to us in the Eucharist and says: It is I. At the altar, deacon and priest serve the one Bread and the one Word, and the boat of the Church is brought safely to the shore.

2027-04-12.title: Monday of the Third Week of Easter
readings: They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which Stephen spoke; his face was like the face of an angel
Blessed are they who follow the law of the Lord! (or: Alleluia)
Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life
2027-04-12.alt: Easter weekday. The Alleluia sounds again at the Gospel acclamation; the Paschal candle is lit at the liturgy until Pentecost; the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus. All this week the Gospel is the Bread of Life discourse of John 6. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-12.verse: Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you.
theo: Stephen first appears in the Acts of the Apostles as a man chosen to wait on tables. The Twelve had asked the community to pick seven men “of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom” to care for the daily distribution of food to the widows, so that the apostles could give themselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word. Stephen's name stands first on the list. But today we see that the man appointed to serve bread is also a man of the word: “full of grace and power,” he “did great wonders and signs among the people.” Members of the synagogue of the Freedmen, Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia, begin to argue with him, and “they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke.” When argument fails, accusation begins. False witnesses are brought: “This man never stops saying things against this holy place and the law.” St Luke tells the story so that we hear the trial of Jesus again; there too false witnesses spoke about the Temple (Mark 14:57–58). The disciple is walking the road of his Master. And at the very moment of accusation Luke gives us one quiet, luminous line: all who sat in the council looked at him, “and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.” The man accused of speaking against Moses carries the radiance of Moses, whose face shone when he came down from Sinai after speaking with God. The Psalm gives us Stephen's inner prayer: “Even though princes sit plotting against me, your servant will meditate on your statutes.” The quarrel here is a family quarrel among Jews, for Stephen is himself a Jew; Luke does not blame a whole people, and neither does the Church (Catechism 597).

The Gospel takes us to the morning after the feeding of the five thousand. The crowd has noticed that Jesus did not get into the boat with his disciples, so they take boats from Tiberias and cross to Capernaum looking for him. “Rabbi, when did you come here?” Jesus does not answer the question; he answers the heart: “you are looking for me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.” They had seen bread; they had not seen the sign. They wanted another meal, not the One who gives it. So Jesus lifts their eyes: “Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you.” They reply like good, practical people: “What must we do to perform the works of God?” They expect a list. Jesus gives them one word: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.” Faith is both God's work in us and our first work for God; every good deed grows out of it. Through this whole week the Church reads the great discourse on the Bread of Life, step by step, and in the Easter season we read it with the eyes of the newly baptized, who have just received the Eucharist for the first time. Stephen served the bread that perishes to hungry widows and preached the bread that endures. The Church still does both, and both are the work of love.
outline: Opening
Ask: why do I look for Jesus? For what he gives, or for himself?
Point 1 · A face like an angel
Stephen, calm and radiant under false accusation.
Point 2 · Bread seen, sign missed
The crowd wanted loaves, not the Giver.
Point 3 · The one work God asks
Believe in him whom he has sent.
Take-home line
“Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures for eternal life.”
live: Work for the food that endures (John 6:27)
Give ten unhurried minutes today to the food that lasts: read John 6:22–40 slowly, or make a short visit to the Blessed Sacrament.
Meet hostility with peace
If someone speaks unfairly about you today, do not answer in kind. Stay calm like Stephen, and pray for that person by name.
2027-04-12.prayer: Lord Jesus, risen from the dead, you filled your servant Stephen with grace and power and made his face shine before his accusers. Deliver us from seeking you only for the bread that perishes. Give us the faith that is your own work in us, and feed us with the bread that endures for eternal life, until we see your face in glory. Amen. Alleluia.
altar: The crowd wanted more loaves; Jesus wanted to give himself. At the altar he gives the food that endures for eternal life: his own Body and Blood, truly present under the appearances of bread and wine, set apart by the Father's seal.

2027-04-13.title: Tuesday of the Third Week of Easter
readings: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Lord, do not hold this sin against them
Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit (or: Alleluia)
It was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven; my Father gives you the true bread from heaven
2027-04-13.alt: Easter weekday. The Alleluia sounds again at the Gospel acclamation; the Paschal candle is lit at the liturgy until Pentecost; the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus. All this week the Gospel is the Bread of Life discourse of John 6. Liturgical colour: white. Optional memorial of St Martin I, pope and martyr (if it is kept, the vestments are red).
2027-04-13.verse: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
theo: Yesterday we saw Stephen accused; today we see him die. At the end of a long speech in which he retells the whole history of Israel, from Abraham to Solomon's Temple, Stephen speaks with the burning voice of the prophets: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you are forever opposing the Holy Spirit.” These are hard words, but they are the words Moses and the prophets themselves had used in calling their own people back to God (Exodus 33:5; Jeremiah 9:26). Stephen speaks as a son of Israel to his brothers, not as an outsider passing judgment on a nation, and the Church reads his words in that light (Nostra Aetate 4). His hearers are enraged and grind their teeth. But Stephen stands firm: “filled with the Holy Spirit, he gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.” Elsewhere the risen Christ is seated at the Father's right hand; here he stands, as if rising to welcome his first witness, or standing as advocate for the one who is being condemned. They drag Stephen out of the city and stone him, and the witnesses lay their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. Stephen's last two prayers are an echo of the cross: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,” and then, on his knees, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Luke ends gently: “When he had said this, he died”; the Greek says he “fell asleep.” The Psalm is the prayer Jesus himself made his own on the cross: “Into your hand I commit my spirit.” And the last line of the reading quietly opens the next chapter of the story: “And Saul approved of their killing him.” Stephen prayed for his killers, and one of them would become the Apostle of the nations.

In the Gospel the crowd that has eaten the loaves now asks Jesus for a sign: “What sign are you going to give us then, so that we may see it and believe you?” They remind him of the great sign of the desert: “Our ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” Jesus corrects them gently: it was not Moses who gave that bread, “but it is my Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” The crowd, like the Samaritan woman at the well asking for living water, says: “Sir, give us this bread always.” And Jesus answers with one of the great sayings of the Gospel: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.” The manna fed bodies for a day and spoiled by morning; Jesus is bread that gives the life of God and does not spoil. Today the Church also remembers St Martin I, pope from 649 to 655. He defended the truth, against the emperor's policy, that Christ has a true human will as well as his divine will, freely united to the will of the Father. For this he was arrested in Rome, taken to Constantinople, humiliated and condemned, and exiled to the Crimea, where he died in 655 of hunger and hardship. In his letters from exile he wrote of being short of bread. Deprived of the bread that perishes, he lived on the bread of life, and the Church honours him as a martyr.
outline: Opening
Ask: what would my last words be, if I knew they were my last?
Point 1 · The heavens opened
Stephen sees the Son of Man standing for him.
Point 2 · Do not hold this sin against them
A martyr's prayer that bore fruit in Saul.
Point 3 · I am the bread of life
The true bread from heaven.
St Martin I
Hungry in exile, faithful to the truth about Christ.
Take-home line
“Whoever comes to me will never be hungry.”
live: Pray Stephen's prayer (Acts 7:60)
Name one person who has hurt you and pray slowly: Lord, do not hold this sin against them.
Commend your spirit
Before sleeping tonight, pray Psalm 31:5: Into your hand I commit my spirit.
2027-04-13.prayer: Lord Jesus, standing at the right hand of the Father, you received the spirit of your servant Stephen and heard his prayer for those who killed him. Give us his forgiving heart, the courage of St Martin your faithful pope, and an ever greater hunger for you, the true bread from heaven, who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen. Alleluia.
altar: The Father still gives the true bread from heaven. At every Mass Christ, who stood to receive Stephen, comes down upon the altar and gives himself as the bread of life, truly his Body, so that whoever comes to him will never be hungry.

2027-04-14.title: Wednesday of the Third Week of Easter
readings: Those who were scattered went from place to place, proclaiming the word; there was great joy in that city
Let all the earth cry out to God with joy (or: Alleluia)
This is the will of my Father, that all who see the Son and believe in him may have eternal life
2027-04-14.alt: Easter weekday. The Alleluia sounds again at the Gospel acclamation; the Paschal candle is lit at the liturgy until Pentecost; the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus. All this week the Gospel is the Bread of Life discourse of John 6. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-14.verse: This is indeed the will of my Father, that all who see the Son and believe in him may have eternal life; and I will raise them up on the last day.
theo: The day Stephen died, “a severe persecution began against the church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout the countryside of Judea and Samaria.” It looks like the end of the young Church. Devout men bury Stephen “and made loud lamentation over him”; Christian mourning is real mourning, even when it is full of hope. Saul goes from house to house, dragging off men and women to prison. And then St Luke writes one of the most hopeful sentences in the Acts of the Apostles: “Now those who were scattered went from place to place, proclaiming the word.” The persecution that was meant to stamp out the Church scatters it like seed. Before his Ascension the risen Lord had said: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The disciples had stayed in Jerusalem; now, through suffering, the word moves into Judea and Samaria exactly as he said. Tertullian would later write, in substance, that the blood of Christians is seed. Philip, one of the Seven like Stephen, goes down to a city of Samaria. Jews and Samaritans had kept apart for centuries (John 4:9), yet here “the crowds with one accord listened eagerly” to Philip; unclean spirits come out, the paralyzed and the lame are healed, “so there was great joy in that city.” The Psalm becomes the song of Samaria: “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth… Come and see what God has done.” Kerala knows this story well. Malayali Catholics scattered by work and need across the Gulf, Europe, America and every corner of India have often carried the faith with them and planted it where they went: a rosary group in a labour camp, a Malayalam Mass in a borrowed chapel, a family that keeps praying in a foreign city.

In the Gospel Jesus repeats the great word of yesterday, “I am the bread of life,” and then opens his heart about the will of his Father. “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and anyone who comes to me I will never drive away.” No one who comes to him is turned away: not the sinner, not the doubter, not the one who comes late. Then he speaks of his own obedience: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Here we glimpse the mystery St Martin I defended: the Son made man has a true human will, and he freely and lovingly makes it one with the Father's will (Catechism 475). And what is that will? “That I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.” Four times in this chapter Jesus says “I will raise them up on the last day.” The Easter faith is not a vague survival of the soul; it is the resurrection of the body, our own bodies raised and glorified like his. And the Bread of Life is bound to that promise: those who receive the Eucharist receive, as the Catechism says, a pledge of future glory (Catechism 1402–1405). This is the hope with which the devout men buried Stephen, and the hope with which the Church buries her children still: the Lord who feeds us will not lose us.
outline: Opening
Ask: what good has God brought out of a time when my life was scattered?
Point 1 · Scattered like seed
Persecution carries the word to Samaria.
Point 2 · Great joy in that city
Philip among the Samaritans.
Point 3 · I will never drive away
Anyone who comes to Jesus is received.
Point 4 · Raised on the last day
The Father's will: lose nothing.
Take-home line
“I will raise them up on the last day.”
live: Bloom where you are scattered (Acts 8:4)
If you live away from home, find one way this week to share the faith where you are: invite a fellow migrant to Mass, or start a short family prayer.
Come without fear (John 6:37)
Bring to Jesus today the thing you are most ashamed of. He has promised not to drive you away; go to confession if you need to.
2027-04-14.prayer: Lord Jesus, bread of life, you turned the scattering of your Church into the spreading of your word, and you fill whole cities with joy. Receive all who come to you, lose none of those the Father has given you, and raise us up on the last day to see your face. Amen. Alleluia.
altar: The Father wills that none be lost. In the Eucharist the risen Lord gives us his own glorified Body as the pledge of our resurrection: the one who feeds us now will raise us up on the last day.

2027-04-15.title: Thursday of the Third Week of Easter
readings: Look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized?
Let all the earth cry out to God with joy (or: Alleluia)
I am the living bread that came down from heaven
2027-04-15.alt: Easter weekday. The Alleluia sounds again at the Gospel acclamation; the Paschal candle is lit at the liturgy until Pentecost; the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus. All this week the Gospel is the Bread of Life discourse of John 6. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-15.verse: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.
theo: Philip has just seen a whole city rejoice. Now an angel sends him somewhere very different: “Get up and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” Luke adds: “This is a wilderness road.” God sends the evangelist away from the crowd to one man. On the road is an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of the Candace, the queen of the Ethiopians, in charge of her whole treasury. In the Bible “Ethiopia” means the ancient kingdom of Kush, south of Egypt, in today's Sudan; for the people of Jerusalem it was the edge of the known world. This powerful man has travelled well over a thousand kilometres to worship in Jerusalem, and now, seated in his chariot, he is reading the prophet Isaiah aloud, as people did in the ancient world. The Spirit says: “Go over to this chariot and join it.” Philip runs, hears the words, and asks the simple question that begins so many conversions: “Do you understand what you are reading?” The answer is humble and honest: “How can I, unless someone guides me?” The passage is Isaiah's song of the Servant: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer.” “About whom, may I ask you, does the prophet say this?” And Philip, “starting with this scripture,” proclaims to him the good news of Jesus. They come to water, and the man cries out: “Look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized?” By the old law a eunuch could not enter the assembly of the Lord (Deuteronomy 23:1), but Isaiah had promised that God would give faithful eunuchs “a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:3–5). On a desert road that promise is kept. Philip baptizes him, the Spirit snatches Philip away, and the Ethiopian “went on his way rejoicing.” Ancient tradition, cherished in Ethiopia, honours him as one of the first to carry the Gospel to Africa, and the whole Church sees in this story the pattern of Christian initiation: the Scriptures opened, Christ proclaimed, faith, Baptism, and joy.

In the Gospel Jesus says something that should make us humble: “No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me.” Faith is never simply our achievement. St Augustine says, in substance, that the Father draws us not by force but by delight, as a branch held out draws a sheep, or as a child is drawn by the sight of what it loves. The Father drew the Ethiopian through his love of the Scriptures; he draws us too, often through someone who sits beside us and explains. Jesus quotes Isaiah: “And they shall all be taught by God.” Then he speaks in the present tense: “whoever believes has eternal life.” Eternal life begins now. And then the discourse turns a corner. “Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.” “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.” The word “flesh” is the same word St John used for the Incarnation: “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). The bread Jesus will give is not a symbol of his flesh; it is his flesh, given “for the life of the world,” that is, offered on the cross. The Eucharist makes present that one sacrifice of Calvary (Catechism 1366–1367). The Ethiopian was reading of a lamb led to the slaughter; at every Mass we receive that Lamb, the living bread who was slain and lives for ever.
outline: Opening
Ask: who sat beside me and helped me understand the faith?
Point 1 · A wilderness road
God sends the evangelist to one seeker.
Point 2 · How can I, unless someone guides me?
The Scriptures opened.
Point 3 · Look, here is water
Baptism, and a promise kept to the excluded.
Point 4 · The living bread
My flesh for the life of the world.
Take-home line
“Whoever eats of this bread will live forever.”
live: Sit beside someone (Acts 8:31)
Offer to read the Sunday Gospel this week with a child, a godchild or a new Catholic, and explain it simply.
Thank God for your guide
Pray today for the catechist, parent or priest who first opened the Scriptures to you.
2027-04-15.prayer: Father, you sent Philip down the desert road to one seeking heart, and you draw us to your Son by the delight of your love. Open the Scriptures to us, renew in us the joy of our Baptism, and feed us with the living bread, the flesh of Christ given for the life of the world, who lives and reigns with you for ever and ever. Amen. Alleluia.
altar: The Ethiopian read of the Lamb led to the slaughter. On the altar that same Lamb, risen and living, gives us his flesh for the life of the world. This is not a sign of something absent: it is Christ himself, the living bread from heaven.

2027-04-16.title: Friday of the Third Week of Easter
readings: He is an instrument whom I have chosen to bring my name before Gentiles and kings and before the people of Israel
Go out to all the world and tell the Good News (or: Alleluia)
My flesh is true food and my blood is true drink
2027-04-16.alt: Easter weekday. The Alleluia sounds again at the Gospel acclamation; the Paschal candle is lit at the liturgy until Pentecost; the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus. All this week the Gospel is the Bread of Life discourse of John 6. Liturgical colour: white. Every Friday remains a day of penance (Code of Canon Law 1250–1251); follow the norms of your bishops' conference and diocese.
2027-04-16.verse: Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them.
theo: Saul last appeared holding the coats of the men who stoned Stephen and dragging believers from their homes. Today he is “still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord.” He asks the high priest for letters to the synagogues of Damascus, so that he may bring to Jerusalem in chains anyone “who belonged to the Way,” the earliest name for the followers of Jesus. Near Damascus “a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” Saul asks: “Who are you, Lord?” And the answer changes his life and should change ours: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Saul had never laid a hand on Jesus; he had persecuted his disciples. But the risen Lord says: you are persecuting me. Christ and his Church are one, as Head and Body (Catechism 795); what is done to the least of his members is done to him. Saul gets up blind. For three days he neither eats nor drinks, as if he too must pass through a kind of death and burial before rising. Then the Lord calls Ananias, an ordinary disciple of Damascus, who is understandably afraid: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints.” But the Lord has his own plans: “he is an instrument whom I have chosen to bring my name before Gentiles and kings and before the people of Israel.” Ananias goes, lays his hands on the man who came to arrest him, and his first word is: “Brother Saul.” Something like scales falls from Saul's eyes; he is baptized, he eats, and at once he proclaims Jesus in the synagogues: “He is the Son of God.” Saul does not leave the God of Israel; he meets the risen Messiah of Israel's God, and spends the rest of his life proclaiming him. St Paul himself retells this story twice in Acts (22 and 26) and in his letters (Galatians 1:15–16; 1 Corinthians 15:8–10). The Psalm, the shortest in the Bible, sums up his new mission: “Praise the LORD, all you nations!”

In the Gospel the Bread of Life discourse reaches its most realistic words. When Jesus says that the bread he will give is his flesh, his hearers in the synagogue of Capernaum dispute among themselves: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” St John calls them “the Jews”; they are Jesus' own people, as he and all his disciples are, honestly puzzled by a hard saying, and the Church does not read such words as blame on the Jewish people (Catechism 597). What matters is that Jesus does not soften what he has said. He makes it stronger: “Very truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.” In verse 54 St John even uses a Greek verb that means to chew or munch, as if to close every escape into mere symbolism. “For my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink.” The fruit of this food is communion: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them.” And it is a sharing in the very life of the Trinity: “Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.” This is why the Church believes that in the Most Holy Eucharist “the body and blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ and, therefore, the whole Christ is truly, really, and substantially contained” (Catechism 1374). The two readings belong together. On the road to Damascus Jesus said: I am the one you are persecuting, because his disciples are his body. At the altar he says: this is my body, and he makes us his body by feeding us with it. St Augustine told the newly baptized, in substance: be what you see, and receive what you are.
outline: Opening
Ask: what would it take for God to stop me in my tracks?
Point 1 · Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
Christ one with his Church.
Point 2 · Brother Saul
Ananias, afraid but obedient.
Point 3 · True food and true drink
Jesus does not soften his words.
Point 4 · Abide in me
The Body of Christ given and received.
Take-home line
“Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them.”
live: Call someone brother (Acts 9:17)
Greet with real kindness today someone you have feared or avoided, as Ananias greeted Saul.
Receive what you are
At your next Holy Communion say a slow, believing Amen, and then serve one member of Christ's body who needs help.
2027-04-16.prayer: Lord Jesus, you stopped Saul on the road to Damascus, opened his eyes and made the persecutor an apostle. Turn our hearts to you, give us the courage of Ananias to call our enemies brothers and sisters, and let us so receive your true Body and Blood that we may abide in you and you in us, now and for ever. Amen. Alleluia.
altar: My flesh is true food and my blood is true drink. On the altar the bread and wine become, truly, really and substantially, the Body and Blood of Christ, with his soul and divinity. We do not receive a symbol; we receive him, and he makes us his body.

2027-04-17.title: Saturday of the Third Week of Easter
readings: Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Tabitha, get up
How shall I make a return to the Lord for all the good he has done for me? (or: Alleluia)
Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life
2027-04-17.alt: Easter weekday. The Alleluia sounds again at the Gospel acclamation; the Paschal candle is lit at the liturgy until Pentecost; the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus. All this week the Gospel is the Bread of Life discourse of John 6. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-17.verse: Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.
theo: After the storm, a calm. St Luke pauses to give a summary of the young Church: “Meanwhile the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and was built up. Living in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.” Saul has been converted; the persecution has eased; the Church breathes. Then Luke follows Peter as he goes “here and there among all the believers,” a shepherd visiting his flock. At Lydda, on the coastal plain, Peter finds Aeneas, “who had been bedridden for eight years, for he was paralyzed.” His words are brief and clear about who is acting: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; get up and make your bed!” Peter claims nothing for himself. The man gets up, and the whole region of Lydda and Sharon turns to the Lord. In nearby Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, in Greek Dorcas, both names meaning “gazelle,” has died. Luke describes her in one beautiful line: she “was devoted to good works and acts of charity.” When Peter arrives, the widows stand around him weeping, “showing tunics and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was with them.” Her charity speaks for her; the work of her hands is her eulogy. Peter sends everyone out, kneels and prays, then turns to the body: “Tabitha, get up.” In Aramaic his words are almost exactly the words Peter had heard Jesus say in the house of Jairus, “Talitha cum,” little girl, get up (Mark 5:41). Peter had been in that room; now he does what he saw his Master do. Tabitha opens her eyes and sits up; Peter gives her his hand. The Psalm sings our gratitude: “What shall I return to the LORD for all his bounty to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation,” and it reminds us that “precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his faithful ones.” The cup of salvation is lifted at every Mass.

In the Gospel the long discourse on the Bread of Life comes to its painful end. Many of the disciples say: “This teaching is difficult; who can accept it?” Jesus does not chase after them with an easier explanation. He asks: “Does this offend you? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?” And he adds: “It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh is useless. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” Jesus is not taking back what he said about his flesh as true food; he is saying that merely human reasoning, “the flesh” in that sense, cannot grasp this gift. Only the Spirit gives the faith to receive it. The Catechism notes that the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalized them: the Eucharist and the Cross are stumbling blocks (Catechism 1336). “Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.” Jesus lets them go rather than water down the truth. Then he turns to the Twelve with a question full of sorrow and freedom: “Do you also wish to go away?” And Simon Peter answers for all who have ever wanted to leave and stayed: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life. We have come to believe and know that you are the Holy One of God.” Peter does not say: we understand everything. He says: we know you. Faith is not first a solved problem but a trusted person. That same Peter, in today's first reading, raises the sick and the dead in the name of the Lord he refused to leave. Mary, the Mother of the Lord, is the first and most faithful of those who stayed; in this Easter season we greet her each day with joy: Queen of Heaven, rejoice, alleluia.
outline: Opening
Ask: have I ever wanted to walk away from the Church or from a hard teaching?
Point 1 · Jesus Christ heals you
Peter acts in the Lord's name, not his own.
Point 2 · Tabitha, get up
A life of charity, and the power of the risen Lord.
Point 3 · This teaching is difficult
Many turned back; Jesus did not water down the truth.
Point 4 · Lord, to whom can we go?
Faith as trust in a person.
Take-home line
“You have the words of eternal life.”
live: Leave a Tabitha legacy (Acts 9:36)
Do one hidden work of charity this week with your hands: mend, cook, sew or repair something for someone in need.
Stay with Jesus (John 6:68)
If a teaching of the faith troubles you, do not walk away: read what the Catechism says about it and talk it over with a priest.
2027-04-17.prayer: Lord Jesus, you healed Aeneas and raised Tabitha through the faith and prayer of Peter. When your words seem hard to us, keep us from turning back, give us your Spirit who gives life, and let us say with Peter and with all your faithful: Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life. Amen. Alleluia.
altar: Some turned away because Jesus said his flesh is true food. At the altar we stand with Peter and say: we have come to believe and know. We lift up the cup of salvation and receive the Holy One of God, truly present, the bread of eternal life.

2027-04-19.title: Monday of the Fourth Week of Easter
readings: God has given even to the Gentiles the repentance that leads to life
My soul thirsts for God, for the living God (or: Alleluia)
I am the gate for the sheep
2027-04-19.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia returns in the antiphons and the Gospel acclamation; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. In Years B and C the Gospel today is John 10:1–10; John 10:11–18 is read on this Monday only in Year A, when it is not the Sunday Gospel.
2027-04-19.verse: The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly.
theo: Peter comes back to Jerusalem from Caesarea and finds himself in trouble. The believers of Jewish birth have heard that he went into the house of Cornelius, a Roman centurion, and ate with uncircumcised men. To them this looks like a betrayal of everything God gave Israel: the Law, the food laws, the holy separation of God's people. Peter does not shout them down. He does not pull rank as the chief of the apostles. The text says he “began to explain it to them, step by step.” He tells them about the vision at Joppa: a large sheet let down from heaven, full of animals the Law called unclean, and a voice saying, “Get up, Peter; kill and eat.” He tells them his own reply, the reply of a faithful Jew: “By no means, Lord; for nothing profane or unclean has ever entered my mouth.” And he tells them what the voice said a second time: “What God has made clean, you must not call profane.”

Then Peter gives the decisive fact. While he was still speaking in Cornelius's house, “the Holy Spirit fell upon them just as it had upon us at the beginning.” It was a little Pentecost in a Gentile house. Peter remembered the word of the Lord: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” And he ends with a question that silences the room: “If then God gave them the same gift that he gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?” The objectors fall silent, and then they do something beautiful: they praise God. “Then God has given even to the Gentiles the repentance that leads to life.” This is a turning point in the history of the Church. The Gospel is not the property of one people or one culture. The door is open to all. And it was opened not by argument alone but by listening together to what God was doing. The Psalm puts the longing of every human heart into words: “My soul thirsts for God, for the living God.”

In the Gospel Jesus uses a picture every villager understood. At night the shepherds of a village brought their flocks into one walled fold with a single gate, and a gatekeeper watched it. In the morning each shepherd came to the gate and called, and his own sheep knew his voice and came out after him. Jesus says: “He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.” Then he changes the image and says something even more astonishing: “I am the gate.” There is one way in to safety and pasture, and it is Jesus himself. “Whoever enters by me will be saved, and will come in and go out and find pasture.” Thieves come to take; Jesus comes to give. “I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly.” The first reading and the Gospel belong together. The gate that Jesus is cannot be locked against anyone whom the Father calls. Peter learned in Cornelius's house that the gate stands open to the nations. The Church is the fold; Christ is its one gate; and the risen Shepherd still calls each of his sheep by name.
conn: Cornelius.
A centurion of the Italian Cohort stationed at Caesarea, “a devout man who feared God” (Acts 10:1–2). His baptism is told in Acts 10; today Peter retells it in his own words.
Joppa.
The port town, today Jaffa beside Tel Aviv, where Peter was staying at the house of Simon the tanner when he saw the vision (Acts 10:5–6).
The circumcised believers.
Christians of Jewish birth who still kept the Law faithfully. Their question was sincere: how can the holiness God gave Israel be kept if Jews and Gentiles eat together?
“Step by step.”
Luke's word (kathexēs) is the same word he uses in the preface of his Gospel for an orderly account (Luke 1:3). Peter does not argue; he tells what happened, in order.
The same gift.
The Spirit came on Cornelius's household before Baptism, so that no one could deny that God had accepted them. Peter then had them baptized (Acts 10:47–48).
The sheepfold.
A walled enclosure of stone, often shared by several flocks, with one opening. Some shepherds slept across the opening, so that the shepherd was himself the gate.
“Abundantly.”
The Greek perisson means more than enough, overflowing. Christ does not give a thin, careful life but a life that overflows.
Years B and C.
The Lectionary gives John 10:11–18 to this Monday only in Year A. In Years B and C, when it has already been read on Good Shepherd Sunday, John 10:1–10 is read instead.
altar: Jesus is the gate. At every Mass we come in through him: we are washed by his word, fed with his Body and Blood, and led out again to the pasture of daily life.

The Holy Spirit fell on Gentiles who were strangers to Israel. The same Spirit is called down on the bread and wine in the epiclesis, so that they become the Body and Blood of Christ, and on us, so that we become one body in him.
outline: Opening
Ask: who are the people I quietly keep outside the gate?
Point 1 · What God has made clean
Peter's vision at Joppa.
Point 2 · Who was I to hinder God?
The Spirit falls on Cornelius's house.
Point 3 · I am the gate
The Shepherd who calls by name and gives life in abundance.
Closing image
A stone sheepfold at dawn, a shepherd calling, and every sheep running out to him.
Take-home line
“I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly.”
live: Explain, do not attack
When someone in your family or parish disagrees with you, do as Peter did: explain step by step, calmly, what you have seen God do.
Open the gate
Think of one person you have written off as “not our kind.” Greet them, invite them, or pray for them by name today.
Listen for his voice
Spend five quiet minutes with John 10:1–10. Ask: when did I last hear the Shepherd call me by name?
Choose abundance
Notice the thieves of your life: the habits that steal joy and time. Give one of them up this week and give that time to the Lord.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
Christ is both the gate and the shepherd. He is the gate because through him we enter; he is the shepherd because he leads us.
St Gregory the Great (in substance)
He will go in by faith and go out by sight; he passes from believing to contemplating, and he finds pasture in the eternal feast.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
See how Peter answers his critics. He does not say, I am the leader; he tells the story from the beginning, and shows that it was God who led him, so that they are persuaded rather than overruled.
magis: Catechism 754
The Church is a sheepfold whose one and indispensable door is Christ.
Catechism 831
The Church is catholic because she is sent by Christ to the whole of the human race.
Lumen Gentium 13
All are called to belong to the new People of God, which takes nothing away from the riches of any people but purifies, strengthens and raises them up.
Evangelii Gaudium 47 (Pope Francis, 2013)
The Church is called to be the house of the Father, with doors always open.
Catechism 1287–1288
The gift of the Spirit promised to the Messiah and poured out on all the People of God.
saints: St Leo IX
Pope (1049–1054), a reformer who travelled tirelessly to renew the clergy and fight simony; he died on 19 April 1054. The Roman Martyrology commemorates him today.
This week
21 Apr: St Anselm (optional). 23 Apr: St George; St Adalbert (optional). 24 Apr: St Fidelis of Sigmaringen (optional). 25 Apr: Fifth Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-19.prayer: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd and gate of the sheep, you call each of us by name and you came that we may have life in abundance. Open our ears to your voice among all the voices of the world. Give your Church the courage of Peter, who would not hinder the work of the Holy Spirit, and the humility of those who listened to him and praised God. Keep the gate of our hearts open to every person you are calling, and lead us at last to the pasture of eternal life. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-20.title: Tuesday of the Fourth Week of Easter
readings: They spoke to the Hellenists also, proclaiming the Lord Jesus
All you nations, praise the Lord (or: Alleluia)
The Father and I are one
2027-04-20.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia returns in the antiphons and the Gospel acclamation; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-20.verse: My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish.
theo: After the martyrdom of Stephen a persecution broke out in Jerusalem, and many believers fled. What looked like a disaster became a sowing. Those who were scattered “traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch,” and wherever they went they spoke the word. At first they spoke only to fellow Jews. Then some men from Cyprus and Cyrene, whose names we do not even know, did something new at Antioch: they “spoke to the Hellenists also, proclaiming the Lord Jesus.” Here the word means Greek-speaking Gentiles. And “the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number became believers and turned to the Lord.” The first great mission to the Gentiles was not planned by a committee. It was begun by refugees who could not keep silent about Jesus.

The Church in Jerusalem sends Barnabas to see what is happening. Luke gives him one of the finest descriptions in the New Testament: “he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.” When he arrives, he does not look for faults. He “saw the grace of God” and “he rejoiced.” He encourages them to stay faithful. Then he does something humble and wise: he goes to Tarsus to fetch Saul, a converted persecutor whom many still feared, and brings him to Antioch. For a whole year they teach together. And “it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called ‘Christians.’” The name means “Christ's people,” the people who belong to the Anointed One. Antioch, a great city of many nations, became the mother church of the missions. The Psalm sings of Zion as the mother of all peoples: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God,” and of people from Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Ethiopia, it says, “This one was born there.” In the Church, every nation is born again.

The Gospel takes us to the Temple in winter, at the festival of the Dedication, the feast we know as Hanukkah, which remembers the rededication of the Temple after the Maccabees. Jesus is walking in the portico of Solomon. Some of the Temple crowd gather around him: “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.” Jesus answers that his works already speak. And then he gives one of the most consoling promises in the Gospel: “My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them out of my hand.” The security of the sheep does not rest on their strength but on the hand that holds them, and that hand is one with the Father's: “no one can snatch it out of the Father's hand. The Father and I are one.” At the feast that celebrated the dedication of the Temple, Jesus reveals himself as the true dwelling of God among us. The Church has always heard in these words the mystery of the Holy Trinity: the Son is one in being with the Father.
conn: The scattering.
The persecution that followed Stephen's death (Acts 8:1–4). Luke shows how God turns the flight of the believers into the spread of the word.
Phoenicia, Cyprus, Antioch.
The coast of present-day Lebanon, the island home of Barnabas (Acts 4:36), and Antioch on the Orontes in Syria, the third city of the Roman Empire after Rome and Alexandria.
Hellenists.
In Acts 6:1 the word means Greek-speaking Jews; here in Antioch, where the contrast is with “Jews” in verse 19, it means Greek-speaking Gentiles. Some ancient manuscripts read “Greeks.”
Barnabas.
Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles named Barnabas, “son of encouragement” (Acts 4:36). He sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet. His feast is 11 June.
“Christians.”
From Christos, Messiah, Anointed One. Probably first used by outsiders. St Ignatius, bishop of Antioch around 107, would write that he wanted not only to be called a Christian but to be found one.
The Dedication.
Hanukkah, in December, recalling the cleansing and rededication of the Temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). John alone mentions it.
“The Jews.”

In John's Gospel this phrase often refers to some Temple authorities and their followers who opposed Jesus, not to the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his Mother and the apostles were Jews. The Church firmly rejects any blame of the Jewish people for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597).
“One.”
In Greek the word is neuter: not one person, but one in being and in action. The Council of Nicaea (325) confessed the Son “consubstantial with the Father.”
altar: “No one will snatch them out of my hand.” In Holy Communion the hand of the Shepherd holds us most closely: he places himself in our hands and on our tongue, so that we may be held in his.
The first disciples to be called Christians were those who met for a whole year to be taught. The Mass is the school of Christians: the word explained, the Bread broken, the community gathered.
outline: Opening
Ask: what name do people give me, and does it say that I belong to Christ?
Point 1 · Scattered and sowing
Refugees who could not keep silent.
Point 2 · A good man, full of the Spirit
Barnabas sees grace and rejoices.
Point 3 · In the Father's hand
My sheep hear my voice.
Closing image
A shepherd's open hand, with a lamb resting in it, and another hand closed around it.
Take-home line
“No one will snatch them out of my hand.”
live: Speak where you are
If you have moved for work or study, to the Gulf, to Bengaluru, to Europe, see yourself as one of the scattered ones of Acts. Share your faith simply where you now live.
Be a Barnabas
Look for the grace of God in someone else's work this week and tell them so. Encouragement is a ministry.
Bring a Saul
Think of someone gifted but kept at a distance. Introduce them, include them, give them a chance to serve.
Rest in his hand
When you are anxious tonight, open your hand and pray: “No one will snatch me out of your hand, Lord.”
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Hear “one,” and be delivered from Arius, who denied that the Son is equal to the Father; hear “are,” and be delivered from Sabellius, who denied that the Father and the Son are distinct. The Father and I are one: one in substance, yet truly two persons.
St Ignatius of Antioch (in substance)
It is right not only to be called Christians but to be Christians in truth. Christianity is not a matter of persuasive words but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Barnabas came, saw, and rejoiced; he was not jealous that the work had begun without him. This is the mark of a good man: to be glad at the good done by others.
magis: Catechism 253–254
The Trinity is one: the divine persons do not share the one divinity among themselves, but each is God whole and entire; and they are really distinct from one another.
Catechism 242
The Council of Nicaea confessed the Son consubstantial with the Father.
Ad Gentes 2
The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature.
Nostra Aetate 4
The Church rejects any charge against the Jewish people as a whole for the death of Christ and decries every form of antisemitism.
Catechism 1289
The name “Christian” means “anointed” and comes from the name of Christ himself.
saints: St Agnes of Montepulciano

Dominican prioress in Tuscany (died 20 April 1317), known for her prayer, her love of poverty and her gift of peace-making. St Catherine of Siena made a pilgrimage to her tomb. The Roman Martyrology commemorates her today.
This week
21 Apr: St Anselm. 23 Apr: St George; St Adalbert. 24 Apr: St Fidelis. 25 Apr: Fifth Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-20.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Good Shepherd, one with the Father, you know your sheep and give them eternal life, and no one can snatch them out of your hand. Make us worthy of the name Christian, which we have received from you. Give us the courage of the scattered disciples who spoke of you wherever they went, and the generous heart of Barnabas, who rejoiced to see your grace at work in others. Keep us in your hand in every danger, and bring us at last into the joy of the Father, with whom you live and reign in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-21.title: Wednesday of the Fourth Week of Easter · St Anselm
readings: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul
O God, let all the nations praise you! (or: Alleluia)
I have come as light into the world
2027-04-21.alt: Optional memorial: St Anselm, bishop and doctor of the Church (1033–1109). The Easter weekday readings are kept. Regina Caeli at noon until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-21.verse: I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.
