theo: “The word of God continued to advance and gain adherents.” With this short line Luke closes the story of King Herod Agrippa, who had killed James and imprisoned Peter, and who then died miserably. Kings rise and fall; the word goes on. Then the scene moves to Antioch, where the Church has grown rich in gifts. Luke names five “prophets and teachers”: Barnabas from Cyprus, Simeon called Niger, which means “the black,” Lucius of Cyrene in North Africa, Manaen who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul of Tarsus. An African, a Cypriot, a man of the royal court, a former persecutor: already the Church is a gathering of nations and classes. And it is while they are at prayer that the Spirit speaks: “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’”

The first great missionary journey is born in the liturgy. The word Luke uses for “worshiping” is the word from which we get “liturgy.” The Church did not choose missionaries by vote or by talent; it fasted, prayed, listened, and then obeyed. “Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.” And Luke adds: “being sent out by the Holy Spirit.” The community lays on hands; the Spirit sends. The two go down to the port of Seleucia, sail to Cyprus, and begin to proclaim the word in the synagogues at Salamis, with young John Mark as their helper. The Psalm is the perfect prayer for this moment of mission: “Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you.” The blessing given to Israel is meant to shine out to every nation, so that “your way may be known upon earth, your saving power among all nations.”

In the Gospel Jesus cries aloud, almost his last public words in John before the Last Supper: “Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.” Jesus is not a messenger who points away from himself; to see him is to see the Father. “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness.” And he says that he did not come to condemn: “I came not to judge the world, but to save the world.” Yet the word he speaks is not empty. It will stand on the last day as the measure of our lives, because it is the Father's own word. Today the Church remembers St Anselm, the monk of Bec and Archbishop of Canterbury, who spent his life seeking to understand this light. His famous motto was “faith seeking understanding.” He did not believe because he had understood; he believed so that he might understand. He prayed: teach me to seek you, and show yourself to me when I seek. For Anselm, thinking about God was itself a way of praying, and prayer was the light in which thought could see.
conn: Herod Agrippa I.

Grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea AD 41–44. He executed James the brother of John and arrested Peter (Acts 12:1–4); his sudden death at Caesarea is told in Acts 12:20–23 and also by the Jewish historian Josephus.
Simeon called Niger.
Niger is Latin for “black.” He may have been an African; some have suggested he is Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21), but this cannot be shown.
Manaen.
A syntrophos of Herod Antipas: brought up with him as a boy, perhaps a foster brother. The Gospel reached even the circles of the court that had killed John the Baptist.
“Worshiping.”
The Greek leitourgountōn, from which comes “liturgy.” The mission of Paul begins in public prayer and fasting.
Laying on of hands.

An ancient sign of blessing and of handing on a task (Numbers 27:18–23). Here it commissions Barnabas and Saul for a particular mission; in the Church it is the sign used in Confirmation and Holy Orders.
John Mark.
Cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), whose mother's house in Jerusalem was a meeting place of the Church (Acts 12:12). Tradition identifies him with St Mark the Evangelist.
“On the last day.”
John holds together the present and the future: judgement happens already in the response to Christ (John 3:18), and it will be revealed fully on the last day.
St Anselm.

Born at Aosta in the Alps (1033), monk, prior and abbot of Bec in Normandy, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093. Twice exiled for defending the freedom of the Church. Author of the Proslogion and Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man). Declared Doctor of the Church in 1720. Died 21 April 1109.
altar: The mission of Barnabas and Saul was born while the Church was “worshiping the Lord and fasting.” Every mission of the Church comes from the altar and returns to it.

Christ came as light into the world. The paschal candle beside the altar this whole season is the sign of that light, and at the consecration the Light of the world comes among us under the veil of bread and wine.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I have a big decision, do I pray and fast before I act?
Point 1 · Set apart for the work
The Spirit speaks during the liturgy at Antioch.
Point 2 · Light, not darkness
Whoever sees Jesus sees the Father.
Point 3 · Faith seeking understanding
St Anselm, thinker and man of prayer.
Closing image
A monk at a desk by candlelight, pen in hand, praying before he writes.
Take-home line
“I have come as light into the world.”
live: Pray before deciding
Before the next important choice in your family or work, set aside a day of prayer and a small fast, as the Church at Antioch did.
Support missionaries
Pray today for a missionary you know by name, perhaps a priest or sister from your parish serving in North India or abroad, and send them a message.
Walk in the light
Bring one hidden thing into the light this week: a confession, an apology, a truth you have been avoiding.
Think and pray
Take one question about your faith that troubles you, and read about it in the Catechism, beginning and ending with a prayer, as Anselm did.
fathers: St Anselm (in substance)
I do not seek to understand so that I may believe; I believe so that I may understand. For this too I believe: that unless I believe, I shall not understand.
St Anselm (in substance)

Come now, little man, leave your busy cares for a while and rest a little in God. Enter the inner room of your mind, shut out everything except God, and say: now, Lord my God, teach my heart where and how to seek you, where and how to find you.
St Augustine (in substance)
Christ the light says: whoever believes in me will not remain in darkness. This shows that he found all in darkness; but he wills that they should not remain in it.
magis: Catechism 158
“Faith seeks understanding”: the words of St Anselm. A believer desires to know better the One in whom he has put his faith.
Fides et Ratio 42 (St John Paul II, 1998)
St Anselm shows that faith and reason, far from being opposed, help each other: the intelligence of faith.
Catechism 699
The laying on of hands, a sign of the Holy Spirit.
Ad Gentes 4
The Holy Spirit is the principal agent of mission, at work in the Church from Pentecost onward.
Catechism 2725–2726
Prayer as a battle and the error of separating prayer from action and thought.
saints: St Anselm

Bishop and Doctor of the Church. A gentle and humble monk who became a fearless archbishop; a great thinker who wrote some of the most tender prayers of the Middle Ages, including prayers to the Blessed Virgin Mary, whom he called the mother of all things made new. Called the Father of Scholasticism.
This week
23 Apr: St George; St Adalbert. 24 Apr: St Fidelis of Sigmaringen. 25 Apr: Fifth Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, light of the world, whoever sees you sees the Father who sent you. Shine into the darkness of our minds and hearts. As your Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul while your Church was at prayer, call and send in our time missionaries, priests and religious, and make every one of us ready to go where you send. By the prayers of St Anselm, give us a faith that seeks to understand and an understanding that bows in love, so that we may know you more truly and love you more dearly. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-22.title: Thursday of the Fourth Week of Easter
readings: Of this man's posterity God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised
For ever I will sing the goodness of the Lord (or: Alleluia)
Whoever receives one whom I send receives me
2027-04-22.alt: Easter weekday. The paschal candle burns beside the ambo; the Alleluia returns in the antiphons and the Gospel acclamation; the Regina Caeli (Queen of Heaven) replaces the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-22.verse: Very truly, I tell you, whoever receives one whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.
theo: Paul and his companions sail from Cyprus to the mainland of Asia Minor, and Luke slips in a small, painful detail: “John, however, left them and returned to Jerusalem.” Young John Mark turned back. We are not told why: fear of the hard road over the Taurus mountains, homesickness, or disagreement. Later this desertion would cause a sharp quarrel between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39). But the story does not end there. Years afterwards Paul would write from prison: “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful in my ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). And the Church remembers this same Mark as the writer of the Gospel that bears his name. The one who turned back was given a second chance, and he became a pillar. God does not throw away those who fail.

At Antioch in Pisidia, high on the plateau, Paul and Barnabas go to the synagogue on the sabbath. After the reading of the Law and the Prophets the officials invite them to speak: “Brothers, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, give it.” Paul stands up and begins with deep respect: “You Israelites, and others who fear God, listen.” His sermon is a loving retelling of Israel's history: God “chose our ancestors,” brought them out of Egypt “with uplifted arm,” “put up with them in the wilderness” for forty years, gave them the land, the judges, and the kings. Then David, “a man after my heart, who will carry out all my wishes.” And from David's line, as God promised, comes the Savior, Jesus. Paul's first preaching is not a rejection of Israel's story but a proclamation of its fulfilment. The Psalm sings the same faithfulness: “I will sing of your steadfast love, O Lord, forever,” and recalls God's oath to David: “I have found my servant David; with my holy oil I have anointed him.”

Paul ends this part of his speech with John the Baptist, who said: “I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet.” The greatest of the prophets knew he was only a servant. The Gospel takes us back to the Last Supper, just after Jesus has knelt and washed the feet of his disciples. He says: “Very truly, I tell you, servants are not greater than their master, nor are messengers greater than the one who sent them.” If the Lord washed feet, his apostles must do the same. “If you know these things, you are blessed if you do them.” Even the shadow of betrayal is present: Jesus quotes the Psalm, “The one who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me,” so that when it happens the disciples may not lose faith but believe that “I am he.” And then a promise that gives the humblest messenger great dignity: “whoever receives one whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” The servant is small, but the One who sends him is God.
conn: Perga in Pamphylia.
A city near the southern coast of present-day Turkey. From there the road climbed steeply over the Taurus mountains to Antioch in Pisidia, about 1,100 metres above sea level.
Antioch in Pisidia.
Not Antioch in Syria but a Roman colony in the interior of Asia Minor, near modern Yalvaç. Luke records Paul's sermon there as a model of his preaching to Jews.
The synagogue service.
Readings from the Law (Torah) and the Prophets, followed by an exhortation. The pattern of reading and preaching passed into the Christian Liturgy of the Word.
“Others who fear God.”
Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel and attended the synagogue without becoming Jews. Cornelius was one of them (Acts 10:2).
“A man after my heart.”
Paul combines 1 Samuel 13:14, Psalm 89:20 and Isaiah 44:28. David's faults were great, but his heart turned back to God; the Messiah would come from his line (2 Samuel 7:12–16).
Untying sandals.
The task of a slave. Rabbinic teaching said a disciple might do every service for his master except this one. John the Baptist says he is unworthy even of that (Luke 3:16).
“He has lifted his heel.”
Psalm 41:9, the lament of one betrayed by a table companion. To lift the heel against someone was a gesture of contempt.
“I am he.”
In Greek egō eimi, “I am,” echoing the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14). Jesus speaks it as the one who knows the future and holds it.
altar: Jesus said these words at the table of the Last Supper, after washing his disciples' feet. Every Mass holds together the Eucharist and service: the Lord who gives himself in the Bread is the Lord who kneels to wash feet.
The Liturgy of the Word follows the pattern Paul knew in the synagogue: the Scriptures are read, and then the word is explained for the people. The Church received this treasure from Israel.
outline: Opening
Ask: have I ever turned back from something God asked of me?
Point 1 · The one who turned back
John Mark leaves, and is later restored.
Point 2 · A history of faithfulness
Paul retells Israel's story and proclaims its fulfilment.
Point 3 · Servants and messengers
Not greater than the master; received as the master.
Closing image
A basin, a towel, and a pair of dusty sandals by the door.
Take-home line
“Whoever receives one whom I send receives me.”
live: Give a second chance
Think of someone who let you down. Like Paul with Mark, find one way to show that the door is not closed.
Tell God's faithfulness
At the family prayer tonight, let each person name one time God was faithful to your family.
Do the humble task
Choose one hidden service at home or in the parish this week, the kind no one thanks you for, and do it for Jesus.
Receive the messenger
Welcome the priest, the catechist or the house-visiting Vincentian as you would welcome Christ.
fathers: St John Chrysostom (in substance)
Paul does not begin by rebuking his hearers. He begins with the story they love, the kindness of God to their fathers, and so leads them gently to Christ, who is the fulfilment of the promises.
St Augustine (in substance)
John the Baptist was so great that he could have been taken for the Christ; yet he humbled himself and said he was not worthy to loose his sandal. The more he lowered himself, the higher he stood.
St John Chrysostom (in substance)
The sharpness of Paul and the gentleness of Barnabas both served Mark: the one corrected him, the other encouraged him, and so he who had turned back became useful. Let no one despair after a fall.
magis: Catechism 858–859
Jesus is the One sent by the Father; he sends the apostles as the Father sent him, so that whoever receives them receives him.
Catechism 523
St John the Baptist, the Lord's precursor, the voice who prepares his way.
Catechism 2559
Humility is the foundation of prayer.
Catechism 1093–1096
The Liturgy of the Word inherited from the synagogue; the Church's bond with Israel in the liturgy.
Dei Verbum 14–16
The Old Testament as true word of God, and the unity of the two Testaments.
saints: St John Mark

Cousin of Barnabas, companion of Paul and Peter, identified by tradition with St Mark the Evangelist. He turned back at Perga but later became Paul's valued helper. His feast (25 April) is not kept this year because it falls on the Fifth Sunday of Easter.
This week
23 Apr: St George; St Adalbert. 24 Apr: St Fidelis of Sigmaringen. 25 Apr: Fifth Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-22.prayer: Lord Jesus, Servant and Master, you knelt to wash the feet of your disciples and you sent them out as the Father sent you. Make us humble servants, glad to do the lowly tasks of love. Thank you for your faithfulness through all generations, from Abraham and David to this very day. When we turn back like John Mark, call us again and make us useful in your service. Teach us to receive in your messengers your own presence, and in you the Father who sent you. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-23.title: Friday of the Fourth Week of Easter · St George; St Adalbert
readings: God has fulfilled his promise by raising Jesus
You are my Son; this day I have begotten you (or: Alleluia)
I am the way, and the truth, and the life
2027-04-23.alt: Optional memorials: St George, martyr; St Adalbert, bishop and martyr. One of them may be kept with the Easter weekday readings. If a memorial is kept, the liturgical colour is red; otherwise white. Where St George is patron of a country, diocese or parish (as in England, and in many churches dedicated to him in Kerala), he is honoured with a higher rank according to the local calendar.
2027-04-23.verse: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
theo: Paul continues his sermon in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia. He speaks with warmth to his own people and to the God-fearers: “My brothers, you descendants of Abraham's family, and others who fear God, to us the message of this salvation has been sent.” He tells, briefly and honestly, what happened in Jerusalem: those in authority there did not recognize Jesus or understand the prophets read every sabbath, and “even though they found no cause for a sentence of death, they asked Pilate to have him killed.” They took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. Then comes the heart of every apostolic sermon: “But God raised him from the dead.” The Resurrection is God's own answer to the injustice of the Cross. It is not a private feeling of the disciples; it is a public fact with witnesses: “for many days he appeared to those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, and they are now his witnesses to the people.”

Paul tells his hearers that this is good news for them: “what God promised to our ancestors he has fulfilled for us, their children, by raising Jesus.” And he quotes the second Psalm, which today is also our responsorial psalm: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” In the Psalm these words were spoken over the king of Israel on the day of his anointing. Paul hears in them the Father's voice on Easter morning, raising his Son and enthroning him as the true King. The Church reads this passage with care. When Luke speaks of “the residents of Jerusalem and their leaders,” he is not blaming a whole people. Paul himself is a Jew speaking to Jews, and he calls them “brothers” and “children” of the promise. The Church teaches that all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion, and that the Jews are not to be presented as rejected or accursed (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597–598).

The Gospel takes us again to the Upper Room. Jesus knows his friends are frightened: he has spoken of betrayal, of Peter's denial, of going away. So he says: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house there are many dwelling places.” He is going ahead to prepare a place, and he will come back to take them with him. Thomas, honest as ever, objects: “Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?” And Jesus answers with one of the greatest sentences in the Gospel: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” Not a map, but a person. Today the Church honours two martyrs who walked that way to the end. St George, a soldier according to ancient tradition, died for Christ at Lydda in Palestine, probably in the persecution of Diocletian, and has been loved in East and West ever since. St Adalbert, bishop of Prague, gave his life as a missionary among the pagan Prussians in 997. For both, Jesus was the way, and death was only the last step home to the Father's house.
conn: “Descendants of Abraham's family.”
Paul addresses his fellow Jews with the title of the covenant. The God-fearing Gentiles are included as hearers of the same message.
“The tree.”
An expression from Deuteronomy 21:22–23 used by the apostles for the cross (Acts 5:30; 10:39; Galatians 3:13). The one who hung under the curse is the one God vindicated.
“Did not recognize him.”
Acts often speaks of ignorance (Acts 3:17), not to excuse sin but to open the door to repentance. The Church never teaches a collective guilt of the Jewish people (Catechism 597).
Psalm 2.

A royal psalm sung at the enthronement of the king in Jerusalem. The New Testament applies it to the Resurrection (Acts 13:33), to the Baptism and Transfiguration of Jesus, and to his eternal priesthood (Hebrews 1:5; 5:5).
“Dwelling places.”
The Greek monai, from the verb menein, “to abide,” a favourite word of John. Heaven is the place of abiding with the Father.
Thomas.
Called Didymus, the Twin. In John he is the honest questioner (John 11:16; 20:24–29). In India we honour him as our Apostle.
St George.

Martyred at Lydda (Diospolis) in Palestine, probably about 303. An early Roman decree ascribed to Pope Gelasius (494) counted him among saints whose names are rightly revered but whose deeds are known only to God. The story of the dragon is a medieval legend, a picture of Christ's victory over evil.
St Adalbert.

Vojtěch, born in Bohemia about 956, bishop of Prague from 982, monk in Rome, missionary to the Prussians, killed on 23 April 997 near the Baltic coast. His relics are honoured at Gniezno; he is a patron of Poland and of the Czech lands.
altar: “In my Father's house there are many dwelling places.” At every Mass we pray for the dead, “our brothers and sisters who have fallen asleep in the hope of the resurrection,” and we taste already the banquet of the Father's house.

The martyrs offered their bodies as Christ offered his. From the earliest centuries the Eucharist was celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs, and relics of saints are still placed in the altar stone.
outline: Opening
Ask: what troubles my heart most today?
Point 1 · But God raised him
The heart of Paul's preaching.
Point 2 · Do not let your hearts be troubled
Many dwelling places.
Point 3 · I am the way
St George and St Adalbert walk the way to the end.
Closing image
A narrow mountain road at dusk, and a lamp shining in the window of a house at its end.
Take-home line
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
live: Bring your trouble
Name the trouble in your heart, and say slowly ten times today: “Jesus, I believe in you.”
Witness to the Resurrection
Tell one person this week, simply, why you believe that Jesus is risen.
Pray for the persecuted
St George and St Adalbert died for Christ; pray today for Christians who suffer for their faith in our own time, in India and abroad.
Remember the dead
Visit the grave of a family member, or have a Mass offered for them, and pray: may they rest in the Father's house.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
Christ is the way as man and the goal as God. Through Christ the man you go to Christ who is God. Walk by him who is the way, and you will arrive at him who is the truth and the life.
Tertullian (in substance)
The more you mow us down, the more we grow: the blood of Christians is seed.
St Thomas Aquinas (in substance)

If you are looking for where to go, hold fast to Christ, for he is the truth; if you are looking for the way to get there, hold fast to Christ, for he is the way. Better to limp along the way than to run swiftly off it.
magis: Catechism 2473–2474
Martyrdom is the supreme witness to the truth of the faith; the Church keeps the memory of the martyrs with great care.
Catechism 1025
To live in heaven is “to be with Christ”: the elect live in him, yet keep and find their true identity.
Catechism 597–598
The Jews are not collectively responsible for the death of Jesus; all sinners were the authors of his Passion.
Catechism 653–655
The Resurrection fulfils the promises and confirms Christ's divinity: “You are my Son, today I have begotten you.”
Lumen Gentium 42
Martyrdom, by which a disciple is made like the Master, is esteemed by the Church as an exceptional gift and the highest proof of love.
saints: St George

Martyr (died about 303). Honoured from the fourth century at Lydda; patron of soldiers, of England, Georgia, Catalonia and many other places. In Kerala, as Geevarghese Sahada, he is honoured with great devotion by Christians of all the Churches, and many of other faiths also come to his shrines.
St Adalbert

Bishop of Prague and martyr (about 956–997). A gentle pastor who longed for the conversion of his people, he twice withdrew to Rome as a monk and finally went as a missionary to the Prussians, who killed him. Canonized in 999.
2027-04-23.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, way, truth and life, no one comes to the Father except through you. When our hearts are troubled, steady them with faith in you. You have gone ahead to prepare a place for us in the Father's house; keep us on the way that leads there. Through the prayers of St George, who gave his life for you, and of St Adalbert, who preached your Gospel to the end, make us brave witnesses of your Resurrection, and strengthen all who suffer for your name today. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-24.title: Saturday of the Fourth Week of Easter · St Fidelis of Sigmaringen
readings: We are now turning to the Gentiles
All the ends of the earth have seen the saving power of God (or: Alleluia)
Whoever has seen me has seen the Father
2027-04-24.alt: Optional memorial: St Fidelis of Sigmaringen, priest and martyr (1578–1622). The Easter weekday readings are kept. If the memorial is kept, the liturgical colour is red; otherwise white. Regina Caeli at noon until Pentecost.
2027-04-24.verse: Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?”
theo: A week after Paul's sermon in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia, “almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.” The good news has spread through the whole town, among Jews and Gentiles alike. But success brings conflict. Some of the synagogue's leaders, seeing the crowds, are filled with jealousy and contradict Paul. Paul and Barnabas answer boldly: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you.” Notice the word “first.” The apostles never stop going first to the synagogue in every town; God's promises were given to Israel, and Israel keeps its place in God's plan (Romans 11:29). Then they quote the Servant Song of Isaiah, applying it to their own mission: “I have set you to be a light for the Gentiles, so that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.” What was said of the Servant, and of Christ, is now the task of the Church.

The Gentiles hear this with joy; they “were glad and praised the word of the Lord,” and “the word of the Lord spread throughout the region.” Opposition grows; some of the city's leading men and devout women of high standing are stirred up, and Paul and Barnabas are driven out. Luke is describing a local conflict in one city, not the response of the whole Jewish people, and the Church reads such passages without any hostility to the Jews, our elder brothers in faith (Nostra Aetate 4). The apostles do what Jesus told them: they shake the dust off their feet and move on to Iconium. And then the most surprising line of all: “the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.” Driven out, and full of joy. That is Easter joy, which does not depend on success. The Psalm sings it: “All the ends of the earth have seen the victory of our God.”

In the Gospel Philip makes a request that comes from the depths of every human heart: “Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied.” And Jesus answers with gentle surprise: “Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” In the face of Jesus, in his compassion, his words, his wounds, we see the face of God. Then Jesus makes two astonishing promises: those who believe in him will do “greater works” than his, because he is going to the Father; and “I will do whatever you ask in my name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.” Today the Church remembers St Fidelis of Sigmaringen. Mark Roy was a brilliant lawyer in Alsace who was called “the poor man's lawyer” because he defended the poor without payment. Sickened by the dishonesty of his profession, he became a Capuchin friar and took the name Fidelis, “faithful.” He was sent by the newly founded Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith to preach in the Swiss region of Graubünden, in a time of bitter religious and political conflict. On 24 April 1622, after preaching at Seewis, he was attacked and killed. He forgave his attackers as he died. He is honoured as the first martyr of that Congregation. Today Catholics and Protestants, recalling with sorrow the violence of those centuries on all sides, pray and work together as brothers and sisters in Christ.
conn: “Almost the whole city.”
Antioch in Pisidia was a Roman colony with a large Gentile population and a Jewish community with its synagogue. Paul's preaching drew both.
Jealousy.
Luke uses the word for zeal (zēlos). It describes a religious zeal that resented the crowds of Gentiles; Paul himself had once been driven by the same zeal (Galatians 1:14).
“First to you.”
Paul's constant practice (Romans 1:16: “to the Jew first and also to the Greek”). God's call to Israel is not withdrawn (Romans 11:29).
“A light for the Gentiles.”
Isaiah 49:6, the second Servant Song. Simeon used the same words over the infant Jesus in the Temple (Luke 2:32).
“Destined for eternal life.”
Luke stresses that faith is God's gift, received as grace. The Church teaches that God wills all to be saved and that no one is predestined to reject him (Catechism 1037).
Shaking off the dust.
A gesture Jesus taught (Luke 9:5; 10:11): not a curse but a solemn sign that the messengers have done their part and leave the matter to God.
“Greater works.”
Not greater miracles in themselves, but the wider harvest of the Church's mission after Pentecost, which Jesus works through his disciples from the Father's side.
St Fidelis.

Born Mark Roy at Sigmaringen in Swabia in 1578; doctor of law; Capuchin from 1612; killed at Seewis in Graubünden, 24 April 1622; canonized 1746. His Capuchin name echoes Revelation 2:10: “Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life.”
altar: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” At the elevation of the Host the Church shows us the Lord, and we look with faith on the One in whom we see the Father.
“If in my name you ask me for anything, I will do it.” Every prayer of the Mass ends “through our Lord Jesus Christ,” because the Church prays in the name of the Son.
outline: Opening
Ask: does my joy depend on things going well?
Point 1 · A light for the Gentiles
The word goes first to Israel, then to the nations.
Point 2 · Driven out, filled with joy
Shaking off the dust.
Point 3 · Show us the Father
Philip's longing and Jesus' answer; St Fidelis, faithful to the end.
Closing image
Two travellers on a dusty road, shaking their cloaks and singing as they walk.
Take-home line
“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
live: Rejoice in failure
When something you did for God is rejected this week, do not sulk. Shake off the dust, pray for those who rejected it, and keep your joy.
Look at Jesus
Spend ten minutes before the Blessed Sacrament or a crucifix, and pray: Lord, show me the Father.
Ask in his name
Bring one big intention to Jesus every day this week, ending with “in the name of Jesus.”
Be faithful and honest
Like St Fidelis, refuse dishonesty in your work, and help one poor person with your skill, without payment.
fathers: St Irenaeus (in substance)
The glory of God is the human person fully alive, and the life of the human person is the vision of God. The Son reveals the Father, and whoever sees the Son sees the Father.
St Augustine (in substance)

To make a sinner righteous is a greater work than to create heaven and earth; for heaven and earth will pass away, but the salvation of the elect will remain. These are the greater works that Christ does through his disciples.
St Fidelis of Sigmaringen (words traditionally attributed to him)
O Catholic faith, how firm you are, how deeply rooted, how well founded on solid rock! Heaven and earth will pass away, but you will never pass away.
magis: Catechism 516
Christ's whole earthly life reveals the Father: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
Catechism 2614
Prayer in the name of Jesus: “If in my name you ask me for anything, I will do it.”
Catechism 839–840
The Jewish people, to whom God first spoke, and the common hope of Jews and Christians.
Unitatis Redintegratio 3
Those baptized in other Christian communities are rightly called Christians and accepted as brothers and sisters in the Lord.
Catechism 1037
God predestines no one to go to hell; he wills that all should come to repentance.
saints: St Fidelis of Sigmaringen

Priest and martyr. Lawyer turned Capuchin friar, famous for his care for the poor and the sick and for his prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. First martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (Propaganda Fide), founded in 1622, the same year he died.
Tomorrow
Fifth Sunday of Easter. The feast of St Mark the Evangelist (25 April) is not celebrated this year because it falls on a Sunday of Easter.
2027-04-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, in you we see the Father, and in your name we may ask for anything. When the word we bring is welcomed, keep us humble; when it is rejected, keep us full of joy and of the Holy Spirit. Make us a light for the nations, as you sent Paul and Barnabas to be. By the prayers of St Fidelis, who gave up wealth to serve the poor and gave up his life for the faith, make us faithful until death, honest in our work and generous to the needy. Show us the Father, and we will be satisfied. You live and reign for ever and ever. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-26.title: Monday of the Fifth Week of Easter
readings: We bring you good news, that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God
Not to us, O Lord, but to your name give the glory (or: Alleluia)
The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything
2027-04-26.alt: Easter weekday of the fifth week (Year I). The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel, the Paschal candle stays lit beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-26.verse: Jesus answered him, “Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.”
theo: Paul and Barnabas are on their first missionary journey, in the hill country of Lycaonia in the middle of what is now Turkey. Threatened in Iconium, they move on to Lystra, and there they meet a man “who could not use his feet and had never walked, for he had been crippled from birth.” He listens to Paul preaching, and Paul, “looking at him intently and seeing that he had faith to be healed,” calls out: “Stand upright on your feet.” The man springs up and walks. Then something unexpected happens. The crowd shouts in their own language, “The gods have come down to us in human form!” They call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, “because he was the chief speaker,” and the priest of Zeus arrives with oxen and garlands to offer sacrifice. The people of that region told an old story of Zeus and Hermes once visiting in disguise and going unrecognised; perhaps they did not want to make that mistake again. The apostles tear their clothes and rush into the crowd: “Friends, why are you doing this? We are mortals just like you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them.” Paul's first sermon to pure pagans does not begin with the Law of Moses but with creation: God “has not left himself without a witness in doing good,” for he gives “rains from heaven and fruitful seasons,” filling people “with food and your hearts with joy.” The Psalm gives the apostles' answer in one line: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.”

In the Gospel we are back at the Last Supper. Jesus has promised to show himself to those who love him, and Judas, “not Iscariot,” asks a fair question: “Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?” Jesus does not answer with a spectacle. He answers with a dwelling: “Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.” The people of Lystra wanted gods who would come down for a visit and be honoured with oxen. The true God does far more: the Father and the Son come to stay, in the heart of the one who loves and obeys. And they do not leave us to remember everything by our own strength: “the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.” St Augustine, looking back on the years he searched for God outside himself, wrote (in substance): you were within me, and I was outside, looking for you there. In these last weeks before Pentecost the Church asks us to look within, where the Holy Trinity has made a home.
outline: Opening
Ask: when people praise you, where does the glory go?
Point 1 · Mortals just like you
The apostles refuse worship and point to the living God.
Point 2 · Never without a witness
Rain, harvests and joy speak of the Creator.
Point 3 · We will make our home with them
The Trinity dwells in the one who loves; the Spirit teaches and reminds.
Take-home line
“We will come to them and make our home with them.”
live: Give the glory away (Psalm 115:1)
When you are praised today, say inwardly: not to me, Lord, but to your name.
Make room for the Guest (John 14:23)
Spend five quiet minutes tonight with the Lord who lives in you, and ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of one word of Jesus.
2027-04-26.prayer: Living God, maker of heaven and earth and sea, you have never left yourself without a witness: you send the rain, you ripen the harvest, you fill our hearts with joy. Not to us, Lord, but to your name be the glory. Lord Jesus, risen from the dead, come with the Father and make your home in us; and send us the Holy Spirit, the Advocate, to teach us everything and remind us of all you have said. Amen.
altar: The God the people of Lystra mistook for a passing visitor comes to stay. In Holy Communion the risen Lord truly enters the one who receives him, Body and Blood, soul and divinity, so that the promise “we will make our home with them” takes flesh in us.

2027-04-27.title: Tuesday of the Fifth Week of Easter
readings: They called the church together and related all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith for the Gentiles
Your friends make known, O Lord, the glorious splendour of your kingdom (or: Alleluia)
My peace I give to you
2027-04-27.alt: Easter weekday of the fifth week (Year I). The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel, the Paschal candle stays lit beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-27.verse: Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not let them be afraid.
theo: Yesterday the crowd at Lystra wanted to worship Paul; today, stirred up by opponents who have followed him from Antioch and Iconium, the same crowd stones him, drags him out of the city and leaves him for dead. Luke tells the next moment very simply: “when the disciples surrounded him, he got up and went into the city.” The next day he walks on to Derbe. Then comes the surprising part. Instead of taking the short road home, Paul and Barnabas turn back through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, the very towns where they had been threatened and beaten, to strengthen the new disciples. Their message is honest: “It is through many persecutions that we must enter the kingdom of God.” They appoint elders in each church and, “with prayer and fasting,” entrust them “to the Lord in whom they had come to believe.” Here we see the Church taking shape: local communities with their own pastors, handed over to the Lord in prayer. Years later Paul would remind Timothy, himself a young man of Lystra (Acts 16:1), of “what persecutions I endured” there, “Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them” (2 Timothy 3:11). Back in Syrian Antioch the missionaries gather the church and tell “all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith for the Gentiles.” They do not report their own sufferings first; they report what God has done. Note too that the opposition came from some who were stirred up, while Paul and Barnabas were themselves Jews, and Jews were among their first converts; Luke's story is never a charge against a whole people.

In the Gospel Jesus, at the Supper, speaks of a peace that can survive stones: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives.” The world's peace is the absence of trouble, and it lasts only until the next trouble comes. The peace of Christ is his own presence, given on the night before he dies, and it can live in a heart surrounded by trouble. He knows what is coming: “the ruler of this world is coming. He has no power over me; but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father.” And he ends with words of quiet resolve: “Rise, let us be on our way.” The risen Lord's first word to the apostles on Easter evening will be this same gift: “Peace be with you.” Paul, rising from the stones and walking back into the city, shows us what that peace looks like in a human life.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is the difference between a calm day and a peaceful heart?
Point 1 · He got up and went into the city
Paul rises after the stones and goes back.
Point 2 · Through many persecutions
Honest preaching, elders, prayer and fasting.
Point 3 · Not as the world gives
The peace of Christ in the middle of trouble.
Take-home line
“My peace I give to you.”
live: Get up again (Acts 14:20)
Go back today, gently, to one person or task you have been avoiding since a painful setback.
Receive his peace (John 14:27)
At the sign of peace at Mass, or in a quiet moment today, receive Christ's peace consciously and give it to one person who is troubled.
2027-04-27.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, on the night before you died you left us your peace, a peace the world cannot give and cannot take away. When stones are thrown at us, help us to rise again as Paul did and walk back into the city with courage. Strengthen all who suffer for the faith, bless the pastors of your Church, and keep open the door of faith that you have opened for all nations. Who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: Before Holy Communion the priest prays: Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles, Peace I leave you, my peace I give you. The peace promised at the Supper is given at every Mass, from the altar where the risen Lord is truly present.

2027-04-28.title: Wednesday of the Fifth Week of Easter · St Peter Chanel; St Louis Grignion de Montfort
readings: They went up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders to discuss this question
Let us go rejoicing to the house of the Lord (or: Alleluia)
Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit
2027-04-28.alt: Easter weekday of the fifth week (Year I). The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel, the Paschal candle stays lit beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. Optional memorials: St Peter Chanel, priest and martyr (colour red if his Mass is said), and St Louis Grignion de Montfort, priest (white). The Gospel of the vine was also read on Sunday; on this weekday it is heard beside the first great dispute of the Church.
2027-04-28.verse: I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
theo: The door of faith has been opened to the Gentiles, and with that joy comes the Church's first great argument. “Certain individuals came down from Judea” to Antioch and taught: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” These were believers in Jesus; the question was real. Must a Gentile first become a Jew in order to become a Christian? Luke does not hide that there was “no small dissension and debate.” What matters is what the Church did next. No one walked out to found a rival church. Paul and Barnabas “and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to discuss this question with the apostles and the elders.” On the way, through Phoenicia and Samaria, they told of the conversion of the Gentiles “and brought great joy to all the believers.” In Jerusalem they are welcomed by “the church and the apostles and the elders,” some believers from the party of the Pharisees state their view, and “The apostles and the elders met together to consider this matter.” This is the Council of Jerusalem, about the year 49, the pattern for every council since: when the faith is disputed, the Church gathers around the apostles and their successors and waits on the Holy Spirit. The Psalm sings of the city where the tribes go up together: “Jerusalem, built as a city that is bound firmly together.”

The Gospel of the true vine, heard on Sunday, now sounds beside this first dispute. “I am the vine, you are the branches.” Branches do not choose one another; they are joined because each one is joined to the vine. The unity the apostles seek in Jerusalem is not a committee's agreement but life flowing from Christ into every member. Jesus also speaks of a painful grace: “Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.” Anyone who has seen a vine cut back in winter knows that pruning looks like loss. Today the Church remembers two priests who were pruned to the root. St Peter Chanel (1803 to 1841), a French priest of the Society of Mary, laboured for over three years on the Pacific island of Futuna with few visible results, and was clubbed to death on 28 April 1841; within a few years almost the whole island had asked for baptism, and he is honoured as the first martyr of Oceania. St Louis Grignion de Montfort (1673 to 1716) preached missions across western France, often rejected and even banned from dioceses, and wrote of total consecration to Jesus through the hands of the Blessed Virgin Mary; his little book, found long after his death, gave St John Paul II his motto, Totus tuus. Both stayed on the vine, and the fruit came after them.
outline: Opening
Ask: when Christians disagree, what do we usually do?
Point 1 · No small dissension
A real question in the young Church.
Point 2 · They went up to Jerusalem
Disputes brought to the apostles, not to the street.
Point 3 · Pruned to bear more fruit
Abiding in the vine; St Peter Chanel and St Louis de Montfort.
Take-home line
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
live: Bring disagreement to communion (Acts 15:2)
If you are in a dispute in your family, parish or work, seek a calm conversation with the right person instead of complaining to others.
Accept the pruning (John 15:2)
Name one loss or disappointment of this year and offer it to the Father in prayer as pruning for more fruit.
2027-04-28.prayer: Father, you are the vinegrower and your Son is the true vine. Keep us joined to him and to one another, so that, when we disagree, we may seek the truth together in the communion of your Church, as the apostles did in Jerusalem. Prune us where we need it and make us bear fruit that lasts. Through the prayers of St Peter Chanel, who gave his life on Futuna, and of St Louis Grignion de Montfort, who gave himself wholly to Jesus through Mary, make us faithful branches. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: The vine gives its wine, and the wine becomes his Blood. At every Mass the sap of the true Vine flows into the branches: in the Eucharist we, many as we are, become one body, because we all share the one bread and the one cup.

2027-04-29.title: Saint Catherine of Siena, Virgin and Doctor of the Church
readings: God has made no distinction between them and us, cleansing their hearts by faith
Proclaim his marvellous deeds to all the nations (or: Alleluia)
Abide in my love, so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete
2027-04-29.alt: Memorial. Thursday of the Fifth Week of Easter (Year I). The weekday readings are given here; the proper readings of the memorial, 1 John 1:5–2:2 and Matthew 11:25–30, may be used instead. St Catherine is a patron of Italy and of Europe. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-29.verse: As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.
theo: The council in Jerusalem reaches its decision. “After there had been much debate, Peter stood up.” He reminds the assembly that God chose him to bring the Gospel to the Gentiles in the house of Cornelius, and that God “who knows the human heart, testified to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us; and in cleansing their hearts by faith he has made no distinction between them and us.” Then comes the sentence that sums up the whole matter: “we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” Salvation is not earned by keeping a list of customs; it is a gift received in faith, for Jew and Gentile alike. The assembly falls silent and listens to Barnabas and Paul tell of the signs God has worked among the nations. Then James, the leader of the church in Jerusalem, speaks. He reads the prophet Amos, “I will rebuild the dwelling of David, which has fallen,” so that “all other peoples may seek the Lord,” and gives his judgment: “we should not trouble those Gentiles who are turning to God,” asking only a few things that would let Jewish and Gentile believers share one table in peace. Peter speaks first, James confirms, the whole assembly listens: this is how the Church discerns. James also honours the Law of Moses, “read aloud every sabbath in the synagogues”; the decision does not despise Israel's heritage but opens its promises to all.

In the Gospel Jesus tells us where the grace that saves us comes from: “As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.” The love between the Father and the Son is poured out on the disciples, and the commandments are simply the way to stay in it. And the goal is joy: “I have said these things to you so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete.” Few saints show this joy on fire more clearly than St Catherine of Siena (1347 to 1380). The twenty-third or twenty-fourth child of a dyer in Siena, she joined the Dominican lay women called the Mantellate, nursed the sick through plague, made peace between feuding families and cities, and, though she had little schooling, dictated The Dialogue and hundreds of letters. She loved the Church so much that she wrote to the Pope as “sweet Christ on earth,” and she also told him plainly to return from Avignon to Rome, which Gregory XI did in 1377. She died in Rome on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three. Paul VI named her a Doctor of the Church in 1970. She wrote to a disciple (in substance): if you are what you ought to be, you will set the whole of Italy on fire. And she prayed (in substance): eternal Trinity, you are a deep sea; the more I enter, the more I find, and the more I find, the more I seek you.
outline: Opening
Ask: is your faith a burden you carry or a love you live in?
Point 1 · Saved through grace
Peter's word at the council: no distinction between them and us.
Point 2 · Abide in my love
The Father's love for the Son poured out on us.
Point 3 · Set the world on fire
St Catherine: joy, truth and love for the Church.
Take-home line
“Abide in my love.”
live: Receive grace, do not earn it (Acts 15:11)
Make an act of thanksgiving today for one gift you know you did not deserve.
Speak the truth in love, like Catherine
Say one honest and kind word today that you have been avoiding, and pray for the Pope and the bishops.
2027-04-29.prayer: Father, as you have loved your Son, so he has loved us; keep us in his love. You set St Catherine of Siena on fire with love for Christ crucified and for his Church: grant that, through her prayers, we may be saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, speak the truth with courage and charity, and find in your love the joy that is complete. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: St Catherine's confessor and biographer, Blessed Raymond of Capua, records that for long periods she could take almost no food except Holy Communion. She lived from the altar. The Eucharist is the love of the Father and the Son given to us as food, so that we may abide in that love.

2027-04-30.title: Friday of the Fifth Week of Easter · St Pius V
readings: It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose on you no further burden than these essentials
I will give you thanks among the peoples, O Lord (or: Alleluia)
This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you
2027-04-30.alt: Easter weekday of the fifth week (Year I). The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel, the Paschal candle stays lit beside the ambo, and the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus until Pentecost. Liturgical colour: white. Optional memorial of St Pius V, pope (white). Fridays of the Easter season remain days of penance; follow the norms of your bishops' conference. The Lectionary numbers the Psalm 57:8–9, 10 and 12; in the NRSV these are verses 7–8, 9 and 11. Tomorrow, 1 May: St Joseph the Worker, and the month of Mary begins.
2027-04-30.verse: This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
theo: The council in Jerusalem has reached its decision, and now the Church puts it into words and sends it on its way. “The apostles and the elders, with the consent of the whole church,” choose two respected men, Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, to travel with Paul and Barnabas to Antioch with a letter. The letter is warm and humble. It admits that some had gone out “with no instructions from us” and had “unsettled your minds.” It calls Barnabas and Paul “our beloved,” men “who have risked their lives for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ.” And it contains one of the most remarkable sentences in the New Testament: “it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose on you no further burden than these essentials.” The Holy Spirit and us: the apostles do not claim to have invented the answer, nor do they hide behind private visions. The Spirit speaks through the gathered Church and its shepherds. The essentials they ask, avoiding food offered to idols, blood, what is strangled, and sexual immorality, allowed Jewish and Gentile Christians to live and eat together in peace. When the letter is read in Antioch, “they rejoiced at the exhortation.” Good teaching, given with love, brings joy, not fear.

In the Gospel Jesus gives the one commandment that sums up all the rest: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” Not simply as we love ourselves, but as he loves us, to the end: “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.” Then he changes our name: “I do not call you servants any longer… but I have called you friends.” And he reminds us who took the first step: “You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last.” Today the Church remembers St Pius V (1504 to 1572), a shepherd boy from Piedmont who became a Dominican friar and then Pope from 1566. He gave the Church the fruit of the Council of Trent in lasting form: the Roman Catechism (1566), the reformed Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal (1570), used for four centuries; he named St Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church. As Pope he kept the poverty of a friar, visited the sick in hospitals and washed the feet of the poor. In the troubled year 1571 he called on the faithful to pray the Rosary, and in thanksgiving he instituted the feast now kept on 7 October as Our Lady of the Rosary. Like the apostles' letter, his work was meant to hand on the essentials of the faith clearly, so that the friends of Jesus might love one another in the truth.
outline: Opening
Ask: who chose whom, you or God?
Point 1 · It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us
The Church discerns and teaches; the letter brings joy.
Point 2 · I have called you friends
Not servants but friends of Jesus.
Point 3 · Love one another as I have loved you
Fruit that will last; St Pius V hands on the faith.
Take-home line
“You did not choose me but I chose you.”
live: Welcome the Church's teaching (Acts 15:31)
Read one paragraph of the Catechism of the Catholic Church today on a subject you know little about.
Love as he loved (John 15:12)
Do one hidden act of service today for someone who cannot repay you, as St Pius V served the sick.
2027-04-30.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you have called us not servants but friends, and you chose us to go and bear fruit that will last. Give us the Holy Spirit who guided the apostles in Jerusalem, so that we may receive the teaching of your Church with joy and love one another as you have loved us. Through the prayers of St Pius V, who handed on the faith clearly and served the poor humbly, keep your Church faithful and united. Who live and reign for ever and ever. Amen.
altar: “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.” At every Mass that greatest love is made present: the one sacrifice of the Cross offered for his friends, and the risen Lord giving himself to them as food. St Pius V's Missal guarded this mystery with reverence for four hundred years, and the Missal of today proclaims the same faith.

quick: The first Christians were of one heart and soul, and there was no needy person among them.
Faith in the Son of God is the victory that conquers the world.
The Risen Lord gives peace, the Spirit and the power to forgive sins; Thomas confesses: My Lord and my God.
2027-04-04.action: Pray “Jesus, I trust in you” at three o'clock each afternoon this week, and make your Easter confession if you have not yet done so.
2027-04-04.question: Which locked door in my heart do I need to open to the mercy of the Risen Lord?
catechism: “My Lord and my God”: the title Lord expresses faith in the divinity of Jesus.
Only God forgives sins, and he gives this power to his ministers.
Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, is at the heart of the Church's life.
kidsaint: St Faustina

Helen was a poor girl from a village in Poland who loved Jesus very much. She became a sister and worked in the kitchen and the garden. Jesus showed her a picture of himself with rays of light coming from his heart, and asked her to tell everyone: Jesus, I trust in you! Now that picture is in churches all over the world. Lesson: even when we have done wrong, we can trust in Jesus' mercy.
2027-04-04.special: Second Sunday of Easter, Sunday of Divine Mercy, Octave Day of Easter: Gloria and Creed; Easter Sequence optional; double Alleluia at the dismissal; plenary indulgence under the usual conditions.
term: Indulgence

A remission before God of the temporal punishment due to sins already forgiven, granted by the Church from the treasury of the merits of Christ and the saints (CCC 1471). It is plenary when it removes all such punishment. It presupposes the forgiveness of sins in confession and requires a heart detached from sin.

family.explain: Thomas was not with the others when Jesus came. He said: I will not believe unless I touch his wounds. A week later Jesus came again and said: Thomas, put your finger here. Thomas did not need to touch. He said: My Lord and my God! Jesus said: happy are those who believe without seeing. That means us!
family.intention: We pray for everyone who finds it hard to believe, and for all who need God's forgiveness today.
family.ask: Ask: “When do we say ‘sorry’ in our family?” Then each person says sorry to someone for something small, and the others answer: I forgive you.

illus: An illustration

An old fisherman in Kollam had not been to confession for nearly forty years. When he was admitted to hospital after a fall, his granddaughter hung a small Divine Mercy picture beside his bed. For two days he pretended not to see it. On the third night he asked her to read the words at the bottom. She read: Jesus, I trust in you. He was quiet for a long time, then said: call the priest. The next morning the hospital chaplain heard his confession. The nurses said afterwards that he slept peacefully for the first time since he came. Mercy had come through a locked door.

pm.open: Merciful Jesus, risen Lord, come into the locked rooms of our hearts, show us your wounds and give us your peace. Jesus, I trust in you. Alleluia. Amen.
share: The whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul (Acts 4:32). What divides our community, and how can mercy heal it?
This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith (1 John 5:4). Where do I need the victory of faith this week?
My Lord and my God! (John 20:28). When did I last speak to Jesus with that kind of faith?
pm.resp: Give thanks to the Lord for he is good, his love is everlasting.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a home of mercy where every sinner finds the open wounds of Christ.
For priests who hear confessions, that they may be patient and gentle ministers of the Father's forgiveness.
For those who doubt, like Thomas, that the Risen Lord may meet them and lead them to faith.
For the poor and needy in our parish, that no one among us may lack what is necessary.
For our group, that we may trust in Jesus and become merciful as the Father is merciful.
pm.close: Father of mercies, by the wounds of your risen Son you have healed us. Make us witnesses of your mercy and one in heart and soul. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Peter told the crowd that God raised Jesus, the Author of life, and called them to repent so that their sins might be wiped out.
St John says: if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
The risen Jesus showed his hands and feet, ate a piece of fish, opened the Scriptures and made the disciples his witnesses.
2027-04-11.action: Invite someone who usually eats alone to share a meal with your family this week.
2027-04-11.question: Do I believe that Jesus rose in his real body, and does that belief change how I treat my own body and others?
catechism: The risen body of Jesus: real, touchable, yet glorified.
Conversion is the first call of the Gospel.
kidsaint: St Stanislaus

Stanislaus was a bishop in Poland long ago. The king was doing very bad things and hurting people, and Bishop Stanislaus bravely told him to stop. According to tradition, the king was so angry that he killed the bishop while he was saying Mass. Lesson: like the apostles, we must tell the truth about Jesus even when it is hard.
2027-04-11.special: Third Sunday of Easter (Year B). Gloria and Creed; sprinkling with water may replace the Penitential Act. Regina Caeli at noon.
term: Bodily Resurrection

The faith of the Church that Jesus rose from the dead in his own real body, the body that was crucified, now glorified and immortal; not a ghost and not merely a memory (Luke 24:39; Catechism 645). It is also the promise for us: we believe in the resurrection of the body.

family.explain: The disciples were talking together when suddenly Jesus was standing with them! They were scared and thought he was a ghost. Jesus said: look at my hands and feet; touch me! A ghost does not have a body like me. Then he asked for some food, and ate a piece of fish in front of them. Jesus is really alive!
family.intention: We pray for people who are afraid or who find it hard to believe.
family.ask: Ask: “Why did Jesus eat fish in front of his friends?” Then share a meal together and thank Jesus that he is alive.

illus: An illustration

In a parish in Thrissur, a young engineer who had stopped believing told his grandmother that the Resurrection was only a beautiful story the disciples told to comfort themselves. She did not argue. She took out her old Bible, opened it to Luke 24 and asked him to read verse 39 aloud. Then she said: frightened men who think they have seen a ghost do not invent a story about touching wounds and watching him eat fish. And men who invent a comfort do not die for it. He went home and read the whole chapter. A year later he was a catechist.

pm.open: Risen Lord Jesus, stand among us now and say, Peace be with you. Open our minds to understand the Scriptures. Alleluia. Amen.
share: You killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead (Acts 3:15). How have my own sins taken part in the Passion, and how do I receive his forgiveness?
If anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). Do I go to Jesus as my advocate after I sin, or do I hide?
Touch me and see (Luke 24:39). How do I touch the risen Lord today, in the sacraments and in the poor?
pm.resp: Lord, let your face shine on us.
interc: For the Church, that she may proclaim repentance and forgiveness to all nations.
For those who doubt the Resurrection, that the Lord may open their minds and hearts.
For friendship between Christians and the Jewish people, and for an end to all contempt.
For sinners who are afraid to come back, that they may know Jesus as their advocate.
For our group, that we may be witnesses of these things.
pm.close: Father, your Son showed his wounds and opened the Scriptures to his disciples. Make us faithful witnesses of his Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, told the council: there is salvation in no other name than Jesus.
Jesus is the good shepherd who knows his sheep and freely lays down his life for them and takes it up again.
We are God's children now, and we will see him as he is. Today we pray for vocations.
2027-04-18.action: Pray every day this week for vocations from your own parish, and thank your priest.
2027-04-18.question: Do I listen for the Good Shepherd's voice, and what is he calling me to?
catechism: Christ the gate and the Shepherd of the flock.
He lays down his life freely.
We shall see him as he is.
kidsaint: St John Vianney

A parish priest in a small village in France called Ars, about two hundred years ago. He was not very good at studies, but he loved Jesus and his people very much. He prayed for them, visited them, and sat for many hours every day in the confessional so that they could receive God's forgiveness. People came from all over France to see him. Lesson: a good shepherd gives his time and his heart to his sheep.
2027-04-18.special: Fourth Sunday of Easter (Good Shepherd Sunday). World Day of Prayer for Vocations. Gloria and Creed.
term: Vocation

From the Latin vocare, “to call.” God's call to every person: first to holiness through Baptism, and then to a particular way of life, as a priest or deacon, in consecrated life, or as a married or single layperson. On Good Shepherd Sunday the Church prays especially for vocations to the priesthood and consecrated life.

family.explain: Jesus said: I am the good shepherd. A shepherd takes care of his sheep. He knows each one by name, he finds food and water for them, and if a wolf comes, he does not run away. Jesus loves us so much that he gave his life for us on the cross, and then he rose again. He knows each of us by name!
family.intention: We pray for our parish priest, and for boys and girls whom Jesus may be calling to be priests and sisters.
family.ask: Ask: “What could Jesus be calling me to do with my life? Let us pray about it together.”

illus: An illustration

In a parish in Wayanad, a young man told his father he was thinking of the seminary. His father, a planter whose only son he was, refused even to discuss it. That monsoon the father fell seriously ill one night. It was the old parish priest, already over seventy, who came at two in the morning on his motorbike through the rain, sat with him in the hospital until dawn, and gave him the sacraments. When the father recovered, he called his son and said: if you want to be a priest, go. But be a priest like that one.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, Good Shepherd, you know us and we know you. Lead us, feed us, and call many to follow you. Alleluia. Amen.
share: There is no other name under heaven… by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Do I speak the name of Jesus with Peter's courage?
See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God (1 John 3:1). How does it change my day to know that I am God's child?
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). For whom am I called to lay down my life, a little each day?
pm.resp: The stone rejected by the builders has become the cornerstone. Alleluia.
interc: For Pope, bishops, priests and deacons, that they may be shepherds after the heart of Christ.
For an increase of vocations to the priesthood and consecrated life, especially from our own parish and families.
For seminarians, novices and their formators.
For all who do not yet know the Good Shepherd, and for the unity of Christians in one flock.
For parents, the first shepherds of their children.
pm.close: Father, through your Son, the Good Shepherd, you lead your flock to life. Give us shepherds after his own heart, and bring us all to see you as you are. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Barnabas brought Saul, whom all feared, to the apostles; the Church grew in peace and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.
Let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action; God is greater than our hearts.
Jesus: I am the vine, you are the branches; abide in me; apart from me you can do nothing.
2027-04-25.action: Do one costly act of love this week, quietly, as fruit of the Vine.
2027-04-25.question: Where in my life am I trying to bear fruit without abiding in Jesus?
catechism: Communion with Jesus: abide in me.
Apart from me you can do nothing.
kidsaint: St Mark the Evangelist

Mark was a young helper of St Paul and St Peter. Once he got scared and went home, but later he came back and became a great helper. He wrote down the story of Jesus in the Gospel of Mark, the shortest Gospel, full of action! His symbol is a lion. Lesson: even if we get scared or make mistakes, Jesus can still use us to do great things.
2027-04-25.special: Fifth Sunday of Easter, Year B: Gloria and Creed; the feast of St Mark is omitted this year; Regina Caeli at noon.
term: Abide

To remain, stay, dwell (Greek menein). In John's Gospel and letters it describes the lasting union of the disciple with Christ, through faith, love, the word and the Eucharist. To abide is not to visit Jesus sometimes but to live in him.

family.explain: Jesus says: I am the vine, a grape plant, and you are the branches. A branch that stays joined to the plant gets everything it needs and grows lots of grapes. But a branch that is broken off dries up. If we stay close to Jesus, by praying, going to Mass and loving others, his life flows into us, and we do good things.
family.intention: We pray for anyone in our family or among our friends who has drifted away from Jesus, that they may come back and be joined to the Vine again.
family.ask: Ask: “What helps our family stay joined to Jesus?” Choose one thing to do together every day this week, such as night prayer, and keep it faithfully.

illus: An illustration

In a parish near Kochi, a man released from prison after many years began coming to the early Sunday Mass. People moved away from him in the pew. The parish's St Vincent de Paul conference president, a retired bank clerk, noticed. The next Sunday he sat next to the man, invited him for tea, and later found him work at a friend's printing press. When some parishioners complained, he said quietly: Barnabas did this for Paul. Two years later the same man was serving as a volunteer in the parish kitchen for the poor, and people who once avoided him now ask for him by name.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, true vine, we are your branches. Keep us in you, and let your life flow in us so that we bear much fruit. Alleluia. Amen.
share: Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles (Acts 9:27). Who needs me to stand by them as Barnabas stood by Paul?
Let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action (1 John 3:18). What act of love have I been only talking about?
Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). Where am I trying to manage without Jesus?
pm.resp: I will praise you, Lord, in the assembly of your people.
interc: For the Church, that she may live in peace, be built up and grow in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.
For those who are distrusted because of their past, that they may find a Barnabas in our community.
For those whose hearts condemn them, that they may know that God is greater than their hearts.
For all who are being pruned by suffering, illness or loss, that they may bear more fruit.
For our group, that we may abide in Christ every day and love in truth and action.
pm.close: Father, vinegrower of the vineyard of your Church, keep us joined to Christ the true vine, and make us bear fruit that gives you glory. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Peter: not by our power, but the God of our ancestors has glorified his servant Jesus, the Author of life.
Jesus shows his hands and feet and eats broiled fish: his Resurrection is real and bodily.
He opens the Scriptures and sends his disciples as witnesses of forgiveness to all nations.
2027-04-01.action: Pray tonight with your family for the priests of your parish, and thank God for one sign of his help this week.
2027-04-01.question: When good news from God seems too good to be true, do I let my joy turn into disbelief, or into praise?
catechism: The risen body of Jesus, real and glorious.
The Jews are not collectively responsible for Jesus' death.
Conversion: turning to God and away from sin, as Peter preached.
kidsaint: St Hugh of Grenoble

A story tells that Bishop Hugh once dreamed that God was building a house in the mountains and seven stars were leading the way. Soon seven men came to him, led by St Bruno, asking for a quiet place to pray. Hugh gave them a valley in the mountains, and the Carthusian monks still pray there today. Lesson: when God sends people to us, we can help them do his work.
2027-04-01.special: Thursday within the Octave of Easter (solemnity): Gloria; the Easter Sequence may be sung; double Alleluia at the dismissal. First Thursday of the month.
term: Witness

In Greek martys, the word from which “martyr” comes. A witness tells what he has seen and heard, and stakes his life on it. The Apostles were witnesses of the Resurrection, and most of them gave their lives for it.

family.explain: The friends of Jesus were talking together when suddenly Jesus was there with them! They were frightened and thought he was a ghost. Jesus said: look at my hands and my feet, touch me. Then he asked for something to eat, and they gave him a piece of fish. Jesus was really alive, with a real body.
family.intention: We pray for everyone who is afraid, that Jesus may give them his peace.
family.ask: Ask: “What would you say to Jesus if he came into our home tonight?” Then greet one another with: Peace be with you.

illus: An illustration

A young fisherman from Poovar was lost at sea for four days after a storm. His family had already lit lamps for him and the parish had prayed for the dead. On the fifth morning he walked up the beach, thin and burnt by the sun. His old mother would not come near him; she kept saying, it is his spirit. He laughed, sat down on the steps and said, Amma, give me some kanji, I am starving. Only when she saw him eat did she run and hold him. The Risen Lord did the same for his frightened friends: he ate, so that they would believe.

pm.open: Risen Lord Jesus, stand among us now and say to us, Peace be with you. Open our minds to understand your word. Alleluia. Amen.
share: Not by our own power (Acts 3:12). Where am I tempted to take the glory that belongs to God?
Touch me and see (Luke 24:39). How have I experienced the real presence of the Risen Lord?
You are witnesses of these things (Luke 24:48). To whom is the Lord sending me this week?
pm.resp: O Lord, our God, how wonderful your name in all the earth!
interc: For the Church, that she may proclaim repentance and forgiveness to every nation.
For the Jewish people, the first to hear the word of God, that they may grow in faithfulness to his covenant.
For priests, especially those who are tired or discouraged, on this first Thursday.
For all who are frightened or doubting, that the Risen Lord may show them his wounds and give them peace.
For our group, that we may be humble witnesses who give God the glory.
pm.close: Father, you glorified your servant Jesus and raised him from the dead. Make us witnesses of his Resurrection in word and deed. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Peter before the council: the healed man stands here by the name of Jesus, the rejected stone made cornerstone.
There is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved.
At the Sea of Tiberias the Risen Lord fills the net and gives his disciples bread and fish.
2027-04-02.action: Make a visit to the Blessed Sacrament this First Friday and say: “It is the Lord!”
2027-04-02.question: In which empty night of my life do I need to hear Jesus say: cast the net again?
catechism: Salvation in the name of Jesus alone.
Christ the cornerstone of the Church.
The name of Jesus contains all: God and man and the whole economy of salvation.
kidsaint: St Francis of Paola

Francis loved God so much that he went to live alone in a cave when he was only a boy. Later many men joined him, and they lived very simply, eating no meat, to show their love for God. A story tells that once a boatman would not take him across the sea, so Francis spread his cloak on the water and crossed on it! His favourite word was “Charity,” which means love. Lesson: love is the most important word of all.
2027-04-02.special: Friday within the Octave of Easter (solemnity): Gloria; the Easter Sequence may be sung; double Alleluia at the dismissal. No Friday abstinence. First Friday of the month.
term: Ichthys

The Greek word for “fish.” Its letters were read as the first letters of “Iēsous Christos Theou Yios Sōtēr,” Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour. Early Christians drew a fish as a secret sign of their faith.

family.explain: Peter and his friends went fishing all night and caught nothing. In the morning a man on the shore told them to throw the net on the right side. Suddenly the net was full of big fish! John cried out: It is the Lord! Peter jumped into the water to reach him. Jesus had made a fire and cooked breakfast for them.
family.intention: We pray for fishermen and for all who work hard and are tired, that Jesus may bless their work.
family.ask: Ask: “Who in our family works very hard for us?” Make a small breakfast surprise for them tomorrow.

illus: An illustration
