Moses had said the same: this commandment that I am commanding you today is not too hard for you, nor is it too far away (Deuteronomy 30:11). Why are they not burdensome? Because the risen Lord gives us his grace to keep them. A heavy load becomes light when someone strong carries it with us.

And John declares: this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith (1 John 5:4). Thomas, in today's Gospel, moved from doubt to faith. The world tells us that money, power and pleasure are what win. John tells us that the one who believes in the risen Christ has already won. Faith is our victory over fear, over despair and over sin.

Finally John writes: this is the one who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ, not with the water only but with the water and the blood (1 John 5:6). John had seen the soldier's spear open the side of Jesus, and water and blood flow out. Zechariah had foretold: on that day a fountain shall be opened… to cleanse them from sin and impurity (Zechariah 13:1). In the image of Divine Mercy, two rays stream from the Heart of Jesus. St Faustina was told that the pale ray stands for the water that makes souls righteous, and the red ray for the blood that is the life of souls.

So let us stand today before that fountain. Let us thank God for the water of our Baptism and for the Blood we receive at this Mass. Let us keep his commandments with joy, and pray the Chaplet this week for the whole world. Have mercy on us and on the whole world. Jesus, I trust in you. Alleluia. Amen.

Dear brothers and sisters, the disciples are gathered in Jerusalem on the evening of Easter. The two from Emmaus are telling their story. And suddenly Jesus himself stands among them and says: Peace be with you. They are terrified. They think they are seeing a ghost.

Jesus does not scold them. He says: look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have (Luke 24:39). And then he asks: have you anything here to eat? He eats a piece of fish in front of them. Our faith is not in a ghost or a memory. Jesus rose in his real body, the same body that was crucified, now glorified for ever.

Why does this matter for us? Because our bodies matter. The body that works in the field, the body that is sick in the hospital, the body that grows old, is not thrown away. We believe in the resurrection of the body. And because the risen Lord has a body, he can give it to us. At this altar he gives us not a symbol but his own risen Body and Blood.

In the first reading Peter speaks to the crowd in Jerusalem: you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. But then he says: I know that you acted in ignorance. Repent, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out (Acts 3:17, 19). Peter had denied Jesus three times. He knows what forgiveness is. He does not preach blame; he preaches mercy. And the Church teaches that all of us, by our sins, share in the Passion.

St John says the same in the second reading: if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1). When we fall, we are not alone before the Father. Jesus stands beside us, showing his wounds, pleading for us. That is why the sacrament of confession is an Easter sacrament: the risen Lord breathes peace on our sins.

Finally Jesus opens their minds to understand the Scriptures and says: you are witnesses of these things (Luke 24:48). We too have been with him today. We have heard his word, we will receive his Body. Let us go out as witnesses: with peace in our hearts, mercy on our lips, and a table open to those who eat alone. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, when Jesus came to his friends after Easter, they thought he was a ghost! But Jesus said: touch my hands and my feet. Ghosts don't have bodies! And then he ate some fish in front of them. Yum! Jesus is really, really alive.
Today at Mass, Jesus comes to us in Holy Communion. We cannot see his hands, but he is really there. Let us say thank you, Jesus, because you are alive!

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today is Good Shepherd Sunday. In the middle of the Easter season the Church shows us the risen Jesus as the shepherd who knows us by name and leads us home. And today we pray in a special way for vocations.

In the first reading Peter stands before the most powerful council in Jerusalem. Only weeks before, he had denied Jesus to a servant girl. Now, filled with the Holy Spirit, he says: there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). The Good Shepherd has made a frightened sheep into a fearless shepherd.

In the Gospel Jesus says: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). He compares himself with the hired hand who runs away when the wolf comes. Why does the hired hand run? Because he does not care for the sheep. The good shepherd stays, because he loves. And Jesus did not only risk his life; he gave it on the cross, freely, and took it up again on Easter morning.

He also says: I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14). You are not a number to him. He knows your name, your story, your wounds. And he has other sheep too, not yet in the fold. He wants one flock and one shepherd. So we pray today for those far from him and for the unity of all Christians.

St John tells us what that love has made of us: see what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God; and that is what we are (1 John 3:1). One day we will see him as he is. That is where the Shepherd is leading us.

And the Shepherd still calls shepherds. Let us pray for our priests, who give their lives for us. Let us thank them. And let every family ask: could Jesus be calling one of ours? Do not be afraid if he is. There is no greater joy than to follow the Good Shepherd wherever he leads. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: I am the good shepherd. A good shepherd knows all his sheep by name. Jesus knows your name too! He loves you so much that he gave his life for you, and he rose again to be with you always.
Jesus also needs helpers to be shepherds for his people: priests and sisters. Maybe one day he will call you! Let us pray: Jesus, Good Shepherd, help me to listen to your voice.

homily: Dear friends, if you cut a branch from a mango tree, for a day or two it stays green. It looks alive. But it has no future. In a few days its leaves are dry. Jesus says today: I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5).

Look at the first reading. Saul, the former persecutor, comes to Jerusalem, but everyone is afraid of him. Nobody trusts him. Then Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles (Acts 9:27). Barnabas trusted when others feared. He gave Paul a place in the Church.

Where did Barnabas get that courage and that generosity? From the Vine. He was a branch joined to Christ, and the fruit of Christ's life in him was encouragement. Is there someone in our parish, perhaps someone with a bad past, a broken family, a different background, who needs a Barnabas? Will you be that person?

St John tells us in the second reading: little children, let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action (1 John 3:18). Our love must be seen. And if our hearts accuse us, if we feel we are not good enough, John says: God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything. Do not let guilt cut you off from the Vine; bring it to him in confession.

Jesus also speaks of pruning. The Father prunes every fruitful branch to make it bear more fruit. Sometimes life cuts us: illness, loss, failure. It hurts. But in the Father's hands, pruning is not punishment; it is love preparing a greater harvest.

How do we abide in Christ? In prayer every day. In the word of God. Above all in the Eucharist: whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. Today is also the day we would have kept the feast of St Mark, who wrote the Gospel. Let us thank God for him, and for the Blessed Virgin Mary, whose month begins this week. Let us stay joined to the Vine, and bear much fruit. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, a branch on a plant gets its food from the plant. If you break it off, it dries up. Jesus says: I am the vine, you are the branches!
When we pray, go to Mass and love others, we stay joined to Jesus, and we grow good fruit like kindness and joy. Let us say: Jesus, keep me close to you!

homily: Dear friends, a man who could not walk for forty years now clings to Peter and John, and a whole crowd runs together to see. Peter could have enjoyed the attention. Instead he says: why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we had made him walk? (Acts 3:12). The healing belongs to Jesus.
This is a good test for all of us. When God does something good through us, do we keep the credit, or do we pass it on to him? A humble witness points away from himself, to the Risen Lord.

Then Peter says hard words: you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. But at once he adds: I know that you acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17). He does not condemn; he invites. Repent, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out. Peter, who had denied the Lord, knows how good it is to be forgiven.

In the Gospel Jesus stands among his disciples and they think he is a ghost. So he says: look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see (Luke 24:39). And he eats a piece of broiled fish in front of them. Our faith is not in a ghost or an idea. Jesus is truly risen in his body, the same body that was wounded for us.

Luke tells us that in their joy they were disbelieving. Sometimes the good news is so big we are afraid to believe it. Our sins forgiven? Death defeated? Heaven open? Yes. The Lord shows us his wounds so that we may dare to believe.

Then he opens the Scriptures and says: you are witnesses of these things (Luke 24:48). That word is for us too. At this Mass the Risen Lord will stand among us and give us his Body. Let us go home and be his witnesses, beginning in our own Jerusalem, our own family. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, the friends of Jesus thought they were seeing a ghost. Jesus said: touch me! And he ate a piece of fish. Jesus is really alive!
Jesus is alive with a real body, and he loves us. When you are afraid, say: Jesus, give me your peace.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the leaders of the Temple ask Peter and John a question: by what power or by what name did you do this? (Acts 4:7). It is a good question for every Christian. When people see us forgive, serve or hope, they should be able to ask: in whose name do you do this?

Peter answers with the courage of the Holy Spirit: by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead. A few weeks before, he was afraid of a servant girl. Now he is not afraid of the high priest. The Resurrection and the Spirit have changed him.

And Peter says: there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). Jesus is not one teacher among many. He is the Saviour. That is why we pray in his name, are baptized in his name and live in his name.

In the Gospel the disciples have fished all night and caught nothing. Many of us know nights like that: work without fruit, prayers that seem unanswered, efforts that fail. At daybreak Jesus stands on the shore and calls: children, you have no fish, have you? He knows our empty nets.

He tells them to cast the net again, on the right side. They obey, and the net is full. The beloved disciple cries out: it is the Lord! (John 21:7). Love recognizes him first. When we obey his word, even in small things, we begin to see that he was with us all along.

On the shore the Lord has already prepared a fire and breakfast. He says: come and have breakfast. And he takes the bread and gives it to them. This is what he does at every Mass. Today, on this First Friday, let us come to him tired as we are, and let him feed us. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, the disciples fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus told them to try again, and the net was full of fish! John shouted: it is the Lord!
Then Jesus made breakfast for his friends. Jesus takes care of us too. Let us say: thank you, Jesus, for loving us!

homily: Dear friends, the leaders look at Peter and John and see ordinary men, fishermen without formal training. Yet they speak with a boldness that astonishes everyone. And the leaders understand: they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13).

That is the secret of every true witness. Not cleverness, not money, not position, but time spent with Jesus. If we pray, read the Gospel and come to Mass, people will see it in our faces and hear it in our words.

The council orders them never again to speak in the name of Jesus. Peter and John answer: whether it is right in God's sight to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge; for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard (Acts 4:19–20). They are respectful, but they will not deny the truth.

The Gospel tells us something surprising. The Eleven did not believe Mary Magdalene. They did not believe the two disciples from Emmaus. When Jesus came, he upbraided them for their lack of faith and stubbornness (Mark 16:14). The Apostles were not easy believers. Their faith was won by the Risen Lord himself.

And yet, to these same slow disciples, Jesus says: go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation (Mark 16:15). He does not wait until we are perfect. He sends us as we are, forgiven and loved.

Tomorrow is Divine Mercy Sunday. Today is a good day to make a good confession and finish the novena. Let us ask for the grace to be with Jesus, so that we too cannot keep from speaking of him. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, some leaders told Peter and John: do not talk about Jesus! But they said: we cannot stop, because we have seen him alive!
Jesus wants us to tell everyone that he loves them. Who can you tell about Jesus today?

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today the Church does something unusual. In the middle of the Easter season she takes us back to Nazareth, to a quiet house and a young woman at prayer. The Annunciation fell on Holy Thursday this year, so it was moved to today. And how fitting it is: the child announced by the angel is the Lord who has just risen from the dead.

In the first reading King Ahaz is afraid. God offers him a sign, and he refuses with pious words. But God gives a sign anyway: the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall name him Emmanuel, God is with us (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23). God does not wait for our perfect faith before he comes near.

The Letter to the Hebrews tells us what the Son said when he came into the world: a body you have prepared for me; see, God, I have come to do your will (Hebrews 10:5, 7). Before Mary said yes, the Son said yes. The body prepared in Mary's womb would one day be offered on the cross for us, and that same body rose on Easter morning.

Then the angel comes to Mary: Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you. Mary does not run away and does not pretend. She asks an honest question: how can this be? And the angel answers: the Holy Spirit will come upon you; nothing will be impossible with God. Then Mary says the most important yes in history: here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word (Luke 1:38).

Today, when we say the Creed, we will kneel at the words: and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man. We kneel because God became small for us. The great God who made the stars became a tiny child, hidden for nine months. And at this altar he becomes small again, hidden in the bread that is his Body.

So let us ask Mary today for her faith. Ahaz said no out of fear; Mary said yes out of love. Whatever God is asking of you this Easter, a forgiveness, a vocation, a child, a sacrifice, say with her: let it be with me according to your word. Holy Mary, rejoice, for your Son has risen. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago an angel came to a girl named Mary. He said: God wants you to be the mother of his Son, Jesus. Mary said: yes, I am God's servant. And Jesus began to grow inside her, like every baby grows inside its mother.
Today at Mass, when we say “and became man,” we kneel down to say thank you to Jesus for becoming a baby for us. Let us say yes to God like Mary!

intro: The angel's first word to Mary is not a command but an invitation to joy. In Easter week we hear it with new meaning: rejoice, for the Lord is with you.

points.apply: Greet Mary each day this week with the Hail Mary prayed slowly.
Thank God for the grace he gave you before you knew it.
Pray the Regina Caeli at noon each day of this Easter season.

concl: The Annunciation begins with joy and ends with a kingdom that has no end.
Mary, full of grace, rejoices now in her risen Son.
opts.resolve: This Easter season I will pray the Regina Caeli each day and greet Mary with joy.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the angel Gabriel's first word to Mary was not obey, or fear, or listen. It was: rejoice. Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you (Luke 1:28). The Greek word means rejoice. Centuries before, the prophet Zephaniah had cried: sing aloud, O daughter Zion; shout, O Israel! Rejoice and exult with all your heart, O daughter Jerusalem! The LORD, your God, is in your midst (Zephaniah 3:14, 17). Mary is that daughter Zion. In her womb the Lord will truly be in the midst of his people.

Gabriel calls her favored one, which the Church has long rendered full of grace. Before she said yes, God had already filled her with grace. The Church teaches that from the first moment of her conception Mary was preserved from every stain of original sin, by the merits of her Son. God's grace came first, and Mary's yes was the response. It is the same in our lives: God loves us before we love him.

Then the angel announces the child: he will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give to him the throne of his ancestor David. He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32–33). Isaiah had foretold a child whose authority would grow continually, with endless peace for the throne of David (Isaiah 9:7). This week we celebrate that King risen from the dead.

For centuries Christians have honoured this moment three times a day with the Angelus: morning, noon and evening. The psalmist prayed evening and morning and at noon (Psalm 55:17). In the Easter season the Angelus gives way to the Regina Caeli: Queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia; for he whom you were worthy to bear has risen as he said. The joy announced at Nazareth is fulfilled at the empty tomb.

So let us greet Mary today as Gabriel did, with joy. Let us pray the Regina Caeli each day this season. And at this Mass, as we kneel at the words and became man, let us rejoice that the Lord is with us too. Holy Mary, full of grace, pray for us. Alleluia. Amen.

opts.a: Every life from its first moment
intro: At the Annunciation the Son of God began his human life as every one of us began ours: hidden in his mother's womb. This feast teaches us the dignity of every human life from conception.

sub: The Word becomes flesh at Mary's yes.
points.apply: Pray each day for mothers who are expecting a child.
Help one expecting mother or young family this month.
Pray for couples longing for a child and for mothers in difficulty.

concl: Because the Son of God was once an unborn child, every unborn child is precious.
The Church protects life and offers mercy and help to every mother.
opts.resolve: This month I will pray for unborn children and help one mother or family in need.
homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate the moment when the eternal Son of God became man. And how did he become man? Not as a grown man coming down from the sky. He began as every one of us began: a tiny life, hidden in his mother's womb. The angel said: you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will name him Jesus (Luke 1:31). For nine months the Creator of the world was smaller than a seed.

The psalmist prayed: for it was you who formed my inward parts; you knit me together in my mother's womb (Psalm 139:13). This is true of every person. God said to Jeremiah: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5). And the angel tells Mary that Elizabeth is in her sixth month (Luke 1:36). Two hidden children, John and Jesus, each known and loved by God before anyone had seen them.

This is why the Church teaches that human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception (Catechism 2270). It is fitting that St John Paul II signed his great letter on the Gospel of Life on the feast of the Annunciation. Because God himself was once an unborn child, no unborn child is ever unimportant. Every life is a gift and a vocation.

But the angel also said: nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37). God had asked Abraham: is anything too wonderful for the LORD? (Genesis 18:14). These words are for couples who long for a child, for mothers who are frightened by an unexpected pregnancy, and for those who carry the wound of having ended a life. The Church does not condemn and walk away. She protects the child, helps the mother, and offers Christ's mercy to all who repent.

So today, let us thank God for the gift of our own lives. Let us pray for unborn children and their mothers. Let us help expecting families in our parish. And at this Mass, as we kneel at the words and became man, let us adore the God who chose to begin so small. Alleluia. Amen.

Dear friends, St Luke tells us that the first Christians were of one heart and soul, and no one said that anything he owned was his own (Acts 4:32). Why were they like this? Luke gives the reason in the very next sentence: with great power the apostles gave their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. When we really believe that Christ is risen, our grip on things loosens.

Then we meet Barnabas, son of encouragement. He sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet. Later he will be the one who welcomes the converted Saul when everyone else is afraid of him. A generous hand and an encouraging heart go together. Every parish needs its Barnabas.

In the Gospel Nicodemus is puzzled about being born again. Jesus says: the wind blows where it chooses; so it is with everyone born of the Spirit (John 3:8). We cannot see the Spirit, but we can see what he does: a selfish man begins to share, a frightened woman begins to speak, a family begins to pray again.

And Jesus points to the cross: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up (John 3:14). Look at him and live. Let us look at him today, at the altar where his sacrifice is made present, and ask him to make us one heart and soul, and to make each of us a Barnabas for someone this week. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, after Easter the friends of Jesus shared everything they had, so no one was hungry. A kind man called Barnabas gave away his field to help the poor, and everyone called him son of encouragement, because he always made people feel brave and happy. Can you be a Barnabas today? Say something kind to someone who is sad!

homily: Dear friends, the apostles are locked in prison, and in the night an angel opens the doors. Does he tell them to run away? No. He says: go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life (Acts 5:20). God frees us not for our comfort but for our mission.

In the morning the guards find the prison locked, the doors guarded, and nobody inside. It sounds like Easter morning: a sealed tomb, and nobody inside. The risen Lord cannot be locked away, and neither can his word.

Then Jesus says to Nicodemus: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son; God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him (John 3:16–17). God is not waiting to catch us. He is waiting to save us. The only thing that keeps us from the light is our own preference for darkness.

Today we remember St John Baptist de la Salle. He was rich and comfortable, but he saw poor children growing up in darkness, without school and without faith. He gave away his fortune, gathered teachers, and opened schools without fees. He said to his Brothers, in substance: you can work miracles by touching the hearts of children. Let us pray today for every teacher, and let us be people who bring others into the light. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, today is the day of St John Baptist de la Salle, the friend of all teachers. He opened schools for poor children so that they could learn to read and learn about Jesus. Let us say a prayer for our teachers today, and say thank you to them tomorrow!

homily: Dear friends, the apostles stand before the most powerful court in their nation. They are told: stop teaching in this name. And Peter says: we must obey God rather than any human authority (Acts 5:29). These are not proud words. These are the words of a man who once denied Jesus out of fear, and who has now been changed by the Resurrection and the Spirit.

And what does Peter preach to his judges? Not anger. He says God raised Jesus to give repentance and forgiveness of sins. Even to those who opposed him, the risen Lord offers mercy. The Easter message is never a weapon against anyone; it is a door opened to everyone.

Peter says one more thing: we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit. We are never alone when we speak of Jesus. In the Gospel John says that Jesus gives the Spirit without measure (John 3:34). He does not give the Spirit with a teaspoon. He pours him out.

So let us ask today for that Spirit. In our offices, our schools, our families, there are moments when we must choose between what people want and what God wants. Let us ask for the courage of Peter, and the gentleness of Peter too, so that our witness may be both firm and kind. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, the leaders told Peter: stop talking about Jesus! Peter was not afraid any more, because the Holy Spirit made him brave. He said: we must obey God first. When someone asks you to do something wrong, you can say: I want to obey God. The Holy Spirit will help you!

homily: Dear friends, the council wants to kill the apostles, and a wise teacher named Gamaliel stands up. He says: if this plan is of human origin, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them (Acts 5:38–39). Two thousand years later, the Church is still here. Not because we are strong, but because the work is God's.

The apostles are flogged, and they go out rejoicing that they were worthy to suffer for the name of Jesus. What a change from the frightened men behind locked doors! The risen Lord does not take away the suffering, but he fills it with joy.

In the Gospel a boy gives Jesus five barley loaves and two fish. It seems like nothing. Jesus takes them, gives thanks, and distributes them, and five thousand people eat as much as they want (John 6:11). Our gifts always seem small. But in Jesus' hands they become enough, and more than enough.

Notice the words: he took, he gave thanks, he distributed. These are the words of the Mass. And at the end Jesus says: gather up the fragments, so that nothing may be lost. At the altar today he will feed us with the true Bread, his own Body. Let us bring him our five loaves, and leave nothing of his gift wasted. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, a little boy had a small lunch: five small breads and two fish. He gave it all to Jesus. Jesus thanked God and shared it, and more than five thousand people ate! When we give Jesus even a little, he can do great things with it. What will you give Jesus today?

homily: Dear friends, the first Church had a problem. Some widows were being forgotten in the daily distribution of food. The Greek-speaking believers complained. The apostles did not say: everything is fine. They listened, called everyone together and found a solution: seven men full of the Spirit and of wisdom, chosen to serve (Acts 6:3).

Look at the result. The forgotten widows were cared for, the apostles could give themselves to prayer and the word, and the word of God spread. A complaint, when it is heard with humility, can become a grace. Every parish has its forgotten widows. Who are they in ours?

In the Gospel the disciples are rowing at night against a strong wind. John says: it was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them (John 6:17). Many of us know that feeling. Then they see Jesus walking on the water, and he says: it is I; do not be afraid (John 6:20). In Greek it is simply: I AM, the name of God.

The storm may come from inside, like the quarrel over the widows, or from outside, like the wind on the sea. In both, the risen Lord comes to us. Today at this altar he comes again, and says: it is I. Let us take him into our boat, and trust that he will bring us to the shore. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, the friends of Jesus were in a boat at night, and a big wind was blowing. They were afraid. Then Jesus came walking on the water and said: It is I; do not be afraid! When you are scared at night, you can say: Jesus, you are with me. I am not afraid!

homily: Dear friends, Stephen was chosen to serve food to widows. A humble job. But the Spirit does not stay inside job descriptions: the man who served tables was full of grace and power, and his wisdom was so strong that his opponents could not answer him (Acts 6:10).

So they found false witnesses, as they had for Jesus. And at that moment, when anyone else would be angry or afraid, the whole council looked at Stephen and saw that his face was like the face of an angel (Acts 6:15). That is what Easter does to a person. The risen Lord gives a peace that accusations cannot take away.

In the Gospel a crowd crosses the lake looking for Jesus. It sounds wonderful, until Jesus tells them the truth: you are looking for me because you ate your fill of the loaves (John 6:26). They wanted more bread, not the One who gives it. Many of us pray like that: we come when we need something, and disappear when we have it.

Jesus does not send them away. He offers them more than they asked: work for the food that endures for eternal life. And when they ask what work they must do, he gives them one: believe in him whom God has sent (John 6:29). Faith first, and everything else grows from it. At this Mass he gives us that food that endures, his own Body and Blood. Let us seek him today not only for his gifts but for himself. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, the people followed Jesus because he gave them bread to eat. Jesus said: I have an even better bread for you, a bread that makes you live for ever! That bread is Jesus himself, in Holy Communion. Today let us tell Jesus: I love you, not only for what you give me, but because you are you!

homily: Dear friends, today we stand with Stephen at the moment of his death. Stones are flying, but he is looking somewhere else: he gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55). Jesus stands up for his witness. No one who suffers for him suffers alone.

Listen to Stephen's last prayers. Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Then, on his knees: Lord, do not hold this sin against them (Acts 7:59–60). He has learned to pray from the cross. And his prayer was heard in a way no one expected: the young man holding the coats was Saul. St Augustine said, in substance, that if Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul.

In the Gospel the people ask Jesus for a sign like the manna. Jesus says: it was not Moses but my Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. And then: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry (John 6:35). The manna lasted one day. Jesus is the bread that gives the life of God for ever.

Today we also remember St Martin I, a pope who would not change the truth about Jesus to please an emperor. He died in exile, hungry for bread, but fed with the bread of life. Let us ask for their courage and their forgiving hearts, and receive with faith today the bread that never fails. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Stephen was hurt by angry people, but he did not hate them. He prayed: Jesus, forgive them. Jesus is happy when we forgive. And Jesus said: I am the bread of life. When we receive him in Holy Communion, he fills our hearts with his love so that we can forgive too.

homily: Dear friends, after Stephen's death it seemed that everything was falling apart. A great persecution began, and believers fled from Jerusalem in every direction. But St Luke says: those who were scattered went from place to place, proclaiming the word (Acts 8:4). The wind that was meant to blow out the fire only carried its sparks further.

Philip went to Samaria, a people the Jews had kept apart from for centuries. He proclaimed Christ, the sick were healed, and so there was great joy in that city (Acts 8:8). God's word does not stay within our walls. Many of you know what it is to be scattered: for work, for study, for family. Wherever you go, you take the word with you.

In the Gospel Jesus says something every one of us needs to hear: anyone who comes to me I will never drive away (John 6:37). Not the one who has failed, not the one who has been away for years. And he tells us the Father's will: that he should lose nothing of what the Father has given him, but raise it up on the last day.

That is our Easter hope. Not only that our souls live on, but that our bodies will be raised. Every time we receive the Bread of Life, we receive the pledge of that resurrection. So let us come to him without fear, and carry his joy wherever life scatters us. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus said: I will never send away anyone who comes to me. That means you can always come to Jesus: when you are happy, when you are sad, even when you have been naughty! He always opens his arms. Let us run to him today and say: Jesus, here I am!

homily: Dear friends, Philip was busy with a great mission in Samaria, and God sent him to a desert road for one man. The Lord does not only care for crowds. He will send an evangelist across a desert for a single seeking heart.

That man was reading Isaiah and could not understand it. When Philip asked: do you understand what you are reading?, he answered: how can I, unless someone guides me? (Acts 8:31). Many people today are like him: they have a Bible, or a memory of the faith, but no one to sit beside them. You could be that Philip for someone.

Philip started from the passage about the Lamb led to the slaughter and told him about Jesus. Then they came to water, and the man said: look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized? (Acts 8:36). The man the old law had kept outside was welcomed into God's family. He went on his way rejoicing.

In the Gospel Jesus says: I am the living bread that came down from heaven; the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh (John 6:51). The Lamb the Ethiopian read about is the Bread we receive. Let us come to him with faith, and then go out like that man from Africa, on our way rejoicing. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, a man was reading the Bible in his chariot, but he did not understand it. God sent Philip to help him. Philip told him about Jesus, and the man was baptized and was so happy! Whenever you do not understand something about Jesus, ask your parents, your teacher or Father. God loves it when we ask!

homily: Dear friends, Saul was on his way to arrest Christians. Suddenly a light from heaven, and a voice: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? Saul asks: who are you, Lord? And the answer: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting (Acts 9:4–5). Not my disciples. Me.

Jesus is so united with his people that what is done to them is done to him. When we hurt one another, we hurt Christ. When we serve the poor, we serve Christ. The Church is not a club of his admirers; it is his body.

Then comes Ananias, a simple disciple who is afraid of Saul, and rightly so. But he obeys. He goes into the house, lays his hands on the man who came to arrest people like him, and says: Brother Saul (Acts 9:17). With that one word the persecutor becomes family. Who is the Saul in your life to whom you need to say: brother, sister?

In the Gospel Jesus says the strongest words about the Eucharist: my flesh is true food and my blood is true drink. Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood abide in me, and I in them (John 6:55–56). He does not say: this is like my body. He gives himself. So let us receive him with faith, and then go out to be his body for others. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Saul was mean to Christians. But Jesus loved him and spoke to him with a great light. Saul changed and became St Paul, one of Jesus' greatest friends! Jesus can change anyone's heart. And in Holy Communion Jesus gives us his own Body, so that he lives in us and we live in him.

homily: Dear friends, after the persecution the Church had peace and grew in the comfort of the Holy Spirit (Acts 9:31). Peter went from place to place visiting the believers. At Lydda he met Aeneas, paralyzed for eight years, and said: Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; get up (Acts 9:34). Not I heal you. Jesus Christ heals you.

At Joppa a good woman, Tabitha, had died. The widows showed Peter the clothes she had made for them. That was her whole life story: good works and acts of charity. Peter knelt and prayed and said: Tabitha, get up. And she opened her eyes (Acts 9:40). The risen Lord is still raising the dead to life.

In the Gospel many disciples said about the Eucharist: this teaching is difficult; who can accept it? (John 6:60). And they left. Jesus did not run after them to make it easier. He turned to the Twelve and asked: do you also wish to go away?

Peter answered with words we can make our own on the hardest days: Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life (John 6:68). He did not say: we understand everything. He said: we know you. When faith is hard, let us not walk away. Let us stay with him, receive him, and ask him to give us the Spirit who gives life. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Tabitha loved to sew clothes for poor people. Everyone loved her! When she died, Peter prayed and said: Tabitha, get up! And God gave her life again. Some people stopped following Jesus because his words were hard. But Peter said: Jesus, we will stay with you! Let us say it too: Jesus, I will always stay with you!

homily: Dear friends, Peter is in trouble with his own community. He has eaten with Gentiles. And the Christians in Jerusalem, good and faithful Jews, are upset. How does the chief of the apostles answer? Not with anger. He explains, step by step, what God has done.

He tells them about the vision: a sheet full of unclean animals and a voice saying, what God has made clean, you must not call profane (Acts 11:9). Then he tells them that the Holy Spirit fell on Cornelius and his family, just as on the apostles at Pentecost.

And he asks: who was I that I could hinder God? (Acts 11:17). That question is for us too. How often do we stand at the gate and decide who may come in? How often do we hinder God by our prejudice, our caste thinking, our coldness to strangers?
Notice what the listeners do. They fall silent, and then they praise God. That is the sign of a living Church: when the Spirit shows us something new, we stop arguing and we praise.

In the Gospel Jesus says: I am the gate. There is one way into life, and it is Jesus. And he is a shepherd who knows each sheep by name. He does not come like a thief to take from us. He says: I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly (John 10:10).
Today, let us listen for that voice. And let us keep the gate open, in our homes and our parishes, for everyone the Shepherd is calling. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, a shepherd calls his sheep by name, and they come running because they know his voice. Jesus knows your name too!
Jesus says: I am the gate. When we come to Jesus, we are safe, and he gives us a happy, full life. Let us say: Jesus, I am listening!

homily: Dear friends, after Stephen was killed, the believers ran away from Jerusalem. It looked like the end. But Luke tells us that wherever they went, they spoke about Jesus. They were scattered like seed, and the seed grew.

In Antioch some unnamed believers did something new: they told the Greeks about the Lord Jesus. And the hand of the Lord was with them (Acts 11:21). Many of us, too, have been scattered, to the Gulf, to Europe, to other states. God can use our scattering to sow his word.

Then the Church sends Barnabas. Luke says he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. When he saw the grace of God, he rejoiced (Acts 11:23). He did not complain that things were done without his permission. He rejoiced, and he encouraged.

And he went to look for Saul, a man others were afraid of. He gave him a place. Together they taught for a whole year, and in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians. That is our name too. Do we live up to it?

In the Gospel Jesus says: my sheep hear my voice; I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:27–28). Whatever storms we face, we are held. And the hand that holds us is the Father's hand, for Jesus says: the Father and I are one.
Today let us be Barnabas for someone: let us see grace and rejoice. And let us rest in the hand of the Shepherd, from which no one can snatch us. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says he holds his sheep in his hand, so tightly that no one can take them away. You are in Jesus' hand!
At Antioch the friends of Jesus were first called Christians. That is your name too. Let us say: Jesus, I belong to you!

homily: Dear friends, in the church at Antioch the leaders are at prayer. They are worshiping and fasting. And in that prayer the Holy Spirit speaks: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them (Acts 13:2). The greatest missionary journey in history began in a prayer meeting.

The Church did not choose Paul's mission by a committee vote. It prayed, it fasted, it listened, and it obeyed. Then they laid hands on them and sent them off. Whenever we have important decisions, in our families, our parishes, our lives, let us learn from Antioch: pray first, then act.

Look also at who those leaders were: a Cypriot, a man called Niger, the black, a man from Cyrene in Africa, a member of Herod's court, and a former persecutor. The Church was already one family of many nations.

In the Gospel Jesus cries out: I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me should not remain in the darkness (John 12:46). He did not come to condemn but to save. Whoever sees Jesus sees the Father.

Today we remember St Anselm, a monk who became Archbishop of Canterbury. He loved to think about God, but he always thought on his knees. He said: I believe, so that I may understand. He did not stop believing when he had questions; he took his questions into prayer.
Let us ask for that grace today: to let the light of Christ fill both our hearts and our minds, and to be ready, like Barnabas and Saul, to go where the Spirit sends us. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, when the leaders at Antioch were praying, the Holy Spirit chose Barnabas and Saul to go and tell the whole world about Jesus.
When we pray, God can tell us what he wants us to do too. Jesus is the light of the world. Let us say: Jesus, shine in my heart!

homily: Dear friends, in today's first reading there is one small, sad sentence: John, however, left them and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13). John Mark turned back from the mission. Perhaps he was afraid. Perhaps he was homesick. We do not know.

But we know the end of the story. Years later, Paul, who had been angry with him, wrote: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful in my ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). And the Church remembers him as St Mark, the writer of a Gospel. God does not throw away those who fail. If you have turned back from something, he is calling you again.

Then Paul preaches in the synagogue. He begins with respect: you Israelites, and others who fear God, listen. He tells the story of God's faithfulness: Egypt, the desert, the land, the judges, King David. And from David's family, God has brought a Savior, Jesus, as he promised. Our God keeps his promises.
Paul remembers John the Baptist, who said: I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet (Acts 13:25). The greatest prophet knew he was a servant.

In the Gospel Jesus has just washed the feet of his disciples. He says: servants are not greater than their master (John 13:16). If the Lord kneels, we must kneel too. And he gives his messengers a great dignity: whoever receives one whom I send receives me.
Let us ask today for humble hearts, ready to serve, and for the grace never to give up on anyone, not even on ourselves. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, John Mark got scared and went home in the middle of a journey with Paul. But later he came back, and he even wrote one of the four Gospels!
If we make a mistake, Jesus gives us another chance. Let us say: Jesus, help me to try again!

homily: Dear friends, Paul preaches to his own people in the synagogue. He calls them brothers, children of Abraham. He tells them what happened to Jesus: though no cause for death was found, he was condemned, taken down from the tree, laid in a tomb. And then the words that are the heart of our faith: but God raised him from the dead (Acts 13:30).

The Resurrection is God's answer to every injustice. When the world says the last word is death, God says: life. And there are witnesses. The apostles saw him, ate with him, and gave their lives for this truth.

In the Gospel Jesus sees his friends afraid. He says: do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me (John 14:1). He promises a place in his Father's house, with many dwelling places. There is room for you there.
Thomas asks: Lord, how can we know the way? And Jesus answers: I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). The way to the Father is not a set of directions; it is a person to follow.

Today we remember two martyrs. St George, a soldier, refused to deny Christ and was killed in Palestine. Here in Kerala we love him as Geevarghese Sahada. St Adalbert, a bishop, went to preach Christ to a pagan people and was killed in 997. For them, Jesus was the way, even when the way led through death.

We may not be asked to die for Christ. But we are asked every day to choose his way, his truth, his life. Let us ask St George and St Adalbert for courage. Do not let your hearts be troubled. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus said: in my Father's house there are many rooms, and I am getting one ready for you!
St George was a brave soldier who loved Jesus more than anything. Let us say: Jesus, make me brave like St George!

homily: Dear friends, in Antioch of Pisidia almost the whole city comes to hear the word of the Lord. But some are jealous and oppose Paul. And Paul says: it was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you. God never forgets his promise to Israel. Then he turns to the Gentiles, saying: I have set you to be a light for the Gentiles (Acts 13:47).

The apostles are driven out of the city. What do they do? They shake off the dust and go on. And Luke says: the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit (Acts 13:52). Driven out, but full of joy!
That is Easter joy. It does not depend on success, on applause, on things going our way. It comes from the risen Lord living in us. Let us not lose our joy when things go wrong.

In the Gospel Philip says: Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied. And Jesus says: have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9). If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus: his mercy, his patience, his wounds.

Today we remember St Fidelis, a lawyer who helped the poor without payment and then became a Capuchin friar. His name means faithful. He went to preach in Switzerland in a time of great conflict, and he was killed in 1622, forgiving those who attacked him. He was faithful until death.
Let us ask for that faithfulness, and for the joy that no one can take away. And let us look at Jesus, to see the Father. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, Philip wanted to see God the Father. Jesus said: if you look at me, you see the Father!
When we look at Jesus, so kind and loving, we see what God is like. Let us say: Jesus, show me the Father!

homily: Dear friends, at Lystra a man crippled from birth listens to Paul, and Paul sees that he has faith to be healed. Stand upright on your feet! The man springs up and walks (Acts 14:10). And the crowd goes wild: the gods have come down to us in human form! They bring oxen and garlands to worship Paul and Barnabas.

This was a great temptation. Who would not enjoy being treated as a god? But the apostles tear their clothes and run into the crowd: we are mortals just like you (Acts 14:15). They point away from themselves to the living God, who sends rain from heaven and fruitful seasons and fills hearts with joy. The best witness is a finger that points beyond itself.

In the Gospel Jesus tells us what the true God really does. Not a short visit to be honoured with sacrifices, but a dwelling: those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them (John 14:23). The Father and the Son make their home in an ordinary heart that loves and obeys.

And we are not left alone to remember everything. The Holy Spirit, the Advocate, will teach you everything and remind you of all that I have said (John 14:26). In these days of Easter, as Pentecost comes near, let us give every glory back to God, and keep a quiet room in our hearts for the Guest who has come to stay. Amen.
kids: Children, Paul healed a man who had never walked, and the people thought Paul was a god! But Paul said: no, I am just a person like you. Thank God! Jesus says something wonderful: if you love me, my Father and I will come and live in your heart. So your heart can be God's little house. Keep it clean and happy for him!

homily: Dear friends, yesterday the crowd at Lystra wanted to worship Paul as a god. Today, stirred up by others, the same crowd stones him and drags him out of the city, thinking he is dead. Crowds change quickly. Praise and stones can come from the same hands within a few days.

But listen to what happens next: when the disciples surrounded him, he got up and went into the city (Acts 14:20). Not out of the city, into it. And soon Paul and Barnabas go back through every town where they had suffered, to strengthen the new believers: it is through many persecutions that we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). They do not promise an easy road. They promise that the road leads to the kingdom.

Where did Paul find such strength? In the gift Jesus left on the night before he died: peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives (John 14:27). The world's peace means no trouble. Christ's peace means his presence in the middle of the trouble. That is why Paul could rise from the stones.

Each of us has been hit by stones of some kind: criticism, illness, failure, betrayal. The risen Lord does not always stop the stones. He gives us his peace and says, as he said at the Supper: rise, let us be on our way (John 14:31). Let us receive his peace today, and carry it to someone whose heart is troubled. Amen.
kids: Children, some people threw stones at Paul and he fell down. Everyone thought he was dead! But his friends stood around him, and Paul got up and kept telling people about Jesus. Jesus gives us a special present called peace. It is like a calm, warm feeling inside that Jesus is with you, even when something is hard. Tonight, before you sleep, say: Jesus, give me your peace.

homily: Dear friends, the young Church had hardly begun when it faced a serious question. Some believers came to Antioch and taught: unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved (Acts 15:1). Paul and Barnabas disagreed strongly. Luke says honestly: there was no small dissension and debate.

What did they do? Nobody started a new church. They went up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders, and on the way they told of the Gentiles' conversion and brought great joy to all the believers. In Jerusalem the apostles and the elders met together to consider this matter (Acts 15:6). When Christians disagree, the way of the Church is not to split, but to gather with the successors of the apostles and listen to the Holy Spirit.

Jesus tells us why this matters: I am the vine, you are the branches. Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). Branches are united because each one draws life from the same vine. And the vinegrower prunes every fruitful branch to make it bear more. Pruning hurts. It looks like loss. But it is the Father's care.

St Peter Chanel worked for years on a Pacific island with little fruit and was killed there; soon the whole island believed. St Louis de Montfort was rejected again and again, and his writing on giving oneself to Jesus through Mary bore fruit long after his death. Let us stay on the vine, accept the pruning, and trust the Father with the fruit. Amen.
kids: Children, have you seen a grape vine or a pepper vine climbing a tree? The leaves and fruit grow only on branches that stay joined to the plant. Jesus says: I am the vine, you are the branches. When we pray, go to Mass and love one another, we stay joined to Jesus. St Peter Chanel went to a faraway island to tell people about Jesus. He was killed there, but later everyone on the island came to love Jesus. His love bore fruit!

homily: Dear friends, after a long debate in Jerusalem, Peter stands up. He has seen the Holy Spirit fall on the Gentiles in the house of Cornelius. God made no distinction between them and us, he says, cleansing their hearts by faith. And then: we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will (Acts 15:9–11). James confirms it, and the Church opens its doors wide.

Grace means gift. We do not earn God's love by a list of achievements, customs or good works. We receive it, and then our good works flow from it like fruit. The first Christians had to learn this together, and we have to learn it again every day.

Jesus tells us where that grace comes from: as the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love (John 15:9). The love between the Father and the Son is offered to us. His commandments are not a heavy yoke; they are the walls of the house in which we abide in his love. And the purpose is joy: so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete (John 15:11).

St Catherine of Siena lived in that love. A dyer's daughter with little schooling, she prayed for hours, nursed plague victims, made peace between enemies, and spoke the truth even to the Pope, out of love for the Church. She told her friends (in substance) that if they were what they ought to be, they would set Italy on fire. Let us ask her to pray that we may abide in Christ's love, and let that fire spread. Amen.
kids: Children, St Catherine had more than twenty brothers and sisters! When she was small she loved to pray and to tell Jesus everything. When she grew up she looked after sick people when no one else would, and she even wrote letters to the Pope. Jesus says: I love you as my Father loves me; stay in my love. When we stay close to Jesus, we are full of joy, like Catherine!

homily: Dear friends, the Church in Jerusalem has made its decision, and now it writes a letter. Listen to its humble, joyful tone. It calls Paul and Barnabas our beloved. And it says: it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose on you no further burden than these essentials (Acts 15:28).

The Holy Spirit and us. The apostles do not say: we decided by ourselves. Nor: each of you decide for yourself. The Spirit speaks through the Church gathered with its shepherds. And when the letter is read in Antioch, they rejoiced at the exhortation (Acts 15:31). True teaching, given with love, does not crush; it lifts the heart and brings joy.

In the Gospel Jesus says what lies at the heart of every teaching: this is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you (John 15:12). He calls us friends, not servants. And he reminds us: you did not choose me but I chose you, and I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last (John 15:16). Before we ever looked for him, he had chosen us.

St Pius V, a shepherd boy who became Pope, spent his life handing on the essentials of the faith: the Catechism, the Breviary, the Missal. Yet he kept the humility of a friar and served the sick with his own hands. Teaching and love go together. Tomorrow begins the month of Mary; let us ask her, and St Pius V who loved her Rosary, to help us live as chosen friends of Jesus. Amen.
kids: Children, do you have a best friend? Jesus says: you are my friends! He chose you, even before you knew him. And he asks his friends to do one thing: love one another as I love you. St Pius V was a shepherd boy who became the Pope, but he still visited sick people and helped the poor. Tomorrow begins May, Mother Mary's month. Let us say a Hail Mary together every day!

intro: Theme: “My Lord and my God!”
Peace through the wounds, the Spirit who forgives, the doubter who confesses, and mercy that makes one heart and soul.

sub: Hands and side, the proof of love.
q: But he was wounded for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the punishment that made us whole, and by his bruises we are healed.
After he said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
points.apply: Bring one fear or old hurt to the Lord in prayer this week and say to him: “Show me your wounds, and give me your peace.”

sub: The breath of the new creation.
Sent as the Father sent him.
q: A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you; and I will remove from your body the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.
If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.
points.apply: Make a good confession this Easter season, and thank the priest who gives you absolution.

sub: The Lord comes back for one man.
Blessed are those who have not seen.
q: You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God, I will extol you.
Jesus said to him, “Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have come to believe.”
points.apply: At every Mass this week, at the elevation, say silently with Thomas: “My Lord and my God.”

q: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases, his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common.
points.apply: Choose one work of mercy, corporal or spiritual, and do it this week for someone who cannot repay you.

concl: The Risen Lord comes through our locked doors, shows us his wounds and gives us peace and forgiveness.
He leads the doubter to faith and makes his people one in mercy.
2027-04-04.resolve: Pray every afternoon at three this week: “Jesus, I trust in you.”

intro: Theme: “Touch me and see; you are witnesses of these things.”
The Author of life raised, repentance offered, our Advocate with the Father, and the risen body that sends us out.

sub: The God of Abraham glorifies his servant.
q: The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone.
and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses.
points.apply: Spend five minutes before a crucifix this week and let the Lord show you how your sins are part of the story he has forgiven.

q: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, says the Lord GOD, and not rather that they should turn from their ways and live?
Repent therefore, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out,
points.apply: Name one habit you need to turn from, and take one concrete step away from it this week.

sub: So that you may not sin.
The atoning sacrifice for the whole world.
q: There are many who say, “O that we might see some good! Let the light of your face shine on us, O LORD!”
My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous;
points.apply: Go to confession before Good Shepherd Sunday, and thank Jesus for standing beside you before the Father.

q: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and that at the last he will stand upon the earth; and after my skin has been thus destroyed, then in my flesh I shall see God,
You are witnesses of these things.
points.apply: Honour the bodily Resurrection this week: visit someone who is sick, care for your own body, and share a meal with someone alone.

concl: God raised the Author of life and offers forgiveness to all who turn to him.
Jesus is our Advocate and our sacrifice; he rose in his real body, opens the Scriptures and sends us as witnesses.
2027-04-11.resolve: Each day this week, read one Old Testament passage that points to Christ and ask him to open your mind.

intro: Theme: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
The one saving name, the children of God, the Shepherd who lays down his life and takes it up again, and shepherds after his own heart.

q: The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvelous in our eyes.
There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved.
points.apply: Speak the name of Jesus to one person this week, simply and with joy, as the reason for your hope.

sub: We will see him as he is.
q: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.
See what love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God; and that is what we are. The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
points.apply: Begin each day this week by saying: Father, I am your child; let me live as your child today.

sub: I lay it down and take it up again.
q: For thus says the Lord GOD: I myself will search for my sheep, and will seek them out.
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
points.apply: Lay down a little of your life for someone in your care this week: your time, your comfort, your own way.

sub: Pray the Lord of the harvest.
q: I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.
Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
points.apply: Pray as a family every day this week for vocations, and encourage one young person who may be called.

concl: Jesus, the rejected stone and the one saving name, is the Good Shepherd who laid down his life and took it up again.
He makes us children of God, leads us to see him as he is, and still calls shepherds after his own heart.
2027-04-18.resolve: Pray daily this week for vocations from your parish and thank your priest in person.

intro: Theme: “I am the vine, you are the branches.”
Barnabas who welcomed Saul, love in truth and action, abiding in Christ, and the Father's pruning.

sub: The Church at peace and growing.
q: You shall also love the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.
But Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and described for them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him, and how in Damascus he had spoken boldly in the name of Jesus.
points.apply: This week, stand beside one person whom others distrust or avoid.

q: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
Little children, let us love, not in word or speech, but in truth and action.
points.apply: Turn one good intention you have been talking about into a deed before next Sunday.

sub: The vine of Israel and the true vine.
The life of the branch is the life of the vine.
q: Let me sing for my beloved my love-song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill.
I am the vine, you are the branches. Those who abide in me and I in them bear much fruit, because apart from me you can do nothing.
points.apply: Choose a daily way of abiding: a visit to the Blessed Sacrament, the Rosary or ten minutes with the Gospel, and keep it all week.

sub: Glory to the Father in much fruit.
q: You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.
He removes every branch in me that bears no fruit. Every branch that bears fruit he prunes to make it bear more fruit.
points.apply: Offer to the Father one painful situation in your life, asking him to make it fruitful.

concl: Christ is the true vine; joined to him by faith, the word and the Eucharist, we live with his life.
The fruit of abiding in him is love in truth and action, like the welcome Barnabas gave to Paul.
2027-04-25.resolve: Abide with Jesus every day this week, and let one act of love be its fruit.

intro: Theme: “You are witnesses of these things.”
Not by our own power, the Risen Lord who can be touched, and the mission of forgiveness to all nations.

sub: The man who will not let go.
Peter turns the glory to God.
Forgiven sinners call others to repent.
q: and by your offspring shall all the nations of the earth gain blessing for themselves, because you have obeyed my voice.
Repent therefore, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out,
points.apply: Each time you are praised today, say inwardly: “Glory to you, Lord Jesus,” and mean it.

q: what are human beings that you are mindful of them, mortals that you care for them?
Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.
points.apply: Before Communion this week, look at the crucifix and say: “It is you, Lord, truly risen, truly here.”

sub: Repentance and forgiveness for every nation.
Beginning from Jerusalem, beginning from home.
q: The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own people; you shall heed such a prophet.
You are witnesses of these things.
points.apply: Share with one person this week, simply and gladly, why you believe that Jesus is risen.

concl: The power that heals belongs to the Risen Lord, who forgives even those who rejected him.
He is truly risen in his body, and he sends us as witnesses of repentance and forgiveness.
2027-04-01.resolve: Say each morning of this Octave: “Lord, make me a witness of your Resurrection today.”

intro: Theme: “It is the Lord!”
The name above every name, love that recognizes the Lord, and the breakfast he prepares on the shore.

sub: Prisoners, yet the word is not bound.
q: The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone.
There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among mortals by which we must be saved.
points.apply: Begin and end your work today with the sign of the cross, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

sub: “Children, you have no fish, have you?”
q: I am now sending for many fishermen, says the Lord, and they shall catch them;
That disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!”
points.apply: Look back on today before sleeping and name one moment when the Lord was with you without your noticing.

sub: A full net that does not tear.
q: On this mountain the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wines, of rich food filled with marrow, of well-aged wines strained clear.
Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and did the same with the fish.
points.apply: Come to Mass this Sunday a little early, and spend those minutes thanking the Lord for the meal he prepares.

concl: Jesus is the one Saviour, and his name gives courage to the weakest disciple.
He meets us after our empty nights, fills our nets and feeds us from his own hands.
2027-04-02.resolve: Whenever something good happens this week, say in your heart: “It is the Lord!”

intro: Theme: “We cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
Companions of Jesus, obedience to God, and slow disciples sent to the whole creation.

sub: The healed man standing beside them.
A sign no one can deny.
q: The Lord is my strength and my might; he has become my salvation.
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John and realized that they were uneducated and ordinary men, they were amazed and recognized them as companions of Jesus.
points.apply: Give the Lord a fixed quarter of an hour each day this week, so that your words may come from time spent with him.

sub: Obeying God rather than human beings.
q: If I say, “I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name,” then within me there is something like a burning fire shut up in my bones; I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.
for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.
points.apply: If you are pressed this week to stay silent about what is right, answer kindly and truthfully, and pray for the one who pressed you.

points.h: Slow to believe, sent to all
q: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace, who brings good news,
And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.”
points.apply: Make a good confession before Divine Mercy Sunday, and then tell one person what the Lord's mercy means to you.

concl: The Apostles were bold because they had been with Jesus, and they would not deny what they had seen.
The Risen Lord sends forgiven and once-doubting disciples into all the world.
2027-04-03.resolve: Pray daily this week: “Lord, let me be with you, and send me.”

intro: Theme: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
God is with us, the Son's yes, Mary's yes, and the Word made flesh, celebrated in the light of Easter.

q: Look, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall name him Immanuel.
“Look, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall name him Emmanuel,” which means, “God is with us.”
points.apply: Where fear has made you refuse God's help, ask him today for the sign you need, and accept the one he gives.

points.h: A body you have prepared for me
sub: The Son's yes to the Father.
q: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart.
And it is by God's will that we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
points.apply: Offer your body to God each morning this week: your work, your tiredness, your hands, for him.

q: And Samuel said, “Speak, for your servant is listening.”
Then Mary said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.”
points.apply: Each day this week begin your prayer with Samuel's words, then listen in silence for two minutes.

sub: From Nazareth to the empty tomb.
q: O come, let us worship and bow down, let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!
And the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory as of a father's only son, full of grace and truth.
points.apply: At every Sunday Creed, bow deeply at “and became man,” and remember that God became small for you.

concl: God kept his promise to give a sign: the Virgin conceived, and God is with us.
The Son who took flesh from Mary offered it on the cross and raised it at Easter; let us say yes with her.
2027-04-05.resolve: Pray the Regina Caeli every noon until Pentecost, and the Angelus every noon after it.

intro: Theme: “So must the Son of Man be lifted up.”
One heart and soul, born of the Spirit, and the cross that heals.

q: How very good and pleasant it is when kindred live together in unity!
Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common.
points.apply: Choose one possession you could share this week, a vehicle, a room, a skill, and offer it to someone in the parish.

q: A new heart I will give you, and a new spirit I will put within you; and I will remove from your body the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.
The wind blows where it chooses, and you hear the sound of it, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.
points.apply: Thank God today for your baptism, and if you know the date, mark it on the calendar to celebrate each year.

q: So Moses made a serpent of bronze, and put it upon a pole; and whenever a serpent bit someone, that person would look at the serpent of bronze and live.
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.
points.apply: At the elevation at your next Mass, look up at the Host and say silently: my Lord and my God, heal me.

concl: The Resurrection makes a community that shares, so that no one is in need.
The Spirit gives new birth, and the Son lifted up on the cross heals all who look to him.
2027-04-06.resolve: Be a Barnabas to one discouraged person each day this week.

intro: Theme: “God did not send the Son into the world to condemn the world.”
Prison doors opened, the love that saves, and a saint who touched hearts in the classroom.

sub: Back to the Temple at daybreak.
q: The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out, and said, “Go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life.”
points.apply: Ask the Lord to open one door of fear in you, and then go and speak of him where you were afraid to.

points.h: Not to condemn but to save
sub: Judgment is our choice of darkness.
q: For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light.
But those who do what is true come to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that their deeds have been done in God.
points.apply: Make a good confession before the Third Sunday of Easter, and bring into the light what you have kept hidden.

sub: Schools for the poor, without fees.
q: Train children in the right way, and when old, they will not stray.
But when Jesus saw this, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the little children come to me; do not stop them; for it is to such as these that the kingdom of God belongs.”
points.apply: Spend time this week teaching a child something of the faith: a prayer, a Bible story, the sign of the cross done well.

concl: The risen Lord opens prisons and sends his witnesses back to speak.
God sent his Son to save, and St John Baptist de la Salle spent his life bringing children into that light.
2027-04-07.resolve: Pray each day this week for one teacher who formed you.

intro: Theme: “We must obey God rather than any human authority.”
Courage before the council, witnesses with the Spirit, and the Son who gives the Spirit without measure.

q: If I say, “I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name,” then within me there is something like a burning fire shut up in my bones; I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot.
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than any human authority.”
points.apply: Form your conscience this week: read one page of the Catechism on a moral question you face at work or at home.

sub: Two witnesses: the apostles and the Spirit.
q: You are my witnesses, says the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen, so that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.
And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit whom God has given to those who obey him.
points.apply: Tell one person this week, simply and without arguing, what the risen Jesus has done for you.

sub: Setting a seal to God's truth.
q: The spirit of the LORD shall rest on him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.
The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands.
points.apply: Put one worry into the hands of the risen Lord each night this week, naming it aloud in prayer.

concl: The Resurrection made the apostles bold and fearless before the council.
The Son who has all things in his hands gives the Spirit without measure to make us witnesses.
2027-04-08.resolve: Pray the Come, Holy Spirit every morning until Pentecost.

intro: Theme: “He distributed them to those who were seated, as much as they wanted.”
Gamaliel's counsel, the joy of suffering for the name, and the sign of the loaves.

sub: A respected teacher of the Law.
q: The human mind may devise many plans, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will be established.
So in the present case, I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone; because if this plan or this undertaking is of human origin, it will fail;
points.apply: Before judging a new movement or person in the Church, pray for a week and ask: could this be of God?

points.h: Worthy to suffer for the name
sub: Every day, in the Temple and at home.
q: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
As they left the council, they rejoiced that they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name.
points.apply: When you are mocked for your faith this week, answer with a smile and a silent prayer for the one who mocks.

q: So he repeated, “Give it to the people and let them eat, for thus says the LORD, ‘They shall eat and have some left.’”
When they were satisfied, he told his disciples, “Gather up the fragments left over, so that nothing may be lost.”
points.apply: Receive Communion this Sunday with special reverence, and at home waste no food for one whole week.

concl: What is of God cannot be overthrown, and those who suffer for Jesus' name rejoice.
Jesus takes our little gifts, gives thanks and feeds the multitude, and gives himself as the Bread of Life.
2027-04-09.resolve: Offer Jesus one “five loaves” gift each day this week.

intro: Theme: “It is I; do not be afraid.”
The forgotten widows, the seven servants, and the Lord who walks on the dark sea.

sub: Care for the neglected entrusted to their own.
q: who executes justice for the orphan and the widow, and who loves the strangers, providing them food and clothing.
Therefore, friends, select from among yourselves seven men of good standing, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint to this task,
points.apply: Find out this week whether any widow or elderly person in your area lacks food, medicine or company, and do something about it.

q: For the word of the LORD is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness.
